NURSING.definition: How closely a patient follows the treatment plan agreed with their care team, such as taking medicines as directed.
NURSING.example: Poor adherence to his inhaler routine was the likely reason for the repeated admissions this winter.

NURSING.definition: Damage to skin and deeper tissue caused by prolonged pressure, usually over a bony area such as the heel or sacrum.
NURSING.example: A category 2 pressure ulcer was found on her sacrum during the evening skin check.

NURSING.definition: Removal of dead or infected tissue from a wound so that healthy tissue can heal.
NURSING.example: The tissue viability nurse recommended sharp debridement before starting the new dressing regime.

NURSING.definition: Fluid that leaks out of a wound; its amount, colour and smell help nurses judge healing or infection.
NURSING.example: The leg wound produced heavy green exudate, so a swab was sent and the dressing changed daily.

NURSING.definition: New, red, slightly bumpy tissue that fills a healing wound from the base upwards.
NURSING.example: Healthy granulation tissue now covers most of the wound bed, which suggests it is healing well.

NURSING.definition: The splitting open of a surgical wound along its line of closure.
NURSING.example: On day five the abdominal wound showed partial dehiscence, and the surgical team was asked to review.

NURSING.definition: Softening and whitening of skin that has been wet for too long, often around a wound edge.
NURSING.example: Maceration around the ulcer margin showed the dressing was not absorbing enough fluid.

NURSING.definition: A bacterial infection of the deeper skin layers, causing redness, heat, swelling and pain.
NURSING.example: The area of cellulitis on his shin was marked with a pen to track any spread.

NURSING.definition: A condition or factor that makes a particular treatment or procedure unsafe or unsuitable for a patient.
NURSING.example: Her recent stomach bleed is a contraindication to the anti-inflammatory painkiller on the chart.

NURSING.definition: The use of many medicines at once, which raises the risk of side effects and interactions.
NURSING.example: Polypharmacy was flagged at the falls clinic, as Mrs Ahmed takes eleven different medicines daily.

NURSING.definition: Giving medicine hidden in food or drink to a patient who lacks capacity, only after a formal best-interests process.
NURSING.example: Covert administration was agreed by the team and pharmacist and recorded in his care plan.

NURSING.definition: To adjust the amount of a medicine or fluid gradually until the desired effect is reached.
NURSING.example: Nurses were asked to titrate the oxygen to keep his saturations within the target range.

NURSING.definition: A fall in blood pressure on standing up, which can cause dizziness and lead to falls.
NURSING.example: Lying and standing readings confirmed postural hypotension, so she was advised to stand up slowly.

NURSING.definition: A structured check of the factors that make a patient likely to fall, used to plan prevention.
NURSING.example: A falls risk assessment was completed within six hours of admission and a low bed was provided.

NURSING.definition: Being unable to empty the bladder fully or at all.
NURSING.example: A bladder scan showed urinary retention of over 800 millilitres, so the doctor was informed.

NURSING.definition: A hard mass of stool stuck in the bowel that the person cannot pass naturally.
NURSING.example: Faecal impaction was suspected because he had overflow leakage and no bowel movement for eight days.

NURSING.definition: A bladder or kidney infection linked to having a urinary catheter in place.
NURSING.example: To reduce catheter-associated urinary tract infection, the ward reviews every catheter's need daily.

NURSING.definition: A way of working that prevents germs reaching a wound, line or sterile site during a procedure.
NURSING.example: The student nurse used aseptic technique when redressing the central line site.

NURSING.definition: Items such as gloves, aprons, masks and eye protection worn to protect staff and patients from infection.
NURSING.example: Staff must put on personal protective equipment before entering the side room.

NURSING.definition: Extra infection control measures, such as a single room, used when a patient carries an infectious organism.
NURSING.example: Isolation precautions were started after his stool sample tested positive for an infectious organism.

NURSING.definition: When bacteria live on or in the body without causing illness or symptoms.
NURSING.example: The screening swab showed colonisation with resistant bacteria, although she had no signs of infection.

NURSING.definition: The spread of infection from one person, surface or piece of equipment to another.
NURSING.example: Cleaning the commode between patients is essential to prevent cross-infection on the bay.

NURSING.definition: A total calculated from routine observations that shows how unwell a patient is and when to get help.
NURSING.example: His early warning score rose from 2 to 6 overnight, triggering an urgent medical review.

NURSING.definition: To pass a concern to a more senior or specialist colleague so they can act.
NURSING.example: The nurse escalated the falling blood pressure to the registrar straight away.

NURSING.definition: A worsening in a patient's physical or mental condition.
NURSING.example: Early signs of deterioration included new confusion and a rising breathing rate.

NURSING.definition: A life-threatening reaction in which the body's response to infection starts damaging its own organs.
NURSING.example: Sepsis was suspected because she was feverish, confused and had passed no urine since morning.

NURSING.definition: The difference between all fluid taken in and all fluid lost over a set period.
NURSING.example: His fluid balance chart showed a deficit of one litre over twenty-four hours.

NURSING.definition: A state in which the body lacks the energy, protein or nutrients it needs to stay healthy.
NURSING.example: Screening identified a high risk of malnutrition, and a referral to the dietitian was made.

NURSING.definition: Difficulty swallowing food, drink or saliva safely.
NURSING.example: Following her stroke, dysphagia meant she needed thickened fluids until the speech therapist reassessed her.

NURSING.definition: Food, drink or stomach contents passing into the airway or lungs instead of the stomach.
NURSING.example: He coughed during every drink, so the team was concerned about aspiration.

NURSING.definition: Giving liquid nutrition directly into the stomach or gut through a tube.
NURSING.example: Enteral feeding through a nasogastric tube started after her swallow assessment.

NURSING.definition: A sudden, often fluctuating state of confusion and poor attention, usually triggered by illness, drugs or surgery.
NURSING.example: His daughter said he was never this muddled at home, so delirium was screened for.

NURSING.definition: The ability to understand, retain and weigh information to make a particular decision and communicate it.
NURSING.example: Her mental capacity to refuse the dressing change was assessed and documented.

NURSING.definition: A decision made for a person who lacks capacity, based on their wishes, values and welfare.
NURSING.example: A best interests decision about moving to a care home was held with his family and social worker.

NURSING.definition: Protecting children and adults at risk from abuse, neglect or harm, and acting on concerns.
NURSING.example: Unexplained bruising on the toddler's arms was reported to the safeguarding lead.

NURSING.definition: Calm verbal and non-verbal techniques used to reduce a person's distress or aggression safely.
NURSING.example: De-escalation, including a quiet room and a low voice, settled the agitated patient without restraint.

NURSING.definition: Deliberately hurting oneself, for example by cutting or overdosing, often as a way of coping with distress.
NURSING.example: The young woman had a history of self-harm, so a mental health liaison referral was made.

NURSING.definition: Skills, such as sitting, walking or speaking, that most children gain by a certain age.
NURSING.example: At the two-year check, the health visitor noted that he had met all his developmental milestones.

NURSING.definition: A fit in a young child caused by a rapid rise in body temperature, usually harmless.
NURSING.example: The parents were frightened after their daughter's first febrile convulsion, so the nurse explained what to do next time.

NURSING.definition: A common viral chest infection in babies that inflames the small airways and makes feeding and breathing harder.
NURSING.example: The baby with bronchiolitis was taking less than half her usual feeds and needed admission.

NURSING.definition: Care focused on comfort and quality of life for people with illness that cannot be cured.
NURSING.example: The community palliative care team visited to help manage his pain and breathlessness at home.

NURSING.definition: Medicines prescribed in advance and kept at home so symptoms near the end of life can be treated quickly.
NURSING.example: Anticipatory medicines were delivered to the house in case she became distressed overnight.

NURSING.definition: A record of a person's wishes and priorities about their future care, made while they can still decide.
NURSING.example: His advance care plan stated that he wished to die at home rather than in hospital.

NURSING.definition: A small battery pump that delivers medicine slowly under the skin over many hours.
NURSING.example: A syringe driver was set up when she could no longer swallow her tablets.

NURSING.definition: A flare of pain that occurs despite regular pain relief already being given.
NURSING.example: He needed three doses for breakthrough pain yesterday, so his regular pain relief was reviewed.

NURSING.definition: The structured passing of information and responsibility for patients from one shift or team to the next.
NURSING.example: At handover, the night nurse highlighted the patient whose blood sugar had been unstable.

NURSING.definition: A group of professionals from different specialties who plan and deliver a patient's care together.
NURSING.example: The multidisciplinary team agreed she was ready to go home with daily carers.

NURSING.definition: Preparing, from admission onwards, everything a patient needs to leave hospital safely.
NURSING.example: Discharge planning began on day one because he lived alone on the third floor.

NURSING.definition: An arranged set of support services, such as carer visits, provided to someone at home.
NURSING.example: Her discharge was delayed while a package of care with four visits a day was organised.

NURSING.definition: A blood clot that forms in a vein, usually in the leg, and may travel to the lungs.
NURSING.example: Every surgical patient is assessed for venous thromboembolism risk and given stockings if suitable.

NURSING.definition: Checks of colour, warmth, movement, sensation and pulses in a limb to detect impaired blood flow or nerve damage.
NURSING.example: Hourly neurovascular observations were recorded on his casted arm overnight.

NURSING.definition: Involuntary leakage of urine or faeces.
NURSING.example: Her incontinence started after the new water tablet, so the timing of the dose was reviewed.

NURSING.definition: Cleaning hands with soap and water or alcohol rub at key moments to stop the spread of germs.
NURSING.example: The monthly audit showed hand hygiene compliance had fallen to 82 percent on the ward.

NURSING.definition: An action taken to improve a patient's condition or prevent harm.
NURSING.example: The main nursing intervention was two-hourly repositioning to protect his skin.

NURSING.definition: Complete and including all the relevant parts or details.
NURSING.example: A comprehensive geriatric assessment was completed before decisions were made about her future care.

NURSING.definition: Continuing for longer than expected or keeping on happening.
NURSING.example: Persistent low mood after the birth led the midwife to refer her to the perinatal team.

NURSING.definition: Coming after something else in time.
NURSING.example: Her first wound swab was clear, but a subsequent sample grew bacteria.

NURSING.definition: An agreed written set of steps for handling a particular clinical situation.
NURSING.example: The hypoglycaemia protocol was followed and his blood sugar rechecked after fifteen minutes.

NURSING.definition: The number of new cases of a condition or event occurring in a group over a set time.
NURSING.example: The ward's incidence of falls halved after bed alarms and regular checks were introduced.

NURSING.definition: Agreement between patient and professional on a treatment plan reached through shared discussion.
NURSING.example: Concordance improved once the nurse and patient agreed a medicine routine that fitted his working day.

NURSING.definition: Blood pressure that stays higher than the healthy range.
NURSING.example: I'd explain to Mr Lee that his hypertension means his blood pressure is too high and needs regular checks.

NURSING.definition: A blood glucose level that has dropped too low, causing shakiness, sweating or confusion.
NURSING.example: If you feel shaky or sweaty, it may be hypoglycaemia, so check your sugar and have a sugary drink.

NURSING.definition: Swelling caused by fluid collecting in the body's tissues, often in the ankles or legs.
NURSING.example: The oedema in your ankles is fluid building up, so keeping your legs raised should help.

NURSING.definition: A body temperature above the normal range.
NURSING.example: The notes say pyrexia, which simply means your son has a high temperature.

NURSING.definition: Medicine or treatment given to relieve pain.
NURSING.example: Your analgesia is due at two o'clock, but tell me if the pain gets worse before then.

NURSING.definition: To get up and move or walk about, with or without help.
NURSING.example: The physiotherapist would like you to mobilise today, so we'll walk to the window together after lunch.

NURSING.definition: An instruction that a patient must not eat or drink anything, usually before a procedure.
NURSING.example: You're nil by mouth from midnight, so please don't eat or drink anything before your operation.

NURSING.definition: Threads used to hold the edges of a wound together while it heals.
NURSING.example: The practice nurse will remove your sutures in ten days.

NURSING.definition: A collection of blood trapped under the skin or in tissue after an injury or procedure.
NURSING.example: The lump near your cannula site is a small haematoma and should fade over the next week.
NURSING.plain: a large bruise, a pool of blood under the skin

NURSING.definition: An infection anywhere in the urinary system, most often the bladder.
NURSING.example: Your urine test shows a urinary tract infection, so the doctor has prescribed a short course of antibiotics.

NURSING.definition: A thin, flexible plastic tube placed in a vein to give fluids or medicines.
NURSING.example: I'm going to put a cannula in the back of your hand so we can give you fluids.
NURSING.plain: a thin tube in your vein

NURSING.definition: Applied directly to the skin or another body surface rather than swallowed or injected.
NURSING.example: This topical cream goes straight onto the itchy patch twice a day.

NURSING.definition: The ability to control the bladder and bowels.
NURSING.example: The continence nurse will help you with exercises to improve your bladder control.

NURSING.definition: To change a patient's body position to relieve pressure or improve comfort.
NURSING.example: We'll reposition you every two hours to protect your skin from sores.

NURSING.definition: A chair with a toilet pan underneath, used beside the bed.
NURSING.example: Until you're steadier on your feet, please use the commode and call us first.
NURSING.plain: a toilet chair by the bed

NURSING.definition: The person a patient names as their closest relative or main contact.
NURSING.example: Who would you like us to record as your next of kin in case we need to contact someone?
NURSING.plain: your closest relative or main contact

NURSING.definition: Able to walk and move about without help from another person.
NURSING.example: On discharge, Mrs Okafor was independently mobile with a walking frame.

NURSING.definition: Needs help from another person to carry out a stated activity.
NURSING.example: Mr Patel requires assistance with washing and dressing but feeds himself.

NURSING.definition: A standard opening that states the purpose of a referral letter.
NURSING.example: I am writing to refer Mrs Brown, an 82-year-old widow, for continued wound care at home.
NURSING.plain: I am asking you to take over or add to this person's care

NURSING.term: I would be grateful if you could
NURSING.definition: A polite, formal way of making a request in a letter.
NURSING.example: I would be grateful if you could review her leg ulcer twice weekly and adjust the dressings as needed.

NURSING.term: please do not hesitate to contact
NURSING.definition: A formal closing line inviting the reader to get in touch with questions.
NURSING.example: Should you require further information, please do not hesitate to contact me on the ward.
NURSING.plain: feel free to get in touch

NURSING.definition: States in a letter that a patient left hospital to return home.
NURSING.example: Mr Jones was discharged home today after a five-day admission for a chest infection.

NURSING.definition: To watch something carefully for any change.
NURSING.example: Please keep an eye on the wound and call us if it becomes red, hot or smelly.

NURSING.definition: Clear guidance on which warning signs mean the patient should seek help, and how and when to do so.
NURSING.example: Before they left, I gave the parents safety-net advice about breathing difficulty and refusing feeds.
NURSING.plain: what to look out for and when to get help

NURSING.definition: Symptoms or changes that suggest a condition is getting worse and needs prompt attention.
NURSING.example: The warning signs to watch for are a high temperature, new confusion or not passing urine.

NURSING.term: how are you feeling in yourself
NURSING.definition: A gentle question about a patient's general wellbeing and mood, not just one symptom.
NURSING.example: Apart from the knee, how are you feeling in yourself this morning?

NURSING.definition: An open question inviting the patient to share concerns.
NURSING.example: Before you go home tomorrow, is there anything worrying you about managing on your own?

NURSING.term: on a scale of nought to ten
NURSING.definition: A way of asking a patient to rate pain or another symptom with a number.
NURSING.example: On a scale of nought to ten, where ten is the worst pain imaginable, how bad is it now?
NURSING.plain: give it a number from 0 to 10

NURSING.term: can you tell me in your own words
NURSING.definition: A teach-back question that checks a patient has understood information.
NURSING.example: Can you tell me in your own words when you'll take your new tablets?

NURSING.definition: Exactly in the amount and at the times the prescriber has instructed.
NURSING.example: Please keep taking the antibiotics as prescribed until the course is finished, even if you feel better.
NURSING.plain: exactly as the doctor told you

NURSING.definition: A later appointment to check progress after treatment or a hospital stay.
NURSING.example: We've booked a follow-up appointment at the clinic in two weeks to check your wound.

NURSING.definition: A special mattress that spreads or changes pressure to protect the skin.
NURSING.example: A pressure-relieving mattress has been ordered for her bed at home.
NURSING.plain: a special air mattress to protect the skin

NURSING.definition: A device that turns liquid medicine into a fine mist breathed in through a mask.
NURSING.example: The nebuliser will turn this medicine into a mist, so just breathe normally through the mask.
NURSING.plain: a machine that turns medicine into a mist you breathe in

NURSING.definition: Given directly into a vein.
NURSING.example: You'll have intravenous antibiotics for two days, then switch to tablets if you improve.
NURSING.plain: through a drip into a vein

NURSING.definition: Solid waste passed from the bowel.
NURSING.example: We need a stool sample, so please use this pot next time you open your bowels.

NURSING.definition: A condition in which the body has lost more fluid than it has taken in.
NURSING.example: Signs of dehydration in your baby include fewer wet nappies and a dry mouth.
NURSING.plain: not having enough fluid in the body

NURSING.definition: Passing stools less often than usual, or stools that are hard and difficult to pass.
NURSING.example: These painkillers can cause constipation, so drink plenty and tell us if you haven't been for three days.

NURSING.definition: A polite way of signalling that you are about to give the patient information.
NURSING.example: Before I start, I'd just like to explain what the dressing change will involve.
NURSING.plain: let me tell you what will happen

NURSING.definition: A reassuring phrase telling a patient there is no need to hurry.
NURSING.example: Take your time getting up, and hold onto the rail if you feel dizzy.

NURSING.definition: Formal wording in a letter or note stating that someone has been told something.
NURSING.example: Her daughter has been informed of the discharge date and will collect her at noon.

MEDICINE.definition: A list of possible conditions that could explain a patient's symptoms, to be confirmed or ruled out.
MEDICINE.example: The differential diagnosis for her chest pain included reflux, angina and a pulmonary embolism.

MEDICINE.definition: The cause or set of causes of a disease.
MEDICINE.example: The aetiology of his liver disease remains unclear, as he drinks little alcohol.

MEDICINE.definition: The way a disease develops in the body, from first trigger to established illness.
MEDICINE.example: The article reviews current thinking on the pathogenesis of type 1 diabetes.

MEDICINE.definition: A second or further medical condition present in a patient alongside the main one.
MEDICINE.example: Comorbidity such as kidney disease limited the treatment options for her heart failure.

MEDICINE.definition: The proportion of a population that has a condition at a particular time.
MEDICINE.example: The prevalence of diabetes in this practice population is higher than the national average.

MEDICINE.definition: How well a test correctly identifies people who do have the condition.
MEDICINE.example: Because the test has high sensitivity, a negative result makes the diagnosis very unlikely.

MEDICINE.definition: How well a test correctly identifies people who do not have the condition.
MEDICINE.example: The marker has low specificity, so a raised level can occur in many other conditions.

MEDICINE.definition: A test result showing a condition is present when it is actually absent.
MEDICINE.example: A false positive on screening can cause anxiety and unnecessary further investigations.

MEDICINE.definition: A factor that makes a treatment riskier, so benefits and risks must be weighed carefully before using it.
MEDICINE.example: Recent surgery is a relative contraindication to clot-dissolving treatment, not an absolute bar.

MEDICINE.definition: A harmful, unintended response to a medicine taken at a normal amount.
MEDICINE.example: The rash was recorded as an adverse drug reaction and the antibiotic was stopped.

MEDICINE.definition: How the body absorbs, distributes, breaks down and removes a medicine over time.
MEDICINE.example: Changes in pharmacokinetics in older adults mean many drugs stay in the body longer.

MEDICINE.definition: The margin between a medicine's effective level and the level at which it becomes toxic.
MEDICINE.example: Lithium has a narrow therapeutic index, so regular blood level monitoring is essential.

MEDICINE.definition: Gradual adjustment of a medicine's amount to reach the best effect with the fewest side effects.
MEDICINE.example: Slow titration of the beta-blocker reduced his dizziness while controlling his heart rate.

MEDICINE.definition: Planned reduction or stopping of medicines that may no longer help or may cause harm.
MEDICINE.example: A deprescribing review stopped four of her twelve medicines with no loss of symptom control.

MEDICINE.definition: An irregular, often fast heart rhythm arising in the upper chambers, which raises the risk of stroke.
MEDICINE.example: The ECG confirmed atrial fibrillation, so his stroke risk was calculated and anticoagulation discussed.

MEDICINE.definition: Death of part of the heart muscle because its blood supply has been blocked.
MEDICINE.example: Raised troponin and ECG changes confirmed an acute myocardial infarction.

MEDICINE.definition: The percentage of blood pumped out of the left ventricle with each heartbeat.
MEDICINE.example: Her echocardiogram showed a reduced ejection fraction of 30 percent.

MEDICINE.definition: Treatment with medicines that reduce the blood's ability to clot.
MEDICINE.example: Anticoagulation was paused before the biopsy to lower the risk of bleeding.

MEDICINE.definition: Describes an organ or condition that can no longer cope, so symptoms become worse and uncontrolled.
MEDICINE.example: He was admitted with decompensated heart failure, breathless at rest and with marked leg swelling.

MEDICINE.definition: Listening to sounds from the heart, lungs or bowel with a stethoscope.
MEDICINE.example: On auscultation there were crackles at the right lung base.

MEDICINE.definition: A period when a long-term condition suddenly becomes worse.
MEDICINE.example: This is her third exacerbation of COPD this year, each triggered by a viral infection.

MEDICINE.definition: A medicine that relaxes and widens the airways to make breathing easier.
MEDICINE.example: His wheeze improved within minutes of the inhaled bronchodilator.

MEDICINE.definition: A breathing test measuring how much air a person can blow out and how quickly.
MEDICINE.example: Spirometry showed an obstructive pattern that did not reverse after the inhaler.

MEDICINE.definition: A blockage in a lung artery, usually from a clot that travelled from the legs.
MEDICINE.example: A CT scan was requested to exclude a pulmonary embolism after her sudden breathlessness.

MEDICINE.definition: An area of lung filled with fluid or inflammatory material instead of air, often seen in pneumonia.
MEDICINE.example: The chest X-ray showed left lower lobe consolidation consistent with pneumonia.

MEDICINE.definition: How well a person's blood glucose is kept within the target range over time.
MEDICINE.example: His glycaemic control has worsened since he started night shifts.

MEDICINE.definition: A dangerous build-up of acids in the blood when the body lacks insulin and breaks down fat instead.
MEDICINE.example: The teenager presented with vomiting and deep breathing and was diagnosed with diabetic ketoacidosis.

MEDICINE.definition: A state caused by too much thyroid hormone, leading to weight loss, tremor and a fast pulse.
MEDICINE.example: Her palpitations, heat intolerance and weight loss pointed towards thyrotoxicosis.

MEDICINE.definition: Reduced response of the body's cells to insulin, so more is needed to control blood glucose.
MEDICINE.example: Insulin resistance often improves with weight loss and regular exercise.

MEDICINE.definition: A brief episode of stroke-like symptoms from a temporary loss of blood supply, resolving fully within a day.
MEDICINE.example: His ten minutes of slurred speech were treated as a transient ischaemic attack and he was referred urgently.

MEDICINE.definition: Loss of function in a specific area, such as one arm's weakness, pointing to a particular site of damage.
MEDICINE.example: There was no focal neurological deficit, which made a stroke less likely.

MEDICINE.definition: The level of brain stimulation above which a seizure occurs; some drugs and states lower it.
MEDICINE.example: Sleep deprivation may lower the seizure threshold, so regular sleep is advised.

MEDICINE.definition: Damage to nerves outside the brain and spinal cord, often causing numbness or tingling in the feet.
MEDICINE.example: Peripheral neuropathy from long-standing diabetes had left her unable to feel the blister on her toe.

MEDICINE.definition: The spread of cancer from where it started to another part of the body.
MEDICINE.example: The scan showed metastasis to the liver, which changed the treatment aim to control rather than cure.

MEDICINE.definition: Assessing a cancer's size and how far it has spread, to guide treatment and outlook.
MEDICINE.example: Staging scans were arranged before the oncology meeting to plan her treatment.

MEDICINE.definition: Serious infection in a person with very low white cells, often after chemotherapy; an emergency.
MEDICINE.example: Any patient on chemotherapy with a fever must be treated for neutropenic sepsis until proven otherwise.

MEDICINE.definition: Extra treatment given after the main treatment, such as surgery, to lower the chance of cancer returning.
MEDICINE.example: After the bowel resection, adjuvant therapy was offered to reduce the risk of recurrence.

MEDICINE.definition: A period when signs and symptoms of a disease reduce or disappear.
MEDICINE.example: Her lymphoma has been in remission for three years.

MEDICINE.definition: A patient's voluntary agreement to treatment after understanding its purpose, risks, benefits and alternatives.
MEDICINE.example: Informed consent for the endoscopy was obtained after discussing the small risk of perforation.

MEDICINE.definition: In UK practice, a young person under 16 who understands a treatment fully enough to consent to it themselves.
MEDICINE.example: The GP judged the fifteen-year-old to have Gillick competence to consent to contraception.

MEDICINE.definition: The duty to keep a patient's personal and health information private unless there is a lawful reason to share it.
MEDICINE.example: He asked that his diagnosis not be shared with his employer, and confidentiality was respected.

MEDICINE.definition: The professional obligation to be open and honest with patients when something has gone wrong in their care.
MEDICINE.example: Under the duty of candour, the consultant met the family to explain the medication error and apologise.

MEDICINE.definition: A study in which participants are allocated by chance to different treatments so their outcomes can be compared fairly.
MEDICINE.example: A large randomised controlled trial found the new drug reduced hospital admissions by a fifth.

MEDICINE.definition: Research that follows a group of people over time to see who develops a particular outcome.
MEDICINE.example: The cohort study tracked 20,000 nurses for ten years to examine links between shift work and heart disease.

MEDICINE.definition: Distortion of a study result by a third factor linked to both the exposure and the outcome.
MEDICINE.example: The authors adjusted for smoking to reduce confounding in the link between coffee and heart attacks.

MEDICINE.definition: An inactive treatment that looks identical to the real one, used for comparison in trials.
MEDICINE.example: Patients receiving the placebo reported almost as much pain relief as the treatment group.

MEDICINE.definition: How well a treatment works under ideal, controlled conditions such as a trial.
MEDICINE.example: The vaccine showed high efficacy in the trial, though real-world results were slightly lower.

MEDICINE.definition: The rate of death in a population or group over a set period.
MEDICINE.example: Thirty-day mortality after hip fracture fell after a dedicated orthogeriatric service was introduced.

MEDICINE.definition: Illness or poor health, or the rate of a disease in a population.
MEDICINE.example: Obesity is associated with significant morbidity, including joint disease and diabetes.

MEDICINE.definition: Having a condition but showing no symptoms of it.
MEDICINE.example: Most people with early high blood pressure are asymptomatic, which is why screening matters.

MEDICINE.definition: Describes a condition that arises without any known cause.
MEDICINE.example: After extensive tests, his lung scarring was labelled idiopathic.

MEDICINE.definition: Caused by medical treatment or the actions of a healthcare professional.
MEDICINE.example: Her low sodium was thought to be iatrogenic, related to the new water tablet.

MEDICINE.definition: Reduced kidney function, which can affect how medicines are cleared from the body.
MEDICINE.example: Due to his renal impairment, the antibiotic was given less frequently.

MEDICINE.definition: Damage to the liver caused by a medicine or other chemical.
MEDICINE.example: Liver function tests were checked monthly because of the risk of hepatotoxicity.

MEDICINE.definition: Treatment started on the most likely cause before test results confirm the diagnosis.
MEDICINE.example: Empirical treatment with broad-spectrum antibiotics began while blood cultures were pending.

MEDICINE.definition: Treatment given to prevent a disease or complication rather than to treat it.
MEDICINE.example: Clot prophylaxis was prescribed for the duration of his hospital stay.

MEDICINE.definition: The process by which something happens, such as how a drug acts or how an injury occurred.
MEDICINE.example: The mechanism of injury, a fall from a ladder, raised concern about a spinal fracture.

MEDICINE.definition: Agreed standards or features used to make a diagnosis or decision.
MEDICINE.example: She met the diagnostic criteria for rheumatoid arthritis after the antibody results returned.

MEDICINE.definition: To experience or go through a procedure, test or change.
MEDICINE.example: He will undergo a coronary angiogram later this week.

MEDICINE.definition: Existing as a natural, permanent part of something.
MEDICINE.example: Every invasive procedure carries an inherent risk of infection and bleeding.

MEDICINE.definition: Chest pain or tightness that occurs when the heart muscle is not getting enough blood.
MEDICINE.example: Angina is chest pain that happens when your heart isn't getting enough blood, often when you walk uphill.
MEDICINE.plain: chest pain from the heart not getting enough blood

MEDICINE.definition: The feeling of difficult or uncomfortable breathing.
MEDICINE.example: Your notes mention dyspnoea, which just means feeling short of breath.

MEDICINE.definition: A heart rate faster than normal for the person at rest.
MEDICINE.example: Your tachycardia means your heart is beating faster than it should, so we'd like to find out why.

MEDICINE.definition: Describes a growth that is cancerous and can invade or spread.
MEDICINE.example: I'm sorry to tell you the biopsy shows the lump is malignant, which means it is a cancer.

MEDICINE.definition: Describes a growth that is not cancerous and does not spread.
MEDICINE.example: The good news is that the lump is benign, so it isn't cancer.

MEDICINE.definition: Removal of a small piece of tissue so it can be examined under a microscope.
MEDICINE.example: We'd like to do a biopsy, which means taking a tiny sample of the skin to look at in the lab.
MEDICINE.plain: taking a small sample of tissue to test

MEDICINE.definition: Higher than recommended levels of fats, such as cholesterol, in the blood.
MEDICINE.example: Your blood test shows hyperlipidaemia, so we'll talk about diet and a cholesterol tablet.

MEDICINE.definition: Damage to the brain from a blocked or burst blood vessel.
MEDICINE.example: Your father has had a cerebrovascular accident, which means a stroke affecting the left side of his brain.

MEDICINE.definition: Stomach acid flowing back up into the food pipe, causing burning or a sour taste.
MEDICINE.example: Your symptoms suggest gastro-oesophageal reflux, so try eating smaller meals and not lying down straight afterwards.

MEDICINE.definition: Coughing up blood or blood-stained mucus from the lungs or airways.
MEDICINE.example: Any haemoptysis, even a streak of blood when you cough, should be reported to us straight away.

MEDICINE.definition: A brief loss of consciousness from a temporary drop in blood flow to the brain.
MEDICINE.example: The syncope you had in the shop means you fainted, and we need to check your heart rhythm.

MEDICINE.definition: Any abnormal area of tissue, such as a sore, lump or patch seen on skin or a scan.
MEDICINE.example: The scan shows a small lesion on your kidney, which is an area we need to look at more closely.

MEDICINE.definition: A blood glucose level higher than the healthy range.
MEDICINE.example: Thirst and passing urine often are signs of hyperglycaemia, so we'll adjust your diabetes treatment.

MEDICINE.definition: A lower than normal level of haemoglobin, so the blood carries less oxygen.
MEDICINE.example: Your tiredness may be due to anaemia, which means your blood is low in iron-carrying cells.
MEDICINE.plain: not enough healthy red blood cells

MEDICINE.definition: An ultrasound scan that shows the structure and pumping of the heart.
MEDICINE.example: We'll arrange an echocardiogram, which is an ultrasound scan of your heart, a bit like a pregnancy scan.

MEDICINE.definition: Unwanted effects of a medicine besides the intended one.
MEDICINE.example: The most common side effects of this tablet are a dry cough and feeling dizzy when you stand.

MEDICINE.definition: The likely course and outcome of a disease.
MEDICINE.example: With treatment, the prognosis for this type of infection is very good.
MEDICINE.plain: what is likely to happen in the future

MEDICINE.definition: A patient who attends hospital for an appointment or test without staying overnight.
MEDICINE.example: You'll be seen as an outpatient, so you can go home the same day.
MEDICINE.plain: a hospital visit without staying overnight

MEDICINE.definition: The treatment usually tried first for a condition, before other options are considered.
MEDICINE.example: Metformin is the first-line treatment, so it's the tablet we usually start with for type 2 diabetes.
MEDICINE.plain: the usual first treatment we try

MEDICINE.definition: Monitoring a condition closely over time without starting treatment unless it changes.
MEDICINE.example: For now I'd suggest watchful waiting, with a repeat check in three months.
MEDICINE.plain: keeping a close eye on it before treating

MEDICINE.definition: A standard, courteous opening for a referral letter to a specialist.
MEDICINE.example: Thank you for seeing Mr Hassan, a 58-year-old builder with a six-week history of exertional chest pain.
MEDICINE.plain: thank you for looking after this patient

MEDICINE.definition: A formal way of asking a specialist for their assessment and advice.
MEDICINE.example: I would appreciate your opinion on whether further cardiac investigation is warranted.
MEDICINE.plain: please tell me what you think

MEDICINE.term: I would be grateful if you could
MEDICINE.definition: A polite, formal way of making a request in a letter.
MEDICINE.example: I would be grateful if you could assess her for a hip replacement at your earliest convenience.

MEDICINE.definition: Used in letters and notes to state the symptoms a patient came with.
MEDICINE.example: She presented with a three-day history of fever, cough and pleuritic chest pain.

MEDICINE.definition: Introduces the findings from the physical examination in a letter or record.
MEDICINE.example: On examination, his abdomen was soft but tender in the right lower quadrant.

MEDICINE.definition: The record of a patient's previous illnesses, operations and long-term conditions.
MEDICINE.example: Her past medical history includes asthma and a gallbladder operation in 2018.

MEDICINE.definition: Formal wording that introduces the results of tests in a letter.
MEDICINE.example: Investigations revealed a low haemoglobin and raised inflammatory markers.

MEDICINE.definition: With the aim or intention of doing something.
MEDICINE.example: I am referring him to your clinic with a view to starting biological therapy.

MEDICINE.definition: A request for a specialist to see a patient quickly because a serious condition is possible.
MEDICINE.example: I'm making an urgent referral, and the hospital will send you the appointment date in writing.
MEDICINE.plain: a fast-track appointment with a specialist

MEDICINE.definition: Telling patients which symptoms should prompt them to seek help, and when and where to go.
MEDICINE.example: Safety-netting was documented: return if the headache worsens, or you develop a stiff neck or rash.
MEDICINE.plain: telling you what to watch for and when to come back

MEDICINE.term: come back and see me if
MEDICINE.definition: A patient-friendly way of giving conditions for a return visit.
MEDICINE.example: Come back and see me if the cough lasts more than three weeks or you cough up blood.

MEDICINE.definition: An open question to check what the patient already knows before giving information.
MEDICINE.example: Before we go on, what do you understand about why you had the scan?
MEDICINE.plain: what do you already know about

MEDICINE.term: is there anything you'd like to ask
MEDICINE.definition: An invitation for the patient to raise questions, often used near the end of a consultation.
MEDICINE.example: I've given you a lot of information today, so is there anything you'd like to ask?

MEDICINE.term: I'm afraid I have some difficult news
MEDICINE.definition: A warning shot that prepares a patient before bad news is shared.
MEDICINE.example: I'm afraid I have some difficult news about your scan results; would you like your wife to stay?

MEDICINE.term: if that's all right with you
MEDICINE.definition: A polite phrase seeking the patient's agreement before an examination or action.
MEDICINE.example: I'd like to listen to your chest now, if that's all right with you.

MEDICINE.term: do you have any concerns about
MEDICINE.definition: A question inviting the patient to share specific worries about a treatment or plan.
MEDICINE.example: Do you have any concerns about starting the blood thinner?

MEDICINE.definition: The good effects and possible harms of an option, set out so the patient can decide.
MEDICINE.example: Let me go through the benefits and risks of the operation so you can decide what's right for you.
MEDICINE.plain: the good points and possible problems

MEDICINE.definition: A choice reached together by clinician and patient, using evidence and the patient's own values.
MEDICINE.example: Whether to start statins is a shared decision, so tell me what matters most to you.

MEDICINE.definition: Relating to the kidneys.
MEDICINE.example: Your renal function has dropped a little, which means your kidneys aren't filtering quite as well.

MEDICINE.definition: Formal wording in a letter stating the advice given to the patient.
MEDICINE.example: She has been advised to avoid driving until she has been free of blackouts for the required period.

OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.definition: The degree to which a person can carry out everyday tasks without help from others.
OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.example: The aim of the inpatient programme was to restore functional independence before she returned to her flat.

OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.definition: Basic self-care tasks such as washing, dressing, eating, toileting and moving around.
OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.example: His scores on activities of daily living improved steadily after the second week of therapy.

OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.definition: More complex tasks needed to live independently, such as shopping, cooking, managing money and using transport.
OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.example: Although she washes and dresses alone, she needs support with instrumental activities of daily living such as budgeting.

OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.definition: How well a person carries out the activities that fill their day, shaped by person, task and environment.
OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.example: Pain and fatigue were the main barriers to occupational performance identified at the initial interview.

OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.definition: A healthy mix of work, rest, self-care and leisure in a person's daily routine.
OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.example: Caring for his wife around the clock had left him with little occupational balance and no time for himself.

OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.definition: An approach in which the demand of a task is increased step by step as tolerance builds.
OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.example: A graded activity plan started with ten minutes of light housework and increased weekly.

OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.definition: Methods of planning and simplifying tasks so that limited physical energy lasts through the day.
OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.example: Energy conservation techniques, such as sitting to prepare vegetables, helped him manage his breathlessness.

OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.definition: Ways of doing tasks that reduce strain on painful or inflamed joints.
OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.example: The rheumatology group covered joint protection, including using two hands to lift a kettle.

OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.definition: A different way of doing a task that works around a lasting loss of ability.
OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.example: Using a written checklist became a useful compensatory strategy for his memory difficulties.

OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.definition: Items designed or changed to make a task easier or safer for someone with a disability.
OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.example: She was shown adaptive equipment, including a long-handled sponge and a sock aid.

OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.definition: A change made to a home, workplace or setting to improve safety, access or ease of use.
OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.example: Environmental modification, such as removing loose rugs, was recommended to lower the chance of further falls.

OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.definition: A visit to a patient's home before they leave hospital to check they can manage safely there.
OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.example: During the pre-discharge home visit, he was unable to step into the bath without assistance.

OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.definition: Small, precise hand and finger movements, such as writing, buttoning or using cutlery.
OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.example: The school reported that his fine motor skills were behind those of his classmates.

OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.definition: Larger whole-body movements, such as walking, jumping, balancing and climbing stairs.
OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.example: Her gross motor skills were age-appropriate, but she struggled with handwriting.

OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.definition: The way the brain receives, organises and responds to information from the senses.
OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.example: Difficulties with sensory processing may explain why he becomes distressed in the noisy dining hall.

OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.definition: Using sensory input, such as weight, sound or movement, to help regulate arousal and emotion.
OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.example: On the acute mental health ward, sensory modulation tools were offered as an alternative to restrictive practice.

OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.definition: The body's sense of where its parts are and how they are moving, without looking.
OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.example: Reduced proprioception in her left foot made walking on uneven ground difficult.

OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.definition: Which hand a person naturally prefers for skilled tasks.
OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.example: Hand dominance had not yet been established, as the four-year-old switched hands when drawing.

OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.definition: A device worn on the body to support, protect, position or correct a joint or limb.
OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.example: A resting wrist orthosis was fabricated to be worn at night following the tendon repair.

OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.definition: Permanent shortening of muscle or soft tissue that stiffens a joint and limits movement.
OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.example: Daily positioning was essential to prevent elbow contracture in the affected arm.

OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.definition: Swelling caused by excess fluid collecting in body tissues.
OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.example: Hand oedema was managed with elevation and gentle active movement after the fracture.

OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.definition: How far a joint can move in each direction.
OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.example: Range of motion at the shoulder was limited to ninety degrees, affecting her ability to reach shelves.

OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.definition: The force a person can produce when squeezing with the hand, often measured with a dynamometer.
OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.example: Grip strength in the right hand had increased since the previous review.

OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.definition: Higher thinking skills used to plan, organise, start, monitor and complete tasks.
OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.example: Impaired executive function meant he could not sequence the steps of making a hot drink.

OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.definition: Therapy aimed at improving, or finding ways around, problems with attention, memory and thinking.
OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.example: After her brain injury, cognitive rehabilitation focused on attention and daily planning.

OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.definition: Reduced awareness of one side of the body or space, usually after a stroke.
OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.example: Unilateral neglect was evident when he ate only the food on the right side of his plate.

OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.definition: Difficulty carrying out purposeful movements despite having the strength and understanding to do them.
OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.example: Because of apraxia, she held the toothbrush correctly but could not work out how to use it.

OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.definition: Repeating an action, word or thought after it is no longer appropriate.
OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.example: Perseveration was noted as he continued to wipe the same plate during the kitchen assessment.

OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.definition: Planned approaches to balancing activity and rest when tiredness limits daily life.
OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.example: The multiple sclerosis service offers a six-week fatigue management course.

OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.definition: Spreading body weight over a larger area to reduce pressure on vulnerable skin.
OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.example: A cushion offering pressure redistribution was supplied because he sits in his wheelchair most of the day.

OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.definition: Equipment or positioning that helps a person sit or lie in a stable, comfortable and safe way.
OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.example: Lateral postural support was added to the chair because she kept leaning to the left.

OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.definition: Moving between two seated surfaces by sliding across a smooth board.
OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.example: He now completes a sliding board transfer from bed to wheelchair with one person supervising.

OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.definition: How likely a person is to fall, judged from their health, medicines, mobility and surroundings.
OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.example: Her falls risk was considered high because of poor lighting, low blood pressure and rushing to the toilet.

OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.definition: Support to help a person stay in, return to or find work after illness or injury.
OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.example: He was referred for vocational rehabilitation after his back injury kept him off work for four months.

OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.definition: Going back to work gradually, with hours or duties increased over an agreed period.
OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.example: A graded return to work began with two half-days per week on light duties.

OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.definition: Designed to suit the body and reduce strain during work or daily tasks.
OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.example: An ergonomic workstation assessment led to a raised monitor and a forearm support.

OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.definition: Built around the person's own priorities, values and choices rather than the professional's agenda.
OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.example: A client-centred approach meant her wish to return to gardening shaped the whole plan.

OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.definition: Agreeing therapy aims jointly with the patient and, where relevant, their family.
OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.example: Collaborative goal setting identified cooking a simple meal as his first priority.

OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.definition: A planned action or treatment intended to improve a person's health or situation.
OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.example: The intervention combined task practice with advice to the family on safe supervision.

OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.definition: A standard tool used to record change in a person's condition or abilities over time.
OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.example: A validated outcome measure was completed at admission and repeated on discharge.

OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.definition: A first measurement against which later changes can be compared.
OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.example: A baseline of his kitchen skills was recorded before the memory programme started.

OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.definition: A therapist deliberately using their personality, attitude and communication to support the therapy process.
OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.example: Therapeutic use of self, including gentle humour, helped build trust with the withdrawn teenager.

OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.definition: Breaking an activity into its steps and demands to see where a person has difficulty.
OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.example: Task analysis showed that the problem lay in reaching the back of the oven, not in reading the dial.

OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.definition: Teaching a task by having the person complete the last step first, then adding earlier steps.
OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.example: Backward chaining was used, so the child pulled up his own trousers before learning earlier dressing steps.

OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.definition: A teaching method that prevents mistakes during practice, often used with memory problems.
OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.example: Errorless learning helped him master the new microwave without repeating incorrect steps.

OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.definition: Physical, emotional and financial pressure experienced by someone looking after another person.
OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.example: Signs of carer strain were noted, as his daughter was sleeping only four hours a night.

OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.definition: Short-term support at home to help a person regain skills and confidence after illness.
OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.example: Six weeks of reablement allowed her to prepare breakfast and wash without carers.

OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.definition: Organising what a patient will need, and who will provide it, before they leave hospital.
OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.example: Discharge planning began on the day of admission because she lives alone on the second floor.

OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.definition: An agreed set of support services, such as home carer visits, arranged for a person.
OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.example: A package of care of two visits daily was arranged to help with washing and meals.

OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.definition: A person's ability to understand, retain and weigh information to make a particular decision.
OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.example: Her mental capacity to decide where to live was assessed jointly with the social worker.

OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.definition: A decision made for someone who lacks capacity, based on what would benefit them most.
OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.example: A best interests meeting was held to consider whether residential care was the right option.

OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.definition: Being prevented, over a long period, from taking part in meaningful activities by outside circumstances.
OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.example: Long stays in secure units can lead to occupational deprivation and loss of everyday skills.

OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.definition: Activity that matters to a person and gives their day purpose, identity or enjoyment.
OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.example: Access to meaningful occupation, such as folding laundry, reduced his agitation in the care home.

OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.definition: To keep something going at the same level over a period of time.
OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.example: She was unable to sustain attention for more than five minutes during the reading task.

OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.definition: To make an action or process easier or more likely to happen.
OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.example: A perching stool was supplied to facilitate safe meal preparation while seated.

OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.definition: To become worse over time.
OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.example: His ability to manage stairs has deteriorated since the last review, so a stairlift assessment is needed.

OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.definition: To change often and irregularly, for example from good to bad.
OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.example: Her symptoms fluctuate, so she may manage the shower one day but not the next.

OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.definition: To include something as part of a larger whole.
OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.example: Hand exercises were incorporated into his morning routine to improve adherence.

OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.definition: How closely a person follows an agreed treatment or programme.
OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.example: Adherence to the splinting regime was poor because the orthosis rubbed her thumb.

OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.definition: To change something slightly so that it works better or suits a new need.
OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.example: The kitchen was modified with a lowered worktop so he could cook from his wheelchair.

OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.definition: A set of exercises a patient practises at home between therapy sessions.
OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.example: I have written down your home exercise programme, so please do these hand stretches twice a day.
OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.plain: exercises to do by yourself at home

OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.term: tell me about a typical day
OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.definition: An open invitation for a patient to describe their usual routine during an interview.
OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.example: To start with, could you tell me about a typical day, from getting up to going to bed?
OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.plain: describe what you normally do each day

OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.definition: A simple tool, such as a long-handled reacher or sock aid, that makes dressing easier.
OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.example: This dressing aid will help you pull your socks on without bending after your hip operation.
OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.plain: a tool that helps you put clothes on

OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.definition: A plain way of describing self-care and household activities when speaking with patients.
OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.example: Can you tell me which everyday tasks you find hardest since the operation?
OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.plain: things like washing, dressing, cooking and cleaning

OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.term: I'd like to find out how you manage at home
OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.definition: A friendly opening for an assessment of a patient's daily life.
OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.example: Good morning, Mrs Patel. I'd like to find out how you manage at home before we plan your discharge.
OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.plain: I want to understand how you cope with daily life at home

OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.definition: A fixed bar on a wall that a person holds for support and balance.
OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.example: We can fit a grab rail beside the toilet so you have something firm to hold.
OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.plain: a strong handle fixed to the wall to hold on to

OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.definition: A high, sloped stool that lets a person half-sit while working at a counter.
OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.example: A perching stool will let you rest while you prepare food at the kitchen worktop.
OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.plain: a tall stool you lean on while working in the kitchen

OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.definition: A seat that fits on a toilet to make it higher and easier to sit on.
OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.example: Because of your new hip, a raised toilet seat will stop you bending too far.
OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.plain: a seat that makes the toilet higher

OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.definition: A board placed across a bath so a person can sit and then swing their legs in.
OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.example: With the bath board in place, you can sit down first and then lift your legs over.
OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.plain: a seat that rests across the top of the bath

OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.definition: Advice to spread activity out and rest regularly rather than doing too much at once.
OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.example: Try to pace yourself by doing one room of cleaning each day instead of the whole house.
OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.plain: do a little at a time and take breaks

OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.definition: A small button worn around the neck or wrist to call for help in an emergency.
OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.example: As you live alone, a pendant alarm means you can call for help if you fall.
OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.plain: a button you wear that calls for help when pressed

OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.definition: Everyday word for a device that holds a joint or limb in a safe position.
OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.example: Please wear the splint at night to keep your fingers straight while the tendon heals.
OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.plain: a support you wear to hold your hand or wrist still

OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.definition: Weakness affecting one side of the body, often after a stroke; explain it simply to patients.
OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.example: His left hemiparesis means he needs help to fasten buttons and cut food.
OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.plain: weakness on one side of the body

OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.definition: Affecting or involving both sides of the body.
OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.example: She has bilateral carpal tunnel symptoms, so both wrists will need night support.
OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.plain: on both sides

OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.term: I am writing to request a home assessment
OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.definition: A clear opening sentence for a referral letter to a community therapy team.
OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.example: I am writing to request a home assessment for Mr Jones, who is due to be discharged on Friday.
OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.plain: I am asking someone to visit the patient's home to check it is safe

OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.definition: A letter phrase linking a patient's current needs to a recent hospital stay.
OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.example: Following her admission with a fractured wrist, Mrs Lee has needed help with meal preparation.
OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.plain: since she came into hospital

OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.definition: A small amount of physical help from another person to complete a task.
OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.example: He currently requires minimal assistance to put on his socks and shoes.
OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.plain: a little help from someone

OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.definition: Someone being present to watch, without physically helping, in case of risk.
OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.example: She can shower independently but needs supervision for safety because of dizziness.
OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.plain: someone nearby to watch and keep you safe

OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.definition: Able to do a task alone when using equipment.
OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.example: Mr Ahmed is independent with aids for dressing, using a long-handled shoe horn.
OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.plain: able to do it yourself with the right equipment

OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.term: I would be grateful if you could
OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.definition: A polite, formal way of making a request in a professional letter.
OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.example: I would be grateful if you could review his seating needs at your earliest convenience.
OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.plain: please could you

OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.term: please do not hesitate to contact me
OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.definition: A polite closing that invites the reader to get in touch with questions.
OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.example: If you require further information, please do not hesitate to contact me on the number above.
OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.plain: feel free to get in touch

OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.definition: A letter phrase stating that equipment has already been provided to the patient.
OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.example: She has been issued with a bath board and a raised toilet seat.
OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.plain: has been given

OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.definition: The ability to hold on to recent information, such as what someone said minutes ago.
OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.example: Problems with short-term memory mean he may forget whether he has taken his tablets.
OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.plain: remembering things that happened recently

OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.definition: A gentle, non-diagnostic way to describe feeling sad or down for a period.
OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.example: She mentioned low mood since stopping work, so I have suggested she speaks to her GP.
OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.plain: feeling sad or down

OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.definition: Simple methods, such as slow breathing, used to reduce tension and anxiety.
OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.example: We practised relaxation techniques you can use before going into busy shops.
OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.plain: ways to calm your body and mind

OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.definition: Damage to skin and tissue caused by prolonged pressure, often over bony areas.
OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.example: Changing position regularly will help prevent a pressure ulcer on your lower back.
OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.plain: a sore caused by sitting or lying in one position for too long

OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.definition: Any equipment that helps a person walk or move about, such as a frame or stick.
OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.example: Please keep your mobility aid within reach when you get up at night.
OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.plain: something that helps you walk, like a frame or stick

OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.definition: An appointment to choose and fit a wheelchair that suits a person's body and needs.
OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.example: I have referred you for a wheelchair assessment so the chair fits you properly.
OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.plain: a check to find the right wheelchair for you

OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.definition: Clinical term for the arm, including shoulder, elbow, wrist and hand.
OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.example: Upper limb function remains reduced on the right, limiting her ability to write.
OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.plain: arm and hand

OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.definition: Clinical term for the leg, including hip, knee, ankle and foot.
OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.example: Following his lower limb amputation, he will need a wheelchair-accessible bathroom.
OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.plain: leg

OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.definition: Reduced ability in thinking skills such as memory, attention or problem-solving.
OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.example: Mild cognitive impairment may affect how safely she uses the gas cooker.
OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.plain: problems with memory and thinking

OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.definition: Short-term care that gives a regular carer a planned break.
OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.example: Your husband may benefit from a week of respite while you recover from your operation.
OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.plain: a short break for the carer while someone else helps

OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.definition: Changes an employer makes so a disabled worker is not disadvantaged.
OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.example: I have suggested reasonable adjustments, including flexible start times and an adapted chair.
OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.plain: changes at work to make your job easier to do

OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.term: let's break it down into smaller steps
OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.definition: A supportive phrase for making a difficult task feel more manageable.
OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.example: Getting dressed feels overwhelming, so let's break it down into smaller steps and start with your top.
OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.plain: we will do one small part at a time

OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.definition: An open question used to find out a patient's own priorities for therapy.
OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.example: Before we set any goals, can you tell me what matters most to you over the next month?
OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.plain: what is most important for you

OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.term: could you show me how you usually do this
OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.definition: A polite request to observe a patient performing a task in their normal way.
OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.example: Could you show me how you usually do this, so I can see where the difficulty is?
OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.plain: please show me how you normally do it

OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.definition: A planned set of sensory activities spread through the day to help a person stay regulated.
OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.example: His sensory diet includes jumping on a trampoline before lessons to help him settle.
OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.plain: a daily plan of calming or energising activities

OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.definition: Bending movement at a joint that reduces the angle between two body parts.
OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.example: Finger flexion has improved, so you should now be able to make a loose fist.
OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.plain: bending

OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.definition: Straightening movement at a joint that increases the angle between two body parts.
OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.example: Wrist extension is still limited, which is why lifting a pan is painful.
OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.plain: straightening

OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.definition: A letter phrase recommending that a service keeps providing therapy or support.
OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.example: I would recommend continued input from community occupational therapy to progress her kitchen skills.
OCCUPATIONAL_THERAPY.plain: more sessions or support

OPTOMETRY.definition: How clearly a person can see fine detail, usually measured with a letter chart.
OPTOMETRY.example: Visual acuity was 6/9 in the right eye and 6/36 in the left without correction.

OPTOMETRY.definition: A focusing problem where the eye does not bend light correctly onto the retina.
OPTOMETRY.example: Uncorrected refractive error remains a leading cause of reduced vision in school-age children.

OPTOMETRY.definition: A refractive error in which distant objects look blurred while near objects are clearer.
OPTOMETRY.example: Her myopia has increased by half a dioptre since last year's examination.

OPTOMETRY.definition: A refractive error in which light focuses behind the retina, making close focusing harder.
OPTOMETRY.example: Moderate hyperopia may cause headaches and tired eyes when the child reads for long periods.

OPTOMETRY.definition: Uneven curvature of the cornea or lens that causes blurred or distorted vision at all distances.
OPTOMETRY.example: Astigmatism of two dioptres was corrected with toric lenses.

OPTOMETRY.definition: The gradual, age-related loss of the eye's ability to focus on near objects.
OPTOMETRY.example: At forty-six, he reported symptoms typical of presbyopia, holding menus further away to read.

OPTOMETRY.definition: The eye changing its focusing power, mainly through the lens, to see objects at different distances.
OPTOMETRY.example: Reduced accommodation was measured, consistent with her complaint of blur after short periods of reading.

OPTOMETRY.definition: A significant difference in prescription between a person's two eyes.
OPTOMETRY.example: Untreated anisometropia in early childhood can lead to reduced vision in the more blurred eye.

OPTOMETRY.definition: Reduced vision in an eye that did not develop normal sight in childhood, despite a healthy eye.
OPTOMETRY.example: Patching was advised to treat amblyopia in the left eye.

OPTOMETRY.definition: A misalignment in which the two eyes do not point at the same object.
OPTOMETRY.example: A small-angle strabismus was detected on cover testing during the child's first visit.

OPTOMETRY.definition: Difficulty turning both eyes inward together to keep close objects single and clear.
OPTOMETRY.example: Convergence insufficiency was thought to explain his eye strain and occasional doubling when studying.

OPTOMETRY.definition: Using both eyes together as a team to produce a single image and judge depth.
OPTOMETRY.example: A full binocular vision assessment was carried out because of her headaches after screen work.

OPTOMETRY.definition: The fluid pressure inside the eye.
OPTOMETRY.example: Intraocular pressure was raised in both eyes on two separate readings.

OPTOMETRY.definition: A common, slowly progressive optic nerve disease where the eye's drainage angle remains open.
OPTOMETRY.example: Open-angle glaucoma often causes no symptoms until a significant amount of side vision is lost.

OPTOMETRY.definition: The size of the central hollow of the optic disc compared with the whole disc.
OPTOMETRY.example: The cup-to-disc ratio was larger in the right eye, raising suspicion of glaucoma.

OPTOMETRY.definition: An area of the field of vision where sight is reduced or missing.
OPTOMETRY.example: An inferior visual field defect was found in the left eye and repeated to confirm it.

OPTOMETRY.definition: The innermost retinal layer made up of nerve fibres travelling to the optic nerve.
OPTOMETRY.example: Imaging showed thinning of the retinal nerve fibre layer in the upper part of the disc.

OPTOMETRY.definition: A non-contact scan using light to produce detailed cross-sectional images of the retina.
OPTOMETRY.example: Optical coherence tomography revealed fluid beneath the macula.

OPTOMETRY.definition: Measurement of the pressure inside the eye.
OPTOMETRY.example: Contact tonometry was repeated after the air-puff reading appeared high.

OPTOMETRY.definition: Magnified examination of the eye using a bright, adjustable beam of light.
OPTOMETRY.example: Slit-lamp biomicroscopy showed a clear cornea and a quiet anterior chamber.

OPTOMETRY.definition: Inspection of the back of the eye after drops have widened the pupil.
OPTOMETRY.example: A dilated fundus examination was performed because of his new floaters.

OPTOMETRY.definition: An eye drop that widens the pupil to allow a better view inside the eye.
OPTOMETRY.example: A mydriatic was instilled, and the patient was advised that near vision would blur for several hours.

OPTOMETRY.definition: Measuring a prescription after drops temporarily stop the eye's focusing muscle.
OPTOMETRY.example: Cycloplegic refraction revealed much more hyperopia than the initial test had suggested.

OPTOMETRY.definition: Gradual damage to the central retina in older people, affecting detailed central vision.
OPTOMETRY.example: Age-related macular degeneration was diagnosed after she noticed straight lines looking wavy.

OPTOMETRY.definition: Small yellow deposits under the retina, commonly seen with ageing and early macular disease.
OPTOMETRY.example: Scattered drusen were noted at both maculae, with no sign of bleeding.

OPTOMETRY.definition: An advanced dry form of macular degeneration with patches of lost retinal tissue.
OPTOMETRY.example: Geographic atrophy had expanded towards the centre of the right macula.

OPTOMETRY.definition: Visual distortion in which straight lines appear bent or wavy.
OPTOMETRY.example: New metamorphopsia in an older patient requires prompt assessment for wet macular disease.

OPTOMETRY.definition: Damage to the small blood vessels of the retina caused by diabetes.
OPTOMETRY.example: Background diabetic retinopathy was seen, with a few small haemorrhages in each eye.

OPTOMETRY.definition: Any disease affecting the macula, the central part of the retina.
OPTOMETRY.example: Exudates near the fovea suggested diabetic maculopathy needing hospital review.

OPTOMETRY.definition: Clouding of the eye's natural lens that causes blurred vision and glare.
OPTOMETRY.example: A dense cataract in the left eye explained his difficulty driving at night.

OPTOMETRY.definition: Clouding of the membrane behind an implanted lens months or years after cataract surgery.
OPTOMETRY.example: Posterior capsule opacification was the likely cause of her gradual blur two years after surgery.

OPTOMETRY.definition: Separation of the gel inside the eye from the retina, common with ageing.
OPTOMETRY.example: Posterior vitreous detachment was confirmed, and no retinal tear was found.

OPTOMETRY.definition: Lifting of the retina away from the back wall of the eye; a sight-threatening emergency.
OPTOMETRY.example: A shadow spreading across her vision raised concern about retinal detachment.

OPTOMETRY.definition: Seeing flashes of light that are not really there.
OPTOMETRY.example: He described photopsia in the outer edge of his vision, especially in dim light.

OPTOMETRY.definition: Small dots, threads or cobweb shapes that drift across vision, caused by changes in the vitreous.
OPTOMETRY.example: A sudden shower of floaters should be examined on the same day.

OPTOMETRY.definition: A condition in which the cornea thins and bulges into a cone shape.
OPTOMETRY.example: Increasing irregular astigmatism in a young adult raised suspicion of keratoconus.

OPTOMETRY.definition: Infection of the cornea, a serious risk for contact lens wearers.
OPTOMETRY.example: Sleeping in contact lenses greatly increases the risk of microbial keratitis.

OPTOMETRY.definition: A scratch on the clear front surface of the eye.
OPTOMETRY.example: Fluorescein staining showed a small corneal abrasion after the branch caught her eye.

OPTOMETRY.definition: Long-term inflammation of the eyelid margins, causing crusting, itching and soreness.
OPTOMETRY.example: Crusting along the lashes was consistent with blepharitis.

OPTOMETRY.definition: Blockage or poor function of the eyelid glands that produce the oily layer of tears.
OPTOMETRY.example: Meibomian gland dysfunction was contributing to the rapid evaporation of her tears.

OPTOMETRY.definition: How long the tear film stays intact after a blink before dry spots appear.
OPTOMETRY.example: Tear break-up time was reduced to four seconds in both eyes.

OPTOMETRY.definition: Inflammation of the thin membrane covering the white of the eye and inner eyelids.
OPTOMETRY.example: Watery discharge and redness in both eyes suggested viral conjunctivitis.

OPTOMETRY.definition: Inflammation inside the front of the eye, often causing pain, redness and light sensitivity.
OPTOMETRY.example: Cells in the anterior chamber confirmed anterior uveitis, and she was referred urgently.

OPTOMETRY.definition: Swelling of both optic discs caused by raised pressure within the skull.
OPTOMETRY.example: Bilateral disc swelling suggested papilloedema, so the patient was sent to the emergency department.

OPTOMETRY.definition: An abnormal pupil response showing reduced signal from one optic nerve or retina.
OPTOMETRY.example: A relative afferent pupillary defect on the right pointed to optic nerve disease.

OPTOMETRY.definition: Seeing two images of a single object.
OPTOMETRY.example: Sudden diplopia with a drooping eyelid requires same-day medical assessment.

OPTOMETRY.definition: Involuntary, repetitive movement of the eyes.
OPTOMETRY.example: Long-standing nystagmus was noted, and the patient reported it had been present since birth.

OPTOMETRY.definition: Treatments aimed at slowing the worsening of short-sightedness in children.
OPTOMETRY.example: Myopia control options were discussed because both parents are highly short-sighted.

OPTOMETRY.definition: The distance from the front to the back of the eye.
OPTOMETRY.example: Axial length is measured every six months to track the progression of her myopia.

OPTOMETRY.definition: Wearing specially designed rigid lenses overnight to reshape the cornea temporarily.
OPTOMETRY.example: With orthokeratology, he can see clearly during the day without glasses.

OPTOMETRY.definition: Learning to look slightly away from an object so a healthier part of the retina sees it.
OPTOMETRY.example: Eccentric viewing training helped her read large print despite the central scarring.

OPTOMETRY.definition: The ability to see objects that differ only slightly in shade from their background.
OPTOMETRY.example: Reduced contrast sensitivity made it hard for him to see kerbs on grey days.
