OPTOMETRY.definition: The minimum level of sight required by law to hold a driving licence.
OPTOMETRY.example: With both eyes open, he no longer meets the visual standard for driving.

OPTOMETRY.definition: Sending a patient for specialist assessment within hours because of a possible sight-threatening problem.
OPTOMETRY.example: A same-day referral was made to the eye casualty department for suspected retinal tear.

OPTOMETRY.definition: The way a condition develops or worsens over time.
OPTOMETRY.example: Field tests every six months will help detect any progression of the glaucoma.

OPTOMETRY.definition: To find or notice something that is not obvious.
OPTOMETRY.example: Routine eye examinations can detect diabetic changes before vision is affected.

OPTOMETRY.definition: Showing no signs or complaints of a condition, even if it is present.
OPTOMETRY.example: The patient was asymptomatic, yet the scan showed early macular changes.

OPTOMETRY.definition: In binocular vision, the amount by which one eye turns away from the aligned position.
OPTOMETRY.example: A small outward deviation became noticeable when the child was tired.

OPTOMETRY.definition: To check something regularly over a period to see whether it changes.
OPTOMETRY.example: We will monitor the naevus with photographs at each annual visit.

OPTOMETRY.definition: Being the real or basic cause, though not immediately obvious.
OPTOMETRY.example: Recurrent styes may reflect underlying blepharitis that needs long-term lid care.

OPTOMETRY.definition: Everyday UK term for a hospital's emergency eye department.
OPTOMETRY.example: I'd like you to go to eye casualty this afternoon so they can check your retina properly.
OPTOMETRY.plain: the hospital's emergency department for eyes

OPTOMETRY.definition: Everyday word for myopic; distant objects look blurred.
OPTOMETRY.example: Your son is slightly short-sighted, which is why the board at school looks fuzzy.
OPTOMETRY.plain: you can see close up but things far away look blurred

OPTOMETRY.definition: Everyday word for hyperopic; the eye works harder to focus, especially up close.
OPTOMETRY.example: You are long-sighted, so your eyes have to work harder when you read.
OPTOMETRY.plain: close things are harder to focus on than distant things

OPTOMETRY.definition: A plain way to describe intraocular pressure above the usual range.
OPTOMETRY.example: Your test showed raised eye pressure, so I'd like a specialist to check your optic nerves.
OPTOMETRY.plain: the pressure inside your eye is higher than usual

OPTOMETRY.definition: Eye drops that widen the pupils so the back of the eye can be examined.
OPTOMETRY.example: After the dilating drops, your vision will be blurry and bright light may feel uncomfortable.
OPTOMETRY.plain: drops that make your pupils bigger

OPTOMETRY.definition: Vision that is unclear or out of focus.
OPTOMETRY.example: When did you first notice the blurred vision in your right eye?
OPTOMETRY.plain: things look fuzzy or unclear

OPTOMETRY.definition: Plain wording for photopsia, used when giving warning advice.
OPTOMETRY.example: If you notice flashing lights or new floaters, please contact us or eye casualty the same day.
OPTOMETRY.plain: sudden flickers or sparks of light in your vision

OPTOMETRY.term: a curtain or shadow across your vision
OPTOMETRY.definition: Plain wording to describe a possible warning sign of retinal detachment.
OPTOMETRY.example: Go to the eye department straight away if you see a curtain or shadow across your vision.
OPTOMETRY.plain: part of your sight becomes dark, as if something is blocking it

OPTOMETRY.definition: Everyday term for amblyopia, useful when talking to parents.
OPTOMETRY.example: Wearing the patch for two hours a day should help her lazy eye see better.
OPTOMETRY.plain: an eye that did not learn to see clearly in childhood

OPTOMETRY.definition: Everyday word for strabismus, when the eyes point in different directions.
OPTOMETRY.example: I noticed a small squint when your son looked at the toy close up.
OPTOMETRY.plain: one eye turns in, out, up or down

OPTOMETRY.definition: Everyday term for diplopia.
OPTOMETRY.example: Does the double vision go away when you cover one eye?
OPTOMETRY.plain: seeing two of everything

OPTOMETRY.definition: Glasses with lenses that gradually change power for distance, middle and near vision.
OPTOMETRY.example: Varifocals take a week or two to get used to, so move your head rather than your eyes at first.
OPTOMETRY.plain: glasses that let you see far and near without changing pairs

OPTOMETRY.definition: Glasses that make close work such as reading clearer.
OPTOMETRY.example: Most people need reading glasses in their forties as the eye's focusing weakens.
OPTOMETRY.plain: glasses just for close-up things like reading

OPTOMETRY.term: I am referring this patient urgently
OPTOMETRY.definition: A clear, direct opening for an urgent referral letter.
OPTOMETRY.example: I am referring this patient urgently for assessment of a suspected wet macular change in the left eye.
OPTOMETRY.plain: I am asking for this person to be seen quickly

OPTOMETRY.definition: A referral for non-urgent specialist assessment, seen in the normal waiting time.
OPTOMETRY.example: A routine referral has been made for cataract assessment, as his vision now affects daily tasks.
OPTOMETRY.plain: a request to see a specialist that is not an emergency

OPTOMETRY.definition: A formal letter phrase introducing documents sent with the letter.
OPTOMETRY.example: Please find enclosed a copy of today's visual field results and scan images.
OPTOMETRY.plain: I have sent these with this letter

OPTOMETRY.definition: A cautious phrase linking examination results to a likely diagnosis without overstating certainty.
OPTOMETRY.example: The findings are consistent with early open-angle glaucoma, although further testing is needed.
OPTOMETRY.plain: the results suggest

OPTOMETRY.definition: Vision at the edges of the visual field, outside the point you look at directly.
OPTOMETRY.example: Glaucoma first affects your peripheral vision, which is why regular tests matter.
OPTOMETRY.plain: side vision

OPTOMETRY.definition: A common condition where tears do not keep the eye surface comfortable and moist.
OPTOMETRY.example: Your gritty, tired eyes after computer work are typical of dry eye.
OPTOMETRY.plain: your eyes do not make enough good-quality tears

OPTOMETRY.definition: Warm items held on closed eyelids to soften blocked gland oils.
OPTOMETRY.example: Use warm compresses on your eyelids for five minutes every morning.
OPTOMETRY.plain: something warm held gently over your closed eyes

OPTOMETRY.definition: Regular gentle cleaning of the eyelid edges to remove crusts and debris.
OPTOMETRY.example: Daily lid hygiene will help control the crusting along your lashes.
OPTOMETRY.plain: cleaning your eyelids carefully each day

OPTOMETRY.definition: Clear safety advice given when a lens wearer has a red or painful eye.
OPTOMETRY.example: Please stop wearing your contact lenses until the redness has completely settled.
OPTOMETRY.plain: take your lenses out and do not use them for now

OPTOMETRY.definition: Direct safety advice about driving after drops or a change in vision.
OPTOMETRY.example: Your pupils are still wide, so you should not drive until your vision is clear again.
OPTOMETRY.plain: do not drive before

OPTOMETRY.definition: A record phrase meaning a result falls inside the expected healthy range.
OPTOMETRY.example: Eye pressures and visual fields were within normal limits in both eyes.
OPTOMETRY.plain: normal

OPTOMETRY.definition: A phrase reporting that a condition or result has not changed since the last check.
OPTOMETRY.example: The appearance of the optic discs remains stable compared with last year's photographs.
OPTOMETRY.plain: has not changed

OPTOMETRY.definition: Plain wording to explain a cataract to a patient.
OPTOMETRY.example: You have some clouding of the lens inside your eye, which is called a cataract.
OPTOMETRY.plain: the clear lens inside your eye has become misty

OPTOMETRY.definition: A lens or device that makes print and objects look bigger.
OPTOMETRY.example: A lighted magnifier may help you read your post and medicine labels.
OPTOMETRY.plain: a lens that makes things look bigger

OPTOMETRY.definition: Bright, well-directed light that makes tasks easier for people with reduced vision.
OPTOMETRY.example: Good lighting over your chair will make reading much easier.
OPTOMETRY.plain: plenty of bright light where you need it

OPTOMETRY.definition: Time spent looking at phones, tablets, computers or television.
OPTOMETRY.example: Try to take regular breaks from screen time to rest your eyes.
OPTOMETRY.plain: time spent looking at phones, tablets or computers

OPTOMETRY.definition: Time spent outside in daylight, linked with a lower chance of developing short-sightedness in children.
OPTOMETRY.example: More time outdoors each day may help reduce the chance of your daughter becoming short-sighted.
OPTOMETRY.plain: time playing or being outside

OPTOMETRY.definition: Everyday term for an eye examination that checks vision and eye health.
OPTOMETRY.example: I'd recommend a sight test every year because you have diabetes.
OPTOMETRY.plain: an eye check-up

OPTOMETRY.definition: A reassuring way to explain a small change in the lenses a patient needs.
OPTOMETRY.example: Your prescription has changed slightly, so new glasses will make distance vision a little sharper.
OPTOMETRY.plain: you need slightly different lenses

OPTOMETRY.definition: Safety-netting advice telling a patient to get care quickly if symptoms appear.
OPTOMETRY.example: Seek urgent attention if your eye becomes very painful or your sight gets worse.
OPTOMETRY.plain: get help straight away

OPTOMETRY.definition: The light-sensitive layer lining the back of the eye.
OPTOMETRY.example: The photographs show that your retina is healthy, with no sign of diabetic changes.
OPTOMETRY.plain: the layer at the back of the eye that senses light

OPTOMETRY.definition: The small central area of the retina responsible for fine detail and reading vision.
OPTOMETRY.example: The macula is the part of your eye you use to read and recognise faces.
OPTOMETRY.plain: the centre of the back of the eye used for detail

OPTOMETRY.definition: The nerve that carries visual signals from the eye to the brain.
OPTOMETRY.example: Glaucoma slowly damages the optic nerve, so we check it carefully at every visit.
OPTOMETRY.plain: the cable that carries signals from your eye to your brain

OPTOMETRY.definition: The clear, curved window at the front of the eye.
OPTOMETRY.example: The scratch is on your cornea, which is why your eye feels so sore.
OPTOMETRY.plain: the clear front surface of the eye

OPTOMETRY.definition: Describes eyes that feel as if they contain sand or dust.
OPTOMETRY.example: Do your eyes feel gritty, or is it more of an aching pain?
OPTOMETRY.plain: feeling like there is sand in your eye

OPTOMETRY.definition: An informal phrase meaning to watch or check something regularly.
OPTOMETRY.example: It's nothing to worry about now, but we'll keep an eye on that freckle at the back of your eye.
OPTOMETRY.plain: check it regularly

OPTOMETRY.definition: A phrase for asking whether close relatives have had a particular condition.
OPTOMETRY.example: Do you have any family history of glaucoma, for example a parent or brother or sister?
OPTOMETRY.plain: whether anyone in your family has had

PHARMACY.definition: How closely a patient takes their medicines in the way agreed with the prescriber.
PHARMACY.example: Poor adherence to his inhaler routine probably explains the repeated flare-ups described in the referral.

PHARMACY.definition: A shared agreement between patient and clinician about whether and how medicines will be taken.
PHARMACY.example: The medicines review aimed to reach concordance on when she would take her evening tablets.

PHARMACY.definition: A condition or factor that makes a particular medicine or treatment unsafe for a patient.
PHARMACY.example: Previous angioedema is a contraindication to restarting that class of blood pressure medicine.

PHARMACY.definition: A change in how a medicine works caused by another medicine, food or substance.
PHARMACY.example: The pharmacist flagged a drug interaction between the newly prescribed antibiotic and the patient's warfarin.

PHARMACY.definition: How the body absorbs, spreads, breaks down and removes a medicine over time.
PHARMACY.example: Age-related changes in pharmacokinetics mean some older patients clear medicines more slowly than younger adults.

PHARMACY.definition: What a medicine does to the body and how its effect relates to its concentration.
PHARMACY.example: The lecture compared the pharmacodynamics of short-acting and long-acting sleeping tablets.

PHARMACY.definition: The share of a medicine that reaches the bloodstream unchanged after it is given.
PHARMACY.example: When switching from intravenous to oral treatment, the team considered the lower bioavailability of the tablets.

PHARMACY.definition: The time it takes for the amount of a medicine in the blood to fall by half.
PHARMACY.example: Because of its long half-life, the medicine can still cause drowsiness the following morning.

PHARMACY.definition: The margin between the level of a medicine that helps and the level that harms.
PHARMACY.example: Lithium has a narrow therapeutic index, so regular blood tests are part of every review.

PHARMACY.definition: To change a dose step by step until the wanted effect is reached safely.
PHARMACY.example: The cardiologist asked the GP to titrate the beta blocker slowly while checking pulse and blood pressure.

PHARMACY.definition: Taking many medicines at the same time, which can increase the chance of harm.
PHARMACY.example: Polypharmacy was identified as a likely factor in the resident's recent falls.

PHARMACY.definition: The planned, supervised reduction or stopping of medicines that no longer offer enough benefit.
PHARMACY.example: The frailty clinic uses a structured approach to deprescribing for patients on more than ten medicines.

PHARMACY.definition: A harmful, unintended response to a medicine used in the normal way.
PHARMACY.example: The widespread rash was reported as a suspected adverse drug reaction through the national reporting scheme.

PHARMACY.definition: An exaggerated immune response to a substance, such as a medicine or one of its ingredients.
PHARMACY.example: Her notes record hypersensitivity to penicillin, so an alternative antibiotic was supplied.

PHARMACY.definition: Checking that a patient's list of medicines is complete and correct when their care moves between settings.
PHARMACY.example: Medicines reconciliation on admission revealed that his regular diuretic had been left off the chart.

PHARMACY.definition: An approved list of medicines that clinicians in an organisation are expected to prescribe from.
PHARMACY.example: The requested inhaler is not on the local formulary, so the team suggested an equivalent option.

PHARMACY.definition: Describes use of a medicine outside the conditions stated in its licence.
PHARMACY.example: The consultant recommended off-label use for the child, and the discussion with the parents was documented.

PHARMACY.definition: Sold under its approved chemical name rather than a manufacturer's brand name.
PHARMACY.example: The patient was reassured that the generic tablets contain the same active ingredient as her previous ones.

PHARMACY.definition: An inactive ingredient in a medicine, such as a filler, binder or colouring.
PHARMACY.example: The pharmacist checked whether any excipient contained gelatin, as the patient follows a vegetarian diet.

PHARMACY.definition: Covered with a layer that stops a tablet dissolving until it has passed the stomach.
PHARMACY.example: Enteric-coated tablets should be swallowed whole and must not be crushed or chewed.

PHARMACY.definition: Designed to release the medicine gradually over a longer period than standard forms.
PHARMACY.example: Modified-release preparations cannot simply be swapped for standard tablets without adjusting the timing.

PHARMACY.definition: A medicine made up in the pharmacy for one patient when no suitable licensed product exists.
PHARMACY.example: An extemporaneous preparation was arranged because the toddler could not swallow the available capsules.

PHARMACY.definition: Reduced kidney function, which can slow the removal of some medicines from the body.
PHARMACY.example: In patients with renal impairment, several antibiotics need dose adjustment guided by kidney function tests.

PHARMACY.definition: Damage to the liver caused by a medicine or another chemical.
PHARMACY.example: Liver function tests were repeated because hepatotoxicity is a known risk with the new tuberculosis treatment.

PHARMACY.definition: Harmful to the kidneys.
PHARMACY.example: Giving two nephrotoxic medicines to a dehydrated patient raises the risk of acute kidney injury.

PHARMACY.definition: A medicine that reduces the blood's ability to form clots.
PHARMACY.example: Any patient on an anticoagulant should be asked about unusual bruising or bleeding at each review.

PHARMACY.definition: Coordinated action to use antibiotics and similar medicines wisely so that resistance develops more slowly.
PHARMACY.example: Under the antimicrobial stewardship programme, every intravenous antibiotic is reviewed after two days.

PHARMACY.definition: The ability of bacteria or other microbes to survive medicines that previously killed them.
PHARMACY.example: Public campaigns on antimicrobial resistance explain why antibiotics will not help most coughs and colds.

PHARMACY.definition: Treatment given to prevent a disease rather than to treat one already present.
PHARMACY.example: Malaria prophylaxis was discussed with the traveller, along with advice on avoiding mosquito bites.

PHARMACY.definition: How well a treatment produces its intended result, usually measured in controlled studies.
PHARMACY.example: The trial showed similar efficacy for both medicines, but fewer patients stopped the newer one.

PHARMACY.definition: How well patients can cope with a medicine's side effects over time.
PHARMACY.example: Tolerability, rather than effectiveness, was the main reason patients abandoned the original regimen.

PHARMACY.definition: An inactive substance or dummy treatment given for comparison in a study.
PHARMACY.example: Half the participants received the active medicine and half received a placebo of identical appearance.

PHARMACY.definition: A study in which people are assigned by chance to different treatments so results can be fairly compared.
PHARMACY.example: The guideline relies mainly on one large randomised controlled trial conducted in older adults.

PHARMACY.definition: The ongoing monitoring and assessment of medicines' safety once they are in general use.
PHARMACY.example: Pharmacovigilance data later revealed a rare liver problem that the original trials had missed.

PHARMACY.definition: A mistake made while a prescription is being prepared, checked or handed to the patient.
PHARMACY.example: The dispensing error was reported, and the team changed how look-alike medicines are stored on the shelves.

PHARMACY.definition: A medicine with strict legal rules on storage, supply and record keeping because it can be misused.
PHARMACY.example: Every controlled drug supplied must be entered in the register and checked by a second member of staff.

PHARMACY.definition: Measuring the level of a medicine in the blood to guide safe and effective dosing.
PHARMACY.example: Therapeutic drug monitoring showed that the antibiotic level was too high, so the next dose was delayed.

PHARMACY.definition: A larger first dose given to reach an effective level quickly before regular doses continue.
PHARMACY.example: The hospital letter explains that the loading dose was given on the ward and regular dosing should continue.

PHARMACY.definition: A medicine that calms a person or makes them drowsy.
PHARMACY.example: Starting a sedative in a frail patient already at risk of falls needs careful justification.

PHARMACY.definition: A medicine that relieves pain.
PHARMACY.example: A simple analgesic taken regularly may control her arthritis pain better than occasional stronger tablets.

PHARMACY.definition: A strong pain-relieving medicine that acts on specific nerve receptors and carries a risk of dependence.
PHARMACY.example: The pain team recommended reviewing the opioid every few weeks and reducing it once healing progresses.

PHARMACY.definition: A state in which the body adapts to a substance and stopping it suddenly causes unpleasant symptoms.
PHARMACY.example: Long-term use of the sleeping tablets had led to dependence, so a slow reduction plan was agreed.

PHARMACY.definition: Unpleasant physical or mental effects that occur when a medicine the body depends on is stopped.
PHARMACY.example: She developed withdrawal symptoms, including anxiety and sweating, after stopping her antidepressant abruptly.

PHARMACY.definition: The combined effect of medicines that block acetylcholine, linked with confusion, constipation and falls in older people.
PHARMACY.example: The review aimed to lower his anticholinergic burden by replacing the bladder medicine and an old antihistamine.

PHARMACY.definition: A delay in the heart's electrical recovery between beats that increases the risk of dangerous rhythms.
PHARMACY.example: An ECG was requested to check for QT prolongation before adding a second antipsychotic.

PHARMACY.definition: To slow or block a process, such as an enzyme breaking down a medicine.
PHARMACY.example: Grapefruit juice can inhibit the liver enzyme that breaks down several cholesterol-lowering medicines.

PHARMACY.definition: To break down a substance chemically inside the body.
PHARMACY.example: Some people metabolise codeine unusually quickly, which can lead to dangerous levels of morphine.

PHARMACY.definition: The specific way a medicine produces its effect in the body.
PHARMACY.example: The leaflet describes the mechanism of action in simple terms for patients starting the new treatment.

PHARMACY.definition: Able to be mixed or given together without a harmful change.
PHARMACY.example: The nurse asked the pharmacist whether the two infusions were compatible through the same line.

PHARMACY.definition: Happening or being used at the same time.
PHARMACY.example: Concurrent use of the two sedating medicines was recorded as a significant safety concern.

PHARMACY.definition: The rate at which new cases of a condition appear in a population over a period.
PHARMACY.example: The study reported a lower incidence of stomach bleeding when a stomach-protecting medicine was added.

PHARMACY.definition: An agreed written set of steps for carrying out a clinical task.
PHARMACY.example: The anticoagulation protocol states when blood tests must be repeated after any change in treatment.

PHARMACY.definition: The safe getting rid of something, such as unused medicines or used needles.
PHARMACY.example: The leaflet explains disposal of used needles in a sharps bin returned to the pharmacy.

PHARMACY.definition: A product taken to add vitamins, minerals, herbs or other substances to the diet.
PHARMACY.example: She had not mentioned the herbal supplement she was taking alongside her antidepressant.

PHARMACY.definition: A written instruction allowing named professionals to supply or give a medicine to a defined group without a prescription.
PHARMACY.example: Under a patient group direction, the pharmacist can supply emergency contraception after a private consultation.

PHARMACY.definition: Available to buy without a prescription.
PHARMACY.example: Many over-the-counter cold remedies contain paracetamol, so patients may take too much without realising.

PHARMACY.definition: The official document describing a licensed medicine's approved uses, risks and handling.
PHARMACY.example: The pharmacist checked the summary of product characteristics to confirm whether the tablets could be split.

PHARMACY.definition: The system that keeps products such as vaccines within a set temperature range from maker to patient.
PHARMACY.example: A fridge failure broke the cold chain, so the affected vaccines were quarantined until advice was received.

PHARMACY.definition: The length of time a product remains safe and effective when stored correctly.
PHARMACY.example: Once opened, the eye drops have a much shorter shelf life than the sealed bottle.

PHARMACY.definition: Giving medicine hidden in food or drink without the patient knowing, allowed only under strict legal safeguards.
PHARMACY.example: Covert administration was agreed at a best-interests meeting, and the pharmacist advised which tablets could be mixed with food.

PHARMACY.definition: An unwanted effect of a medicine, in everyday words; clinicians may write 'adverse effect'.
PHARMACY.example: The most common side effect of this tablet is a mild upset stomach, which usually settles.
PHARMACY.plain: an unwanted effect of a medicine

PHARMACY.definition: Relief of pain, usually by medicine.
PHARMACY.example: Regular analgesia was advised for the first few days after the injury.
PHARMACY.plain: pain relief; painkillers

PHARMACY.definition: Blood pressure that stays higher than the healthy range.
PHARMACY.example: Your hypertension, which simply means high blood pressure, is the reason for this new tablet.
PHARMACY.plain: high blood pressure

PHARMACY.definition: A blood glucose level that is higher than it should be.
PHARMACY.example: Signs of hyperglycaemia include feeling very thirsty and passing more urine than usual.
PHARMACY.plain: high blood sugar

PHARMACY.definition: A blood glucose level that has dropped too low, causing shakiness, sweating or confusion.
PHARMACY.example: If you notice signs of hypoglycaemia, such as shaking or sweating, have a sugary drink straight away.
PHARMACY.plain: low blood sugar; a 'hypo'

PHARMACY.definition: A medicine that makes the kidneys pass more water and salt.
PHARMACY.example: Take the diuretic in the morning so you are not getting up to the toilet at night.
PHARMACY.plain: a water tablet

PHARMACY.definition: A medicine that prevents or reduces nausea and vomiting.
PHARMACY.example: The doctor has prescribed an antiemetic to take before your chemotherapy sessions.
PHARMACY.plain: anti-sickness medicine

PHARMACY.definition: Applied directly to the skin or another body surface rather than swallowed.
PHARMACY.example: This is a topical cream, so apply a thin layer to the affected skin only.
PHARMACY.plain: put on the skin

PHARMACY.definition: By mouth.
PHARMACY.example: The antibiotic is taken orally, so you can swallow it with a glass of water.
PHARMACY.plain: by mouth; swallowed

PHARMACY.definition: Placed under the tongue so the medicine dissolves and is absorbed there.
PHARMACY.example: The sublingual spray works quickly, so use it as soon as the chest pain starts.
PHARMACY.plain: put under the tongue to dissolve

PHARMACY.definition: Taken only when symptoms occur rather than at fixed times.
PHARMACY.example: Use the blue inhaler as required, whenever you feel wheezy or short of breath.
PHARMACY.plain: only when you need it

PHARMACY.definition: A device that turns liquid medicine into a fine mist to be breathed in.
PHARMACY.example: The nebuliser is useful when you are too breathless to use your normal inhaler properly.
PHARMACY.plain: a machine that turns medicine into a mist you breathe in

PHARMACY.definition: The correct way of using an inhaler so the medicine reaches the lungs.
PHARMACY.example: Let's check your inhaler technique, because a small change can make the medicine work much better.
PHARMACY.plain: the way you use your inhaler

PHARMACY.definition: Stomach acid flowing back up into the food pipe, causing burning discomfort.
PHARMACY.example: Gastro-oesophageal reflux can be worse when you lie down soon after a large meal.
PHARMACY.plain: heartburn; acid reflux

PHARMACY.definition: A medicine that helps the bowels empty more easily.
PHARMACY.example: Because the painkiller can cause constipation, I'd suggest a gentle laxative as well.
PHARMACY.plain: a medicine to help you open your bowels

PHARMACY.definition: Discomfort or pain in the upper stomach, often after eating.
PHARMACY.example: Your dyspepsia may improve if you take the anti-inflammatory tablet with food.
PHARMACY.plain: indigestion

PHARMACY.definition: An unpleasant sensation that makes a person want to scratch.
PHARMACY.example: The letter notes pruritus as a possible reaction, so please tell us if you feel itchy.
PHARMACY.plain: itching

PHARMACY.definition: A moisturising product that softens skin and helps keep water in.
PHARMACY.example: Apply the emollient several times a day, smoothing it gently in the direction of hair growth.
PHARMACY.plain: a moisturiser

PHARMACY.definition: Swelling caused by fluid collecting in the body's tissues.
PHARMACY.example: Ankle oedema can happen with this blood pressure tablet, so let us know if your ankles swell.
PHARMACY.plain: swelling caused by extra fluid

PHARMACY.definition: Raised levels of fats, such as cholesterol, in the blood.
PHARMACY.example: The statin was started to treat your hyperlipidaemia and lower your risk of heart disease.
PHARMACY.plain: high cholesterol

PHARMACY.term: are you taking any other medicines
PHARMACY.definition: A key question to check for interactions before supplying a medicine.
PHARMACY.example: Before I give you this, are you taking any other medicines, including herbal remedies or vitamins?
PHARMACY.plain: do you use any other tablets, sprays, creams or remedies?

PHARMACY.term: I am writing to inform you
PHARMACY.definition: A formal opening for a letter that passes on information to another professional.
PHARMACY.example: I am writing to inform you that Mrs Ahmed reported dizziness after starting her new blood pressure tablet.
PHARMACY.plain: this letter is to let you know

PHARMACY.term: I would be grateful if you could review
PHARMACY.definition: A polite formal request asking a colleague to reassess a patient or treatment.
PHARMACY.example: I would be grateful if you could review his pain medicines, as he reports increasing drowsiness.
PHARMACY.plain: please could you look again at

PHARMACY.definition: An instruction to take a medicine while eating or just after a meal.
PHARMACY.example: Take with or after food, because these tablets can irritate the stomach if taken alone.
PHARMACY.plain: take it during a meal or straight after eating

PHARMACY.definition: When the stomach has no food in it, usually before a meal.
PHARMACY.example: This thyroid tablet works best on an empty stomach, so take it before breakfast.
PHARMACY.plain: when you have not eaten for a while, usually before a meal

PHARMACY.definition: An instruction to keep taking a medicine for the full length prescribed.
PHARMACY.example: Please finish the course exactly as the prescriber advised, even if you feel better sooner.
PHARMACY.plain: keep taking it for as long as you were told

PHARMACY.term: do not take more than the label says
PHARMACY.definition: A plain safety warning about not going over the stated amount.
PHARMACY.example: Do not take more than the label says, even if the pain is bad; phone us instead.
PHARMACY.plain: never take extra doses

PHARMACY.definition: A feeling of sleepiness or heaviness that makes it hard to stay alert.
PHARMACY.example: This antihistamine can cause drowsiness, so take it in the evening if possible.
PHARMACY.plain: feeling sleepy

PHARMACY.definition: An instruction not to drink alcohol while taking a medicine.
PHARMACY.example: Please avoid alcohol while you take this antibiotic, as it can make you very unwell.
PHARMACY.plain: don't drink alcohol

PHARMACY.term: do not drive or operate machinery
PHARMACY.definition: A warning given when a medicine may affect alertness or coordination.
PHARMACY.example: If the tablets make you sleepy, do not drive or operate machinery until you know how they affect you.
PHARMACY.plain: don't drive or use dangerous equipment

PHARMACY.definition: A prescription for regular medicine that can be reordered without a new consultation each time.
PHARMACY.example: You can order your repeat prescription online, and we'll have it ready within a few days.
PHARMACY.plain: a regular prescription you can reorder

PHARMACY.definition: A device that organises medicines by day and time to help patients take them correctly.
PHARMACY.example: We could set up a compliance aid with compartments for each day, which may make things easier.
PHARMACY.plain: a pill organiser box marked with days and times

PHARMACY.definition: A way of asking a patient to explain instructions back to check understanding.
PHARMACY.example: Could you tell me in your own words how you'll take the new tablets each day?
PHARMACY.plain: explain it back to me your way

PHARMACY.term: I can see this is worrying you
PHARMACY.definition: An empathic phrase that recognises a patient's concern before giving information.
PHARMACY.example: I can see this is worrying you, so let's go through the possible side effects together.
PHARMACY.plain: I understand you are worried

PHARMACY.term: refer you back to your GP
PHARMACY.definition: To send a patient to their family doctor for further assessment.
PHARMACY.example: Your symptoms need a closer look, so I'm going to refer you back to your GP today.
PHARMACY.plain: ask your family doctor to see you again

PHARMACY.definition: An infection anywhere in the system that makes and carries urine, most often the bladder.
PHARMACY.example: A urinary tract infection often causes stinging when you pass urine and needing to go more often.
PHARMACY.plain: a water infection; a bladder infection

PHARMACY.definition: Ongoing difficulty falling asleep or staying asleep.
PHARMACY.example: Insomnia can be a side effect of this medicine, so try taking it earlier in the day.
PHARMACY.plain: trouble sleeping

PHARMACY.definition: A drop in blood pressure on standing up, causing dizziness or fainting.
PHARMACY.example: Postural hypotension is common with this tablet, so stand up slowly from a chair or bed.
PHARMACY.plain: feeling dizzy when you stand up

PHARMACY.definition: A sudden, severe allergic reaction affecting breathing or circulation that needs emergency treatment.
PHARMACY.example: If you show signs of anaphylaxis, such as swelling of the lips or difficulty breathing, call 999.
PHARMACY.plain: a severe allergic reaction that can be life-threatening

PHARMACY.term: please do not hesitate to contact me
PHARMACY.definition: A polite formal closing offering further help or information.
PHARMACY.example: If you need further details about his medicines, please do not hesitate to contact me at the pharmacy.
PHARMACY.plain: please get in touch with me if you need anything

DENTISTRY.definition: An area of a tooth damaged by decay, from early mineral loss to an open cavity.
DENTISTRY.example: Bitewing radiographs revealed a carious lesion between the two upper premolars.

DENTISTRY.definition: Loss of minerals from enamel or dentine caused by acid.
DENTISTRY.example: Chalky white spots near the gum line indicate early demineralisation from frequent sugary drinks.

DENTISTRY.definition: The return of minerals to weakened enamel, helped by saliva and fluoride.
DENTISTRY.example: With fluoride varnish and dietary change, early lesions may undergo remineralisation instead of needing fillings.

DENTISTRY.definition: The sticky layer of bacteria that builds up on tooth surfaces, also called plaque.
DENTISTRY.example: Disclosing tablets helped the child see where dental biofilm remained after brushing.

DENTISTRY.definition: Hard deposits on teeth formed when plaque absorbs minerals from saliva.
DENTISTRY.example: Heavy calculus on the lower front teeth was removed before the gum condition was reassessed.

DENTISTRY.definition: Loss of the fibres and bone that hold a tooth in its socket.
DENTISTRY.example: Charting showed attachment loss of several millimetres around the lower molars.

DENTISTRY.definition: A deepened space between gum and tooth caused by gum disease.
DENTISTRY.example: Each periodontal pocket deeper than expected was recorded on the six-point chart.

DENTISTRY.definition: A quick screening of gum health using a probe in each section of the mouth.
DENTISTRY.example: The basic periodontal examination scores suggested that a full periodontal chart was needed.

DENTISTRY.definition: Bleeding when a probe is gently passed along the gum, a sign of inflammation.
DENTISTRY.example: Bleeding on probing fell sharply after the patient began cleaning between her teeth daily.

DENTISTRY.definition: Bone loss reaching the area where the roots of a multi-rooted tooth divide.
DENTISTRY.example: Furcation involvement on the upper first molar makes its long-term prognosis uncertain.

DENTISTRY.definition: Movement of a tooth in its socket beyond what is normal.
DENTISTRY.example: Increased tooth mobility was noted in the lower incisors, consistent with advanced bone loss.

DENTISTRY.definition: A faulty relationship between the upper and lower teeth when they meet.
DENTISTRY.example: The orthodontic referral describes a severe malocclusion with a large overjet.

DENTISTRY.definition: The way the upper and lower teeth come together when the jaws close.
DENTISTRY.example: After the crown was fitted, the occlusion was checked with articulating paper.

DENTISTRY.definition: Pain or poor function of the jaw joint and the muscles used for chewing.
DENTISTRY.example: Clicking and morning jaw pain suggested a temporomandibular disorder linked to stress.

DENTISTRY.definition: Inflammation of the tooth's inner soft tissue that cannot heal on its own.
DENTISTRY.example: Lingering pain after cold suggested irreversible pulpitis, so root canal treatment was offered.

DENTISTRY.definition: Situated around the tip of a tooth root.
DENTISTRY.example: The radiograph showed a periapical area of bone loss at the lower left first molar.

DENTISTRY.definition: A dark area on an X-ray where less dense tissue lets radiation pass through.
DENTISTRY.example: A well-defined radiolucency at the root tip was consistent with chronic infection.

DENTISTRY.definition: Relating to treatment of the inside of a tooth, such as the root canals.
DENTISTRY.example: The referral requested specialist endodontic assessment because the canals were severely curved.

DENTISTRY.definition: Filling and sealing the cleaned root canal space.
DENTISTRY.example: A post-operative radiograph confirmed satisfactory obturation to the end of each canal.

DENTISTRY.definition: A filling, crown or other repair that replaces lost tooth structure.
DENTISTRY.example: The old restoration had a broken margin, allowing decay to develop underneath.

DENTISTRY.definition: A tooth-coloured filling material made from resin mixed with fine particles.
DENTISTRY.example: The chipped front tooth was repaired with composite matched to the natural shade.

DENTISTRY.definition: A silver-coloured filling material made by mixing mercury with other metals.
DENTISTRY.example: Use of amalgam has been reduced, especially in children and pregnant patients, under current regulations.

DENTISTRY.definition: A tooth or implant part that supports a bridge, crown or denture.
DENTISTRY.example: The canine was chosen as an abutment because of its long, stable root.

DENTISTRY.definition: The direct bonding of living bone to the surface of an implant.
DENTISTRY.example: Heavy smoking can delay osseointegration and increase the chance of implant failure.

DENTISTRY.definition: Inflammation around a dental implant with loss of the supporting bone.
DENTISTRY.example: Peri-implantitis was diagnosed after bleeding, pus and bone loss were found around the implant.

DENTISTRY.definition: The part of the jawbone that forms and supports the tooth sockets.
DENTISTRY.example: After several extractions, the alveolar bone had shrunk, complicating implant placement.

DENTISTRY.definition: Painful inflammation of a tooth socket after extraction when the blood clot is lost.
DENTISTRY.example: Alveolar osteitis was more likely because the patient smoked on the day of the extraction.

DENTISTRY.definition: The lower jawbone.
DENTISTRY.example: The panoramic radiograph showed an unerupted tooth lying deep within the mandible.

DENTISTRY.definition: The upper jawbone, which holds the upper teeth.
DENTISTRY.example: The upper molar roots lie very close to the sinus floor in the posterior maxilla.

DENTISTRY.definition: An injection of local anaesthetic that numbs one side of the lower jaw, lip and chin.
DENTISTRY.example: An inferior alveolar nerve block was given before the lower molar was prepared.

DENTISTRY.definition: Altered feeling such as tingling or numbness, sometimes following nerve injury.
DENTISTRY.example: Persistent paraesthesia of the lower lip was recorded after the wisdom tooth surgery.

DENTISTRY.definition: A substance added to some anaesthetics that narrows blood vessels to prolong numbness and reduce bleeding.
DENTISTRY.example: An anaesthetic without a vasoconstrictor was chosen after discussion with the patient's cardiologist.

DENTISTRY.definition: The stopping of bleeding, by the body itself or by clinical measures.
DENTISTRY.example: Haemostasis was achieved with sutures and pressure before the patient left the surgery.

DENTISTRY.definition: Death of jawbone linked to some bone-strengthening or cancer medicines, often after extraction.
DENTISTRY.example: Because she takes a bisphosphonate, the risk of medication-related osteonecrosis of the jaw was explained before extraction.

DENTISTRY.definition: The amount of saliva produced over a set time, measured when dry mouth is suspected.
DENTISTRY.example: A low salivary flow rate helped explain the patient's rapid new decay.

DENTISTRY.definition: A concentrated fluoride coating painted onto teeth to help prevent decay.
DENTISTRY.example: Fluoride varnish is applied twice a year for children assessed as being at higher risk.

DENTISTRY.definition: A thin protective coating placed in the grooves of back teeth to prevent decay.
DENTISTRY.example: A fissure sealant was placed on the newly erupted permanent molars.

DENTISTRY.definition: Loss of tooth surface caused by acids not made by bacteria, such as from drinks or reflux.
DENTISTRY.example: The pattern of erosion on the inner surfaces of the upper teeth suggested frequent reflux.

DENTISTRY.definition: Wear of the teeth caused by tooth-to-tooth contact.
DENTISTRY.example: Marked attrition of the canines was consistent with the night-time grinding his partner described.

DENTISTRY.definition: Wear of teeth caused by external objects, such as overly hard brushing.
DENTISTRY.example: Notches at the gum line were attributed to abrasion from a hard toothbrush.

DENTISTRY.definition: A developmental defect in which enamel forms with too little mineral, leaving it soft and discoloured.
DENTISTRY.example: Molar hypomineralisation made the child's back teeth sensitive and prone to rapid breakdown.

DENTISTRY.definition: Short, sharp pain from exposed dentine reacting to cold, heat, sweetness or touch.
DENTISTRY.example: Gum recession had exposed root surfaces, causing dentine hypersensitivity to cold drinks.

DENTISTRY.definition: The cause or set of causes of a disease or condition.
DENTISTRY.example: The aetiology of the tooth wear appears to combine acidic diet and grinding.

DENTISTRY.definition: The likely course and outcome of a condition or treatment.
DENTISTRY.example: The prognosis for the cracked molar is poor, so extraction was discussed as an option.

DENTISTRY.definition: Next to or beside something.
DENTISTRY.example: Decay had spread from the filling to the adjacent tooth surface.

DENTISTRY.definition: Injection of local anaesthetic into the tissue close to a tooth to numb it.
DENTISTRY.example: Buccal infiltration provided enough numbness to restore the upper premolar.

DENTISTRY.definition: The spread of infection between patients, staff or equipment.
DENTISTRY.example: Strict cross-infection control includes changing gloves and cleaning surfaces between every patient.

DENTISTRY.definition: The process of cleaning and sterilising instruments so they are safe to reuse.
DENTISTRY.example: Each instrument tray is tracked through decontamination before it returns to the surgery.

DENTISTRY.definition: A treatment that produces fine airborne droplets, such as using a high-speed drill.
DENTISTRY.example: During outbreaks, extra protective equipment is required for any aerosol-generating procedure.

DENTISTRY.definition: Fear of dental treatment that may lead people to avoid care.
DENTISTRY.example: Severe dental anxiety had kept the patient away for years until the pain became unbearable.

DENTISTRY.definition: Use of medicines to relax a patient who remains awake and able to respond.
DENTISTRY.example: Conscious sedation was offered so the anxious patient could have the extractions in one visit.

DENTISTRY.definition: A white patch in the mouth that cannot be wiped off and may become cancerous.
DENTISTRY.example: The leukoplakia on the floor of the mouth was biopsied because of the patient's smoking history.

DENTISTRY.definition: The formation of sores or breaks in the lining of the mouth.
DENTISTRY.example: Any ulceration lasting longer than three weeks without a clear cause should be urgently referred.

DENTISTRY.definition: Relating to the correction of the position of teeth and jaws.
DENTISTRY.example: Orthodontic treatment was postponed until the patient's gum health had improved.

DENTISTRY.definition: Describes a tooth that is blocked from coming through fully, often a wisdom tooth.
DENTISTRY.example: The impacted lower wisdom tooth was pressing against the root of the molar in front.

DENTISTRY.definition: The process of a tooth coming through the gum into the mouth.
DENTISTRY.example: Delayed eruption of the upper canine prompted an X-ray to check its position.

DENTISTRY.definition: The first set of teeth, which are later replaced by permanent teeth.
DENTISTRY.example: Decay in the primary dentition still needs treatment, as it can cause pain and infection.

DENTISTRY.definition: Having no natural teeth.
DENTISTRY.example: The edentulous patient reported that his lower denture moved when he ate.

DENTISTRY.definition: An artificial replacement for a missing body part, such as teeth.
DENTISTRY.example: A removable prosthesis was planned to replace the three missing upper teeth.

DENTISTRY.definition: Infection of the inner lining of the heart, a rare risk after some dental procedures in vulnerable patients.
DENTISTRY.example: Routine antibiotic cover is not advised, but his risk of infective endocarditis was discussed with his cardiologist.

DENTISTRY.definition: Long-term gum infection that damages the bone and tissues holding the teeth.
DENTISTRY.example: Periodontitis, which is a form of gum disease, can make teeth loose if it is not treated.
DENTISTRY.plain: gum disease that can loosen teeth

DENTISTRY.definition: Inflammation of the gums, usually caused by plaque, which can be reversed.
DENTISTRY.example: The bleeding when you brush is gingivitis, and better cleaning should settle it within weeks.
DENTISTRY.plain: red, swollen or bleeding gums

DENTISTRY.definition: Decay of tooth tissue caused by acid from bacteria feeding on sugars.
DENTISTRY.example: These caries are at an early stage, so we may be able to stop them without fillings.
DENTISTRY.plain: tooth decay

DENTISTRY.definition: Habitual grinding or clenching of the teeth, often during sleep.
DENTISTRY.example: The worn edges suggest bruxism, which is common when people are stressed.
DENTISTRY.plain: teeth grinding or clenching

DENTISTRY.definition: Dryness of the mouth, usually from reduced saliva.
DENTISTRY.example: Your blood pressure tablets may be causing xerostomia, so sip water and chew sugar-free gum.
DENTISTRY.plain: a dry mouth

DENTISTRY.definition: The removal of a tooth.
DENTISTRY.example: If the tooth cannot be saved, an extraction under local anaesthetic is the other option.
DENTISTRY.plain: having a tooth taken out

DENTISTRY.definition: A professional clean to remove hard deposits and stains from teeth.
DENTISTRY.example: A scale and polish today will remove the tartar your toothbrush can't reach.
DENTISTRY.plain: a professional clean of your teeth

DENTISTRY.definition: Removing infected or damaged pulp from inside a tooth and sealing the space.
DENTISTRY.example: Root canal treatment can usually save the tooth and stop the pain.
DENTISTRY.plain: cleaning out the infected nerve inside the tooth and sealing it

DENTISTRY.definition: A collection of pus caused by a bacterial infection in or around a tooth.
DENTISTRY.example: The swelling is a dental abscess, and draining it will relieve the pressure.
DENTISTRY.plain: a painful pocket of infection near a tooth

DENTISTRY.definition: Persistent unpleasant breath odour.
DENTISTRY.example: Most halitosis comes from bacteria on the tongue and between the teeth, so cleaning these helps.
DENTISTRY.plain: bad breath

DENTISTRY.definition: A medicine injected to numb one area so treatment can be done without pain.
DENTISTRY.example: I'll give you a local anaesthetic first, so you'll feel a small scratch and then numbness.
DENTISTRY.plain: an injection to numb the area

DENTISTRY.definition: An image of teeth or bone made using X-rays.
DENTISTRY.example: I'd like to take a radiograph to see the root of this tooth.
DENTISTRY.plain: an X-ray

DENTISTRY.definition: A removable plate holding artificial teeth.
DENTISTRY.example: Take your denture out at night and clean it with a soft brush.
DENTISTRY.plain: false teeth

DENTISTRY.definition: Teeth that give short, sharp pain with cold, heat or sweet foods.
DENTISTRY.example: Using a toothpaste for sensitive teeth twice a day often reduces the twinges within weeks.
DENTISTRY.plain: teeth that hurt with hot, cold or sweet things

DENTISTRY.definition: Cleaning the spaces between teeth with floss or small brushes.
DENTISTRY.example: Daily interdental cleaning is the best way to stop your gums bleeding.
DENTISTRY.plain: cleaning between your teeth with floss or small brushes

DENTISTRY.definition: A painful tooth socket where the healing blood clot has been lost after an extraction.
DENTISTRY.example: Smoking in the first few days increases the chance of a dry socket, so please avoid it.
DENTISTRY.plain: a painful hole where the healing clot has come away

DENTISTRY.definition: Advice to leave toothpaste fluoride on the teeth after brushing.
DENTISTRY.example: After brushing, remember to spit, don't rinse, so the fluoride keeps protecting your teeth.
DENTISTRY.plain: spit out the toothpaste but don't wash it away with water

DENTISTRY.definition: A reassuring phrase warning that pushing is felt even when the area is numb.
DENTISTRY.example: You may feel some pressure as I loosen the tooth, but it shouldn't be sharp or painful.
DENTISTRY.plain: you might feel pushing, but not pain

DENTISTRY.term: raise your hand if you want me to stop
DENTISTRY.definition: A phrase agreeing a stop signal so the patient feels in control.
DENTISTRY.example: Raise your hand if you want me to stop at any point, and I'll pause straight away.
DENTISTRY.plain: lift your hand and I will stop

DENTISTRY.definition: To fade gradually, as numbness does after an anaesthetic.
DENTISTRY.example: The numbness should wear off in about two to three hours.
DENTISTRY.plain: go away slowly

DENTISTRY.term: avoid hot drinks until the numbness has gone
DENTISTRY.definition: Aftercare advice to prevent burns or bites while the mouth is still numb.
DENTISTRY.example: Please avoid hot drinks until the numbness has gone, as you could burn your mouth without noticing.
DENTISTRY.plain: don't have hot drinks while your mouth is still numb

DENTISTRY.definition: How often sugary foods or drinks are consumed, a key cause of decay.
DENTISTRY.example: Reducing the frequency of sugar intake matters more than the total amount, so keep sweets to mealtimes.
DENTISTRY.plain: how often you have sugary food and drinks

DENTISTRY.definition: A formal opening for a referral letter to another clinician.
DENTISTRY.example: I am writing to refer Mr Okafor for assessment of a non-healing ulcer on the side of his tongue.
DENTISTRY.plain: this letter asks you to see this patient

DENTISTRY.term: I would appreciate your opinion on
DENTISTRY.definition: A polite formal request for a specialist's advice in a letter.
DENTISTRY.example: I would appreciate your opinion on whether the upper molar can be saved with endodontic treatment.
DENTISTRY.plain: please tell me what you think about

DENTISTRY.definition: A phrase used in notes and letters to introduce what the clinician found.
DENTISTRY.example: On examination, there was a firm swelling over the lower left molar region.
DENTISTRY.plain: when I checked

DENTISTRY.definition: Painful when touched or pressed.
DENTISTRY.example: The tooth is tender when I tap it, which suggests the infection has reached the root.
DENTISTRY.plain: sore when touched or pressed

DENTISTRY.definition: Restricted mouth opening, often from muscle spasm or infection.
DENTISTRY.example: The letter notes trismus after the wisdom tooth removal, which should ease with gentle exercises.
DENTISTRY.plain: difficulty opening your mouth fully

DENTISTRY.definition: Difficulty swallowing.
DENTISTRY.example: Because the swelling is causing dysphagia, you need to be seen at the hospital today.
DENTISTRY.plain: difficulty swallowing

DENTISTRY.definition: A rinse that reduces bacteria in the mouth for a short period.
DENTISTRY.example: Use the antiseptic mouthwash for a week, but long-term use can stain the teeth.
DENTISTRY.plain: a germ-killing mouth rinse

DENTISTRY.definition: A prescription toothpaste with more fluoride than standard types, for people at high risk of decay.
DENTISTRY.example: I'm prescribing a high-fluoride toothpaste to protect the exposed roots of your teeth.
DENTISTRY.plain: a stronger toothpaste that protects against decay

DENTISTRY.definition: An artificial root, usually titanium, placed in the jaw to support a replacement tooth.
DENTISTRY.example: A dental implant could replace the missing tooth without filing down the teeth beside it.
DENTISTRY.plain: an artificial tooth root fixed into the jaw

DENTISTRY.definition: A cap made to cover and strengthen a damaged tooth.
DENTISTRY.example: After root canal treatment, a crown will protect the tooth from cracking.
DENTISTRY.plain: a cap that covers and protects a damaged tooth

DENTISTRY.definition: A fixed false tooth attached to the natural teeth on one or both sides of a gap.
DENTISTRY.example: A bridge would fill the gap, but the neighbouring teeth would need some preparation.
DENTISTRY.plain: a fixed false tooth held by the teeth beside it

DENTISTRY.definition: A thin, tooth-coloured layer bonded to the front of a tooth to improve its appearance.
DENTISTRY.example: A veneer can cover the stained front tooth, but some enamel usually has to be removed.
DENTISTRY.plain: a thin tooth-coloured cover for the front of a tooth

DENTISTRY.definition: A fixed or removable device used to move teeth into a better position.
DENTISTRY.example: Your orthodontic appliance needs careful cleaning, especially around the wires.
DENTISTRY.plain: a brace

DENTISTRY.definition: The last tooth at the back of each side of each jaw.
DENTISTRY.example: Your lower third molar is only partly through the gum, which is why food gets trapped.
DENTISTRY.plain: a wisdom tooth

DENTISTRY.definition: A hard plastic guard worn over the teeth, usually at night, to reduce grinding damage.
DENTISTRY.example: An occlusal splint worn at night should protect your teeth and may ease the jaw ache.
DENTISTRY.plain: a mouthguard worn at night

DENTISTRY.definition: A short-term filling placed until permanent treatment can be done.
DENTISTRY.example: The temporary filling may wear down, so avoid chewing on that side until your next visit.
DENTISTRY.plain: a short-term filling until the permanent one is done

DENTISTRY.term: is there anything worrying you about the treatment
DENTISTRY.definition: An open question inviting the patient to share concerns before consent.
DENTISTRY.example: Before we start, is there anything worrying you about the treatment that you'd like to ask?
DENTISTRY.plain: do you have any worries you want to talk about?

DENTISTRY.definition: A later visit to check healing or the results of treatment.
DENTISTRY.example: I'll book a follow-up appointment in two weeks to check how the gum is healing.
DENTISTRY.plain: a return visit to check how things are healing

PHYSIOTHERAPY.definition: How far a joint can move in each direction, usually measured in degrees.
PHYSIOTHERAPY.example: Active range of motion at the left shoulder was limited to 90 degrees of flexion because of pain.

PHYSIOTHERAPY.definition: The body's sense of where its joints and limbs are without looking at them.
PHYSIOTHERAPY.example: After the ankle sprain, poor proprioception made single-leg standing unsteady, so balance board work was added.

PHYSIOTHERAPY.definition: A structured observation or measurement of how a person walks.
PHYSIOTHERAPY.example: Gait analysis showed a shortened step on the right and reduced push-off through the forefoot.

PHYSIOTHERAPY.definition: An instruction allowing the patient to put as much weight through a limb as comfort permits.
PHYSIOTHERAPY.example: The orthopaedic team documented weight-bearing as tolerated following fixation of the tibial plateau fracture.

PHYSIOTHERAPY.definition: Lasting shortening of muscle or soft tissue that stops a joint moving fully.
PHYSIOTHERAPY.example: Daily positioning and stretching aim to prevent a knee flexion contracture in this bed-bound patient.

PHYSIOTHERAPY.definition: Increased muscle tone that resists movement more strongly the faster the limb is moved.
PHYSIOTHERAPY.example: Spasticity in the right elbow flexors has increased since the stroke, making dressing harder for her.

PHYSIOTHERAPY.definition: Joints moving further than the usual range, sometimes linked with pain or instability.
PHYSIOTHERAPY.example: Generalised hypermobility may explain her recurrent patellar subluxations, so strengthening is prioritised over stretching.

PHYSIOTHERAPY.definition: Relating to how nerves and muscles work together to produce movement.
PHYSIOTHERAPY.example: Neuromuscular control of the knee was poor during landing, with the joint collapsing inwards.

PHYSIOTHERAPY.definition: An excessive fear of movement because the person expects it to cause pain or injury.
PHYSIOTHERAPY.example: High kinesiophobia scores suggested his avoidance of bending was driven by fear rather than tissue damage.

PHYSIOTHERAPY.definition: Gradually reintroducing feared activities in planned steps to rebuild confidence.
PHYSIOTHERAPY.example: Graded exposure began with lifting an empty box and progressed towards loading the dishwasher.

PHYSIOTHERAPY.definition: Exercise where a muscle works while lengthening under load, often used for tendon problems.
PHYSIOTHERAPY.example: The trial compared eccentric loading with heavy slow resistance for runners with Achilles pain.

PHYSIOTHERAPY.definition: A painful tendon condition linked with overload, with reduced tolerance to activity.
PHYSIOTHERAPY.example: Patellar tendinopathy is common in jumping sports and usually responds to progressive loading over months.

PHYSIOTHERAPY.definition: Relating to muscles, bones, joints, tendons and ligaments together.
PHYSIOTHERAPY.example: Musculoskeletal conditions account for a large share of primary care consultations and sickness absence.

PHYSIOTHERAPY.definition: Symptoms such as pain, numbness or weakness caused by an irritated or compressed nerve root.
PHYSIOTHERAPY.example: L5 radiculopathy was suspected because of pain into the dorsum of the foot and weak big-toe extension.

PHYSIOTHERAPY.definition: Abnormal skin sensations such as tingling or pins and needles.
PHYSIOTHERAPY.example: She reported intermittent paraesthesia in the thumb and index finger, worse at night.

PHYSIOTHERAPY.definition: Techniques that help move secretions out of the lungs.
PHYSIOTHERAPY.example: Airway clearance was taught twice daily using the active cycle of breathing techniques.

PHYSIOTHERAPY.definition: Using a simple device that encourages slow, deep breaths to expand the lungs, often after surgery.
PHYSIOTHERAPY.example: Incentive spirometry was encouraged hourly after the laparotomy to reduce the risk of chest complications.

PHYSIOTHERAPY.definition: Neck and shoulder muscles that assist breathing when the work of breathing is high.
PHYSIOTHERAPY.example: On review he was using his accessory muscles, with a respiratory rate of 28.

PHYSIOTHERAPY.definition: Partial collapse of lung tissue so that part of the lung holds less air.
PHYSIOTHERAPY.example: Basal atelectasis on the chest film was treated with sitting out, deep breathing and early walking.

PHYSIOTHERAPY.definition: Positioning the body so gravity helps secretions drain from particular areas of the lungs.
PHYSIOTHERAPY.example: Postural drainage was modified because head-down tilt was poorly tolerated with his reflux.

PHYSIOTHERAPY.definition: The ability to carry out daily activities such as washing, dressing and walking without help.
PHYSIOTHERAPY.example: The main rehabilitation aim is functional independence at home before she returns to living alone.

PHYSIOTHERAPY.definition: A standard test or questionnaire used to track change in a patient over time.
PHYSIOTHERAPY.example: A timed walk test was chosen as the primary outcome measure for the pulmonary rehabilitation course.

PHYSIOTHERAPY.definition: Hands-on treatment of joints and soft tissues by a clinician.
PHYSIOTHERAPY.example: Manual therapy alone gave short-term relief, so it was combined with an active exercise programme.

PHYSIOTHERAPY.definition: Passive, controlled movements applied to a joint to reduce pain or stiffness.
PHYSIOTHERAPY.example: Grade III joint mobilisation of the glenohumeral joint was used to improve external rotation.

PHYSIOTHERAPY.definition: Muscles, tendons, ligaments and other non-bony body tissues.
PHYSIOTHERAPY.example: The scan excluded a fracture, suggesting a soft tissue injury to the lateral ankle ligaments.

PHYSIOTHERAPY.definition: Describing a muscle contraction that produces force without the joint moving.
PHYSIOTHERAPY.example: Isometric quadriceps holds were started on day one, as knee bending was still too painful.

PHYSIOTHERAPY.definition: Nearer to the centre of the body or to where a limb attaches.
PHYSIOTHERAPY.example: Proximal hip weakness may be contributing to his knee pain during stair descent.

PHYSIOTHERAPY.definition: Further from the centre of the body or from where a limb attaches.
PHYSIOTHERAPY.example: Sensation was reduced distally, with numbness worst in the toes of both feet.

PHYSIOTHERAPY.definition: Looseness of ligaments that allows more joint movement than expected.
PHYSIOTHERAPY.example: Ligamentous laxity was noted on anterior drawer testing compared with the uninjured ankle.

PHYSIOTHERAPY.definition: How likely a person is to fall, judged from factors such as balance, medicines and history.
PHYSIOTHERAPY.example: Her falls risk is high given two falls this year, postural dizziness and poor vision.

PHYSIOTHERAPY.definition: The movement of rising from a seated position, often timed or counted as a test.
PHYSIOTHERAPY.example: He managed five sit-to-stand repetitions in 19 seconds, using his arms on the second attempt.

PHYSIOTHERAPY.definition: An external device such as a splint or brace that supports or controls a body part.
PHYSIOTHERAPY.example: An ankle-foot orthosis was supplied to reduce foot drop and improve toe clearance when walking.

PHYSIOTHERAPY.definition: The layer of muscles at the base of the pelvis supporting the bladder, bowel and womb.
PHYSIOTHERAPY.example: Supervised pelvic floor training is first-line treatment for stress urinary incontinence in women.

PHYSIOTHERAPY.definition: Exercise-based treatment for dizziness and imbalance caused by inner-ear problems.
PHYSIOTHERAPY.example: Vestibular rehabilitation, including gaze stability exercises, was offered for her persistent dizziness after labyrinthitis.

PHYSIOTHERAPY.definition: The nervous system's ability to reorganise itself in response to practice and experience.
PHYSIOTHERAPY.example: Intensive task practice after stroke is thought to work partly through neuroplasticity.

PHYSIOTHERAPY.definition: Increased sensitivity of the nervous system so that pain is felt more easily and more widely.
PHYSIOTHERAPY.example: Widespread tenderness and pain out of proportion to findings raised the possibility of central sensitisation.

PHYSIOTHERAPY.definition: Signs or symptoms that may indicate serious disease and need urgent medical review.
PHYSIOTHERAPY.example: Red flags such as saddle numbness or new bladder problems were screened for and were absent.

PHYSIOTHERAPY.definition: The expected course and likely outcome of a condition.
PHYSIOTHERAPY.example: The prognosis for return to running is good, although full recovery may take several months.

PHYSIOTHERAPY.definition: A structured process of gathering information to understand a patient's problem and needs.
PHYSIOTHERAPY.example: The initial assessment included a subjective history, observation of posture and strength testing.

PHYSIOTHERAPY.definition: A treatment or action taken to change a patient's condition or outcome.
PHYSIOTHERAPY.example: No single intervention was superior; exercise, education and pacing were all moderately effective.

PHYSIOTHERAPY.definition: To use other movements or body parts to make up for weakness or pain.
PHYSIOTHERAPY.example: She compensates for weak hip abductors by leaning her trunk over the stance leg.

PHYSIOTHERAPY.definition: To limit an amount, activity or movement.
PHYSIOTHERAPY.example: Pain continues to restrict his overhead reaching, so work duties have been adjusted.

PHYSIOTHERAPY.definition: To keep something going over time; also, to suffer an injury.
PHYSIOTHERAPY.example: He sustained a hamstring strain while sprinting and could not sustain jogging for more than two minutes.

PHYSIOTHERAPY.definition: To change something slightly to make it more suitable.
PHYSIOTHERAPY.example: The squat was modified to a partial depth because of patellofemoral pain.

PHYSIOTHERAPY.definition: The length of time something lasts.
PHYSIOTHERAPY.example: Symptom duration of more than twelve weeks was the cut-off for inclusion in the chronic pain study.

PHYSIOTHERAPY.definition: How hard or strong an activity, or a symptom, is.
PHYSIOTHERAPY.example: Exercise intensity was set at a level where she was slightly breathless but could still talk.

PHYSIOTHERAPY.definition: Next to or very near something else.
PHYSIOTHERAPY.example: Stiffness at adjacent spinal levels may increase load on the segment above a fusion.

PHYSIOTHERAPY.definition: To reduce or block a process or activity.
PHYSIOTHERAPY.example: Knee swelling can inhibit quadriceps activation, so effusion is managed before strengthening is progressed.

PHYSIOTHERAPY.definition: Happening after something else.
PHYSIOTHERAPY.example: Subsequent sessions focused on returning to stairs and outdoor walking.

PHYSIOTHERAPY.definition: To make an action or process easier.
PHYSIOTHERAPY.example: A raised chair was provided to facilitate safe transfers after the hip replacement.

PHYSIOTHERAPY.definition: Continuing for a long time or longer than expected.
PHYSIOTHERAPY.example: Persistent low back pain was managed with a combined physical and psychological approach.

PHYSIOTHERAPY.definition: Present but not obvious, and often the real cause of a problem.
PHYSIOTHERAPY.example: Repeated ankle sprains may reflect underlying balance deficits rather than bad luck.

PHYSIOTHERAPY.definition: To become or make smaller or less.
PHYSIOTHERAPY.example: Morning stiffness diminished over six weeks as her daily walking increased.

PHYSIOTHERAPY.definition: The state of being whole, intact and structurally sound.
PHYSIOTHERAPY.example: Skin integrity over the heels was checked at each visit because of reduced sensation.

PHYSIOTHERAPY.definition: Existing or happening at the same time.
PHYSIOTHERAPY.example: Concurrent heart failure limited how quickly his exercise programme could be progressed.

PHYSIOTHERAPY.definition: Stiff and not easily bent; also strict and inflexible.
PHYSIOTHERAPY.example: A rigid flatfoot that does not change on tiptoe needs a different approach from a flexible one.

PHYSIOTHERAPY.definition: Loss of fitness, strength and stamina caused by inactivity or prolonged bed rest.
PHYSIOTHERAPY.example: After three weeks in intensive care, marked deconditioning meant she needed two people to stand.

PHYSIOTHERAPY.definition: Involving professionals from several different health disciplines working together.
PHYSIOTHERAPY.example: The multidisciplinary team agreed a discharge date once stairs and kitchen tasks were safe.

PHYSIOTHERAPY.definition: Exercise treatment carried out in a warm pool, using water for support and resistance.
PHYSIOTHERAPY.example: Hydrotherapy allowed him to practise walking with less load through his painful knees.

PHYSIOTHERAPY.definition: To judge carefully how well something works or how effective it is.
PHYSIOTHERAPY.example: The trial evaluated whether early walking after knee replacement shortened hospital stay.

PHYSIOTHERAPY.definition: Relating to the lower part of the back, between the ribs and the pelvis.
PHYSIOTHERAPY.example: Your lumbar spine, the lower part of your back, is stiff but the scan shows nothing serious.

PHYSIOTHERAPY.definition: A standard opening for a referral letter that states its purpose at once.
PHYSIOTHERAPY.example: I am writing to refer Mr Patel, a 64-year-old retired builder, for further management of his right shoulder pain.
PHYSIOTHERAPY.plain: I'm asking another health worker to see you and help.

PHYSIOTHERAPY.term: I would be grateful if you could
PHYSIOTHERAPY.definition: A polite, formal way of making a request in a professional letter.
PHYSIOTHERAPY.example: I would be grateful if you could review her pain medication, as night pain is limiting her sleep.

PHYSIOTHERAPY.term: please do not hesitate to contact me
PHYSIOTHERAPY.definition: A formal closing that invites the reader to get in touch with questions.
PHYSIOTHERAPY.example: Should you require any further information, please do not hesitate to contact me at the outpatient department.
PHYSIOTHERAPY.plain: Please get in touch if you have questions.

PHYSIOTHERAPY.definition: A clear way to report improvement in a letter or handover.
PHYSIOTHERAPY.example: Mrs Lee has made good progress and can now climb a full flight of stairs with one rail.

PHYSIOTHERAPY.definition: Able to walk and move around without help from another person.
PHYSIOTHERAPY.example: He is now independently mobile indoors with a walking stick and is ready for discharge.
PHYSIOTHERAPY.plain: Able to walk around on your own.

PHYSIOTHERAPY.definition: A set of exercises the patient carries out between appointments.
PHYSIOTHERAPY.example: I've written your home exercise programme on this sheet; try to do it once a day.

PHYSIOTHERAPY.definition: A later appointment to check how the patient is doing.
PHYSIOTHERAPY.example: We'll book a follow-up appointment in two weeks to see how your knee is responding.
PHYSIOTHERAPY.plain: Another visit to check how you are.

PHYSIOTHERAPY.term: on a scale of nought to ten
PHYSIOTHERAPY.definition: A spoken phrase used to ask a patient to rate pain or another symptom.
PHYSIOTHERAPY.example: On a scale of nought to ten, where ten is the worst pain imaginable, how bad is it today?
PHYSIOTHERAPY.plain: Give your pain a number from 0 to 10.

PHYSIOTHERAPY.definition: A polite spoken request asking the patient to demonstrate a movement or point to a symptom.
PHYSIOTHERAPY.example: Could you show me exactly where the pain starts when you lift your arm?

PHYSIOTHERAPY.definition: An informal but polite way to ask a patient to report something.
PHYSIOTHERAPY.example: Please let me know straight away if this stretch causes any sharp pain.

PHYSIOTHERAPY.definition: Affecting both sides of the body.
PHYSIOTHERAPY.example: She has bilateral knee pain, slightly worse on the left side.

PHYSIOTHERAPY.definition: At or towards the front of the body.
PHYSIOTHERAPY.example: The anterior aspect of the knee was tender, so I explained the pain is at the front.

PHYSIOTHERAPY.definition: At or towards the back of the body.
PHYSIOTHERAPY.example: Posterior thigh pain on bending suggests the hamstring, which runs down the back of the leg.

PHYSIOTHERAPY.definition: Further from the middle line of the body; on the outer side.
PHYSIOTHERAPY.example: The lateral ankle ligaments are the ones on the outside, which is where you rolled it.

PHYSIOTHERAPY.definition: Bending a joint so that the angle between the parts becomes smaller.
PHYSIOTHERAPY.example: Knee flexion has reached 100 degrees, which means you can bend it far enough for most chairs.

PHYSIOTHERAPY.definition: Straightening a joint so that the angle between the parts becomes larger.
PHYSIOTHERAPY.example: Full knee extension is important, so let's work on getting the leg completely straight.

PHYSIOTHERAPY.definition: Moving a limb away from the middle line of the body.
PHYSIOTHERAPY.example: Shoulder abduction is painful above 80 degrees, so lifting your arm out sideways hurts halfway up.
PHYSIOTHERAPY.plain: Moving your arm or leg out to the side.

PHYSIOTHERAPY.definition: Swelling caused by fluid collecting in the body's tissues.
PHYSIOTHERAPY.example: There is still some oedema around the ankle, so keep it raised when you sit down.

PHYSIOTHERAPY.definition: The body's response to injury, causing heat, redness, swelling and pain.
PHYSIOTHERAPY.example: The inflammation should settle over the next few days if you avoid overloading the tendon.
PHYSIOTHERAPY.plain: Heat, swelling and soreness while the body heals.

PHYSIOTHERAPY.definition: To get a patient moving, especially walking, or to move a stiff joint.
PHYSIOTHERAPY.example: We would like you to mobilise to the bathroom with the frame this afternoon.

PHYSIOTHERAPY.definition: To walk, used mainly in clinical notes.
PHYSIOTHERAPY.example: The patient ambulated 30 metres with a frame and the supervision of one person.

PHYSIOTHERAPY.definition: Equipment such as a stick, crutches or a frame that helps a person walk safely.
PHYSIOTHERAPY.example: For now, please use your walking aid whenever you go outside, especially on uneven ground.
PHYSIOTHERAPY.plain: A stick, crutches or frame to help you walk.

PHYSIOTHERAPY.definition: Moving from one surface to another, for example from bed to chair.
PHYSIOTHERAPY.example: Her bed-to-chair transfer is now safe with one person standing by.
PHYSIOTHERAPY.plain: Moving from your bed to a chair, or similar.

PHYSIOTHERAPY.definition: Lying flat on the front, face down.
PHYSIOTHERAPY.example: This next exercise is done prone, so could you lie on your front for me, please?

PHYSIOTHERAPY.definition: Lying flat on the back, face up.
PHYSIOTHERAPY.example: Start in supine, lying on your back with your knees bent and feet flat.

PHYSIOTHERAPY.definition: A period when a long-term condition or its symptoms suddenly get worse.
PHYSIOTHERAPY.example: If you have an exacerbation of your back pain, reduce the exercises rather than stopping completely.
PHYSIOTHERAPY.plain: A flare-up, when it suddenly gets worse.

PHYSIOTHERAPY.definition: Starting suddenly and recently, often with severe symptoms.
PHYSIOTHERAPY.example: In the acute stage of the sprain, gentle movement and elevation are most helpful.

PHYSIOTHERAPY.definition: Lasting a long time, usually more than three months.
PHYSIOTHERAPY.example: Chronic neck pain often improves with regular exercise, even if it does not fully disappear.

PHYSIOTHERAPY.definition: Difficult or uncomfortable breathing; shortness of breath.
PHYSIOTHERAPY.example: Dyspnoea limited her to walking 50 metres, so we will practise breathing control together.

PHYSIOTHERAPY.definition: Extreme tiredness that does not fully go away with rest.
PHYSIOTHERAPY.example: Fatigue is common after chemotherapy, and gentle exercise can actually help you feel less tired.

PHYSIOTHERAPY.definition: Spreading activity evenly and taking planned rests to avoid boom-and-bust cycles.
PHYSIOTHERAPY.example: Pacing means doing a little every day rather than a lot on good days and nothing on bad ones.
PHYSIOTHERAPY.plain: Spreading out your activity with rests.

PHYSIOTHERAPY.definition: Showing or causing symptoms.
PHYSIOTHERAPY.example: The disc bulge on the scan may not be symptomatic, as many people without pain have one.

PHYSIOTHERAPY.definition: Not advisable because it could cause harm in this patient's situation.
PHYSIOTHERAPY.example: Heat is contraindicated over the area because of your reduced skin sensation.

PHYSIOTHERAPY.definition: How closely a patient follows an agreed treatment or exercise plan.
PHYSIOTHERAPY.example: Adherence to the exercises has been good, and his strength has improved as a result.

PHYSIOTHERAPY.definition: To make exercises gradually harder as the patient becomes stronger.
PHYSIOTHERAPY.example: If this feels easy by next week, we'll progress your exercises by adding a light weight.
PHYSIOTHERAPY.plain: Make your exercises a bit harder.

PHYSIOTHERAPY.definition: To formally end a hospital stay or a course of treatment.
PHYSIOTHERAPY.example: We plan to discharge you from physiotherapy once you can walk to the shops comfortably.
PHYSIOTHERAPY.plain: Finish your treatment or let you go home.

PHYSIOTHERAPY.definition: A break or crack in a bone.
PHYSIOTHERAPY.example: The fracture in your wrist has healed, so now we need to work on stiffness and grip.

PHYSIOTHERAPY.definition: The position in which a person holds their body when sitting or standing.
PHYSIOTHERAPY.example: No single posture is perfect; changing position often matters more at your desk.

PHYSIOTHERAPY.definition: Control and strength of the trunk muscles that support the spine during movement.
PHYSIOTHERAPY.example: These exercises build core stability, which helps support your back when you lift.
PHYSIOTHERAPY.plain: Strength in your tummy and back muscles.

DIETETICS.definition: A state where intake of energy or nutrients is too low, too high or unbalanced for the body's needs.
DIETETICS.example: Malnutrition is often missed in older inpatients, so screening is completed within 24 hours of admission.

DIETETICS.definition: Age-related loss of muscle mass and strength that affects function.
DIETETICS.example: Sarcopenia was suspected because of slow walking speed and weak grip, despite a normal body weight.

DIETETICS.definition: Severe wasting of muscle and fat driven by illness such as cancer, not fully reversed by feeding.
DIETETICS.example: Cancer cachexia limited how much weight she could regain, so goals focused on comfort and function.

DIETETICS.definition: Dangerous shifts in fluids and electrolytes that can occur when a starved person starts eating again.
DIETETICS.example: Because intake had been minimal for ten days, he was judged at high risk of refeeding syndrome.

DIETETICS.definition: Feeding that uses the gut, usually through a tube when eating by mouth is not enough.
