DIETETICS.example: Enteral nutrition was started on day two of intensive care once the patient was haemodynamically stable.

DIETETICS.definition: Nutrition given directly into a vein when the gut cannot be used.
DIETETICS.example: Parenteral nutrition was considered only after the gut had failed to absorb feed for over a week.

DIETETICS.definition: Passing through the nose into the stomach, describing a type of feeding tube.
DIETETICS.example: Tube position must be confirmed before any feed is given through a nasogastric tube.

DIETETICS.definition: A ranking of carbohydrate foods by how quickly they raise blood glucose.
DIETETICS.example: Swapping to foods with a lower glycaemic index helped smooth her after-meal glucose readings.

DIETETICS.definition: How well blood glucose levels are kept within a target range over time.
DIETETICS.example: Glycaemic control has improved since he reduced sugary drinks and started regular meals.

DIETETICS.definition: A state in which the body's cells respond poorly to insulin, so glucose stays higher.
DIETETICS.example: Central weight gain and insulin resistance are closely linked in polycystic ovary syndrome.

DIETETICS.definition: Abnormal levels of fats such as cholesterol or triglycerides in the blood.
DIETETICS.example: Dietary management of dyslipidaemia focused on reducing saturated fat and increasing soluble fibre.

DIETETICS.definition: A vitamin or mineral needed by the body in small amounts.
DIETETICS.example: Micronutrient status should be checked after bariatric surgery, as absorption of several nutrients falls.

DIETETICS.definition: A nutrient needed in large amounts: carbohydrate, protein or fat.
DIETETICS.example: The macronutrient balance of the plan was adjusted to provide more protein at each meal.

DIETETICS.definition: The proportion of a nutrient that is absorbed and can be used by the body.
DIETETICS.example: Iron from plant foods has lower bioavailability, but vitamin C eaten at the same meal improves absorption.

DIETETICS.definition: Difficulty swallowing food, drink or saliva safely.
DIETETICS.example: Following the stroke, dysphagia meant meals were planned jointly with the speech and language therapist.

DIETETICS.definition: Food prepared to a specific softness or smoothness so it can be swallowed safely.
DIETETICS.example: A texture-modified diet can reduce intake, so energy and protein were boosted in each portion.

DIETETICS.definition: Adding extra energy or nutrients to ordinary food without increasing its volume much.
DIETETICS.example: Food fortification with milk powder and butter raised her intake without making portions larger.

DIETETICS.definition: A prescribed drink or food product providing concentrated energy, protein and nutrients.
DIETETICS.example: An oral nutritional supplement was added because food alone had not stopped his weight falling.

DIETETICS.definition: An autoimmune condition in which gluten damages the lining of the small intestine.
DIETETICS.example: Coeliac disease requires a strict lifelong gluten-free diet, including care with cross-contamination at home.

DIETETICS.definition: Poor absorption of nutrients from the gut into the body.
DIETETICS.example: Pale, greasy stools and weight loss pointed to fat malabsorption linked to pancreatic insufficiency.

DIETETICS.definition: A short-term diet limiting certain fermentable carbohydrates to identify triggers of gut symptoms.
DIETETICS.example: A low-FODMAP diet should be supervised and followed by structured reintroduction, not continued indefinitely.

DIETETICS.definition: Relating to body measurements such as weight, height, arm size or waist size.
DIETETICS.example: Anthropometric measures included mid-upper arm circumference, as standing weight was impossible on the ward.

DIETETICS.definition: Weight in kilograms divided by height in metres squared, used to classify weight.
DIETETICS.example: Body mass index can underestimate risk in people with low muscle mass or certain ethnic backgrounds.

DIETETICS.definition: Losing weight without trying, often a sign of illness or poor intake.
DIETETICS.example: Unintentional weight loss of 8% over three months triggered a full dietetic review.

DIETETICS.definition: The amount of energy a person needs each day for body functions and activity.
DIETETICS.example: Energy requirements were estimated higher than usual because of the large pressure wound.

DIETETICS.definition: The difference between protein taken in and protein broken down, indicating muscle gain or loss.
DIETETICS.example: Negative nitrogen balance in critical illness reflects rapid muscle breakdown despite feeding.

DIETETICS.definition: A blood protein level often affected by inflammation, so a poor marker of nutrition alone.
DIETETICS.example: Low serum albumin was attributed to infection rather than diet, so it was not used to judge nutritional status.

DIETETICS.definition: Blood levels of salts such as sodium, potassium or phosphate that are too high or low.
DIETETICS.example: Daily bloods were taken during the first week of feeding to detect any electrolyte imbalance early.

DIETETICS.definition: A low level of potassium in the blood.
DIETETICS.example: Hypokalaemia after prolonged vomiting was corrected by the medical team before feeds were increased.

DIETETICS.definition: Limiting foods high in phosphate, often needed in advanced kidney disease.
DIETETICS.example: Phosphate restriction was explained using common foods, including processed cheese and some fizzy drinks.

DIETETICS.definition: A medical limit on how much fluid a patient may drink each day.
DIETETICS.example: His fluid restriction includes soup, ice and jelly, which he had not been counting.

DIETETICS.definition: The feeling of fullness that reduces the desire to eat after a meal.
DIETETICS.example: Protein and fibre at breakfast increased satiety, helping him avoid snacking before lunch.

DIETETICS.definition: A written record of everything a person eats and drinks over a set period.
DIETETICS.example: Her three-day food diary showed long gaps between meals and very little protein.

DIETETICS.definition: An interview method asking a person to describe all food and drink taken in the previous day.
DIETETICS.example: A 24-hour recall suggested his intake was about half his estimated needs.

DIETETICS.definition: Describing an environment or factor that encourages weight gain.
DIETETICS.example: The report described an obesogenic environment, with cheap high-energy food available on every street.

DIETETICS.definition: Relating to the treatment of severe obesity, especially weight-loss surgery.
DIETETICS.example: Bariatric patients need lifelong vitamin and mineral supplementation and regular blood monitoring.

DIETETICS.definition: A metabolic state in which the body burns fat and produces ketones for fuel.
DIETETICS.example: Very low carbohydrate diets induce ketosis, which needs medical oversight in people taking certain diabetes medicines.

DIETETICS.definition: Estimating the carbohydrate in meals so insulin can be matched to it.
DIETETICS.example: Carbohydrate counting gave the teenager more flexibility in what she ate at school.

DIETETICS.definition: A type of fat, mainly from animal and some plant sources, linked with raised cholesterol.
DIETETICS.example: Replacing saturated fat with unsaturated oils is a key step in lowering cardiovascular risk.

DIETETICS.definition: Unpleasant symptoms after a food that do not involve the immune system, unlike allergy.
DIETETICS.example: Lactose intolerance often allows small amounts of milk, whereas a milk allergy requires strict avoidance.

DIETETICS.definition: A severe, rapid and potentially life-threatening allergic reaction.
DIETETICS.example: Because of a previous episode of anaphylaxis to peanuts, his care plan stressed strict avoidance and emergency medication.

DIETETICS.definition: A child's weight or growth falling below the expected pattern for their age.
DIETETICS.example: Faltering growth was noted when the infant's weight dropped across two centile lines.

DIETETICS.definition: Feeding an infant only breast milk, with no other food or drink.
DIETETICS.example: Exclusive breastfeeding is recommended for around the first six months of life.

DIETETICS.definition: A lack of a nutrient that is large enough to affect health.
DIETETICS.example: Vitamin D deficiency is common in people who spend little time outdoors or cover most of their skin.

DIETETICS.definition: Enough in amount or quality for a particular need.
DIETETICS.example: Adequate protein intake is especially important while pressure ulcers are healing.

DIETETICS.definition: To add something extra to make up for what is missing.
DIETETICS.example: Breakfast cereal was supplemented with full-fat milk to increase his energy intake.

DIETETICS.definition: To be greater than a stated amount or limit.
DIETETICS.example: Her daily sodium intake exceeded the recommended limit, mostly because of bread and ready meals.

DIETETICS.definition: The relationship between two amounts, shown as how many times one contains the other.
DIETETICS.example: His insulin-to-carbohydrate ratio was reviewed after frequent lows in the afternoon.

DIETETICS.definition: To check something regularly over a period of time.
DIETETICS.example: Weight will be monitored weekly on the ward, using the same scales each time.

DIETETICS.definition: Standards used to judge or decide something; plural of criterion.
DIETETICS.example: She met the criteria for high nutritional risk on the screening tool.

DIETETICS.definition: To put a plan or decision into action.
DIETETICS.example: The care home implemented protected mealtimes, and residents' intake improved within a month.

DIETETICS.definition: To rise and fall irregularly.
DIETETICS.example: Appetite fluctuated with each chemotherapy cycle, so the plan was adapted week by week.

DIETETICS.definition: Not enough for a particular purpose.
DIETETICS.example: Evidence is insufficient to recommend routine vitamin supplements for all adults with this condition.

DIETETICS.definition: To judge the value, quality or effect of something carefully.
DIETETICS.example: The study evaluated whether group education improved diet quality in adults with prediabetes.

DIETETICS.definition: To build up gradually over time.
DIETETICS.example: In kidney failure, potassium can accumulate in the blood, so high-potassium foods may need limiting.

DIETETICS.definition: Before, used in formal writing.
DIETETICS.example: Prior to admission, she had been eating one small meal a day for several weeks.

DIETETICS.definition: Although; used to add a limiting point.
DIETETICS.example: His weight has increased, albeit slowly, since supplements were introduced.

DIETETICS.definition: The result or effect of a treatment or process.
DIETETICS.example: The primary outcome was change in HbA1c after twelve months of dietary intervention.

DIETETICS.definition: To consist of or be made up of.
DIETETICS.example: The programme comprises six group sessions on label reading, cooking skills and portion control.

DIETETICS.definition: A factor that can change and may affect results in a study.
DIETETICS.example: Physical activity was a confounding variable, as the diet group also walked more.

DIETETICS.definition: Blood glucose that is above normal but not yet high enough to be diagnosed as diabetes.
DIETETICS.example: Prediabetes means your sugar levels are a little high, and changes to diet and activity can often bring them down.
DIETETICS.plain: Blood sugar higher than normal, but not diabetes yet.

DIETETICS.definition: A formal opening that states the subject of a letter.
DIETETICS.example: I am writing regarding Mrs Okafor, whom I reviewed today for unintentional weight loss following her chemotherapy.

DIETETICS.definition: A polite, clear way to give advice in speech or writing.
DIETETICS.example: I would recommend having a small snack mid-morning, as you're going a long time without food.

DIETETICS.definition: Formal letter wording meaning a treatment has been started.
DIETETICS.example: He has been commenced on two supplement drinks daily, and his weight will be reviewed in four weeks.

DIETETICS.term: I would be grateful if you could review
DIETETICS.definition: A polite formal request for another clinician to check something.
DIETETICS.example: I would be grateful if you could review her vitamin D level at her next blood test.

DIETETICS.term: how have you been getting on with
DIETETICS.definition: A friendly spoken question to check a patient's experience of advice or treatment.
DIETETICS.example: How have you been getting on with the changes we discussed at your last appointment?

DIETETICS.definition: Used in questions to gather a patient's usual eating pattern.
DIETETICS.example: Could you talk me through a typical day, starting with what you have when you wake up?
DIETETICS.plain: What you usually eat and drink in a normal day.

DIETETICS.definition: Guidance on what to eat and drink for health or a medical condition.
DIETETICS.example: Dietary advice was given on regular meals and reducing sugary drinks, with written information.

DIETETICS.definition: The overall condition of a person's body in terms of nutrition.
DIETETICS.example: Her nutritional status has improved, and she has regained three kilograms since discharge.

DIETETICS.definition: In poor health because the body is not getting the right amount of nutrients.
DIETETICS.example: He is malnourished, so for now we'll focus on getting enough energy and protein rather than a strict diet.
DIETETICS.plain: Not getting enough goodness from food.

DIETETICS.definition: Everything a patient eats and drinks by mouth.
DIETETICS.example: Oral intake remains poor, at roughly a quarter of each meal served on the ward.

DIETETICS.definition: The total amount a person drinks over a set time.
DIETETICS.example: Your fluid intake is low, so try to keep a glass of water beside you during the day.

DIETETICS.definition: A blood glucose level that is higher than the target range.
DIETETICS.example: Hyperglycaemia after meals suggests we should look at the size of your rice and bread portions.

DIETETICS.definition: A blood glucose level that is lower than is safe.
DIETETICS.example: If you feel shaky or sweaty, it may be hypoglycaemia, so check your level and treat it promptly.

DIETETICS.definition: The amount of sugar circulating in the blood.
DIETETICS.example: Your blood glucose readings have come down since you switched to wholegrain bread.

DIETETICS.definition: The amount of a food served or eaten at one time.
DIETETICS.example: Using a smaller plate is a simple way to reduce portion size without feeling deprived.
DIETETICS.plain: How much is on your plate.

DIETETICS.definition: Made from the whole grain, including the outer layer, so higher in fibre.
DIETETICS.example: Choosing wholegrain cereals can help you feel full for longer.
DIETETICS.plain: Brown or whole versions of bread, pasta and rice.

DIETETICS.definition: The part of plant foods the body does not fully digest, helping bowel health.
DIETETICS.example: Increase fibre slowly and drink more fluid, or you may feel bloated at first.
DIETETICS.plain: Roughage from fruit, vegetables, beans and whole grains.

DIETETICS.definition: The nutrition information printed on food packaging.
DIETETICS.example: Let's look at this food label together to see how much salt is in one serving.

DIETETICS.definition: Providing a lot of vitamins, minerals or protein compared with the calories it contains.
DIETETICS.example: Eggs, yoghurt and beans are nutrient-dense choices when your appetite is small.
DIETETICS.plain: Lots of goodness in a small amount.

DIETETICS.definition: Containing a lot of calories in a small amount of food.
DIETETICS.example: While you're losing weight unintentionally, energy-dense foods like full-fat yoghurt are helpful.
DIETETICS.plain: High in calories for its size.

DIETETICS.definition: Less desire to eat than usual.
DIETETICS.example: With a reduced appetite, small meals every few hours are often easier than three large ones.

DIETETICS.definition: In clinical notes, a loss of appetite as a symptom; not the same as the eating disorder.
DIETETICS.example: The notes mention anorexia, which here means his appetite has gone, not an eating disorder.

DIETETICS.definition: Advice to eat small amounts at frequent intervals.
DIETETICS.example: Try eating little and often, perhaps something every two to three hours.
DIETETICS.plain: Small amounts, many times a day.

DIETETICS.definition: Improving nutrition through everyday foods before using prescribed supplements.
DIETETICS.example: We'll start with a food first approach, adding cheese, milk and butter to the meals you already enjoy.
DIETETICS.plain: Using normal food first to build you up.

DIETETICS.definition: Drinks that provide energy and protein, such as milky drinks or smoothies.
DIETETICS.example: Nourishing drinks like hot chocolate made with milk are a good choice between meals.
DIETETICS.plain: Filling drinks that give you energy.

DIETETICS.definition: Letter wording meaning body weight has stopped going up or down.
DIETETICS.example: His weight has stabilised at 58 kilograms over the past month, so supplements will continue.

DIETETICS.definition: The span of body weights linked with the lowest health risk for a person's height.
DIETETICS.example: Your healthy weight range is quite wide, so we don't need to aim for one exact number.
DIETETICS.plain: A weight that is good for your health.

DIETETICS.definition: A target the patient can actually reach in their circumstances.
DIETETICS.example: Let's agree a realistic goal for this month, such as cooking at home four nights a week.

DIETETICS.definition: A fatty substance in the blood; high levels raise the risk of heart disease.
DIETETICS.example: Oats and beans can help lower your cholesterol as part of an overall healthy diet.
DIETETICS.plain: A type of fat in your blood.

DIETETICS.definition: Blood pressure that stays higher than the healthy range.
DIETETICS.example: Because you have hypertension, cutting down on salty foods could help your blood pressure.

DIETETICS.definition: Relating to the stomach and intestines.
DIETETICS.example: Gastrointestinal symptoms such as bloating were recorded alongside each meal in her diary.
DIETETICS.plain: To do with your stomach and bowel.

DIETETICS.definition: Passing stools less often than usual, or with difficulty.
DIETETICS.example: Constipation is common with these painkillers, so fluid and fibre are especially important.
DIETETICS.plain: Finding it hard to open your bowels.

DIETETICS.definition: Loose or watery stools passed more often than usual.
DIETETICS.example: If the diarrhoea continues for more than a couple of days, please contact the ward.

DIETETICS.definition: A feeling that you might vomit.
DIETETICS.example: Cold foods and dry crackers may be easier to manage when nausea is bad.

DIETETICS.definition: Coping with a food, feed or treatment without significant side effects.
DIETETICS.example: She is tolerating the tube feed well, with no vomiting or abdominal pain.

DIETETICS.definition: Giving liquid nutrition through a tube into the stomach or small bowel.
DIETETICS.example: Tube feeding can give your body what it needs while your swallowing recovers.

DIETETICS.definition: Drinks made thicker so they move more slowly and are safer to swallow.
DIETETICS.example: Thickened fluids help stop drinks going down the wrong way while your swallow is weak.
DIETETICS.plain: Thicker drinks that are easier to swallow safely.

DIETETICS.definition: Problems moving food or drink safely from the mouth to the stomach.
DIETETICS.example: Because of his swallowing difficulties, all meals should be soft and moist.

DIETETICS.definition: The natural sugar found in milk and many dairy foods.
DIETETICS.example: Hard cheese contains very little lactose, so you may be able to enjoy it without symptoms.

PODIATRY.definition: Painful irritation of the thick band of tissue under the foot, often worst with the first steps in the morning.
PODIATRY.example: Her heel pain on rising and tenderness at the medial calcaneal tubercle were consistent with plantar fasciitis.

PODIATRY.definition: Deformity in which the big toe angles towards the other toes, with a prominent joint on the inner foot.
PODIATRY.example: Moderate hallux valgus was causing pressure over the first metatarsal head in his narrow work shoes.

PODIATRY.definition: Damage to nerves in the limbs, often causing numbness, tingling or loss of protective feeling in the feet.
PODIATRY.example: Peripheral neuropathy meant he had not noticed the blister until it had broken down.

PODIATRY.definition: Narrowing of the arteries supplying the legs, reducing blood flow and slowing healing.
PODIATRY.example: Absent foot pulses raised concern about peripheral arterial disease, so a vascular referral was made.

PODIATRY.definition: Ratio comparing blood pressure at the ankle with the arm, used to screen for reduced leg circulation.
PODIATRY.example: The ankle-brachial pressure index was low on the left, supporting a diagnosis of arterial insufficiency.

PODIATRY.definition: The process or state of an open wound forming through the skin that does not heal normally.
PODIATRY.example: Recurrent ulceration under the third metatarsal head was linked to high plantar pressure.

PODIATRY.definition: Removal of dead, damaged or infected tissue from a wound to help it heal.
PODIATRY.example: Sharp debridement of the callus rim exposed a small, clean ulcer base.

PODIATRY.definition: Reducing pressure on a vulnerable area of the foot using devices, padding or changes to footwear.
PODIATRY.example: Effective offloading is essential if this plantar ulcer is going to heal.

PODIATRY.definition: An area of thickened, hardened skin that forms where the foot is repeatedly rubbed or pressed.
PODIATRY.example: A thick callus had built up beneath the second metatarsal head and was reduced with a scalpel.

PODIATRY.definition: A hard corn: a small, dense core of thickened skin that presses inwards and causes pain.
PODIATRY.example: A heloma durum on the dorsum of the fifth toe was enucleated and padded.

PODIATRY.definition: An ingrown toenail, where the nail edge grows into the surrounding skin and may become infected.
PODIATRY.example: Recurrent onychocryptosis of the left hallux had not settled with conservative care.

PODIATRY.definition: Fungal infection of the nail, making it thick, discoloured and crumbly.
PODIATRY.example: Nail clippings were sent for culture to confirm suspected onychomycosis before treatment.

PODIATRY.definition: Fungal skin infection of the foot, commonly causing itching, scaling or splitting between the toes.
PODIATRY.example: Scaling and fissuring between the fourth and fifth toes suggested tinea pedis.

PODIATRY.definition: A wart on the foot caused by a viral skin infection, often painful when pressed.
PODIATRY.example: The child's verruca pedis was painful on squeezing, and the family were advised on options.

PODIATRY.definition: Rapid destruction of foot bones and joints in a person with neuropathy, often presenting as a hot, swollen foot.
PODIATRY.example: A warm, swollen foot in a patient with neuropathy should be treated as Charcot neuroarthropathy until proven otherwise.

PODIATRY.definition: Flat foot: the inner arch is low or collapses when standing.
PODIATRY.example: Flexible pes planus was noted bilaterally, but the child was symptom-free and active.

PODIATRY.definition: A foot with an unusually high arch, which can concentrate pressure on the heel and forefoot.
PODIATRY.example: Pes cavus was increasing load on her forefoot, causing painful callus formation.

PODIATRY.definition: Excessive inward rolling of the foot during walking or running.
PODIATRY.example: Gait observation showed overpronation on the right during the mid-stance phase.

PODIATRY.definition: Systematic observation or measurement of how a person walks or runs.
PODIATRY.example: Video gait analysis on the treadmill helped explain the runner's recurrent shin pain.

PODIATRY.definition: Examination of joint range, alignment and movement to understand how the lower limb functions.
PODIATRY.example: A full biomechanical assessment revealed limited ankle dorsiflexion contributing to forefoot overload.

PODIATRY.definition: Devices worn in shoes to support, realign or redistribute pressure on the foot.
PODIATRY.example: Custom orthoses were prescribed to reduce strain on the plantar fascia.

PODIATRY.definition: Pain in the ball of the foot, around the heads of the long foot bones.
PODIATRY.example: His metatarsalgia worsened after long shifts standing on a hard factory floor.

PODIATRY.definition: Thickened tissue around a nerve between the toes, causing burning pain or numbness in the forefoot.
PODIATRY.example: Squeezing the forefoot reproduced her pain, raising suspicion of a Morton's neuroma in the third space.

PODIATRY.definition: Painful, degenerative change in the Achilles tendon, usually from overload.
PODIATRY.example: Morning stiffness and a thickened tendon suggested mid-portion Achilles tendinopathy.

PODIATRY.definition: Cramping leg pain on walking that eases with rest, caused by poor arterial blood supply.
PODIATRY.example: He described intermittent claudication in his calf after walking about two hundred metres.

PODIATRY.definition: A thin nylon fibre pressed against the skin to test whether protective sensation is present.
PODIATRY.example: He could not feel the monofilament at four of the ten sites tested on each foot.

PODIATRY.definition: The sound or trace of blood flow in an artery, assessed with a handheld ultrasound device.
PODIATRY.example: A monophasic Doppler waveform at the dorsalis pedis suggested significant arterial disease.

PODIATRY.definition: The time taken for colour to return to the skin after pressure, a simple check of local circulation.
PODIATRY.example: Capillary refill time in the toes was prolonged, so a vascular assessment was arranged.

PODIATRY.definition: Redness of the skin, often caused by inflammation or infection.
PODIATRY.example: Spreading erythema beyond the wound margin indicated a possible soft tissue infection.

PODIATRY.definition: Softening and whitening of skin that has been kept too wet for too long.
PODIATRY.example: Maceration around the ulcer suggested the dressing was not managing the exudate.

PODIATRY.definition: Yellowish, stringy dead tissue on a wound bed that can delay healing.
PODIATRY.example: The wound bed was covered with slough, which was gently removed at each visit.

PODIATRY.definition: Healthy red, moist new tissue that fills a healing wound.
PODIATRY.example: Healthy granulation tissue now covers most of the ulcer base.

PODIATRY.definition: Infection of bone, a serious complication of deep foot ulcers.
PODIATRY.example: Probe-to-bone contact in the toe ulcer raised concern about underlying osteomyelitis.

PODIATRY.definition: Bacterial infection of the deeper skin layers, causing redness, heat, swelling and pain.
PODIATRY.example: She developed cellulitis of the forefoot after a cracked heel became infected.

PODIATRY.definition: Removal of a narrow strip of the toenail edge, usually under local anaesthetic.
PODIATRY.example: A partial nail avulsion was performed on the medial border of the right hallux.

PODIATRY.definition: Destroying part of the nail-growing tissue with a chemical so the removed nail edge does not regrow.
PODIATRY.example: Chemical matrixectomy with phenol was carried out to prevent regrowth of the ingrowing edge.

PODIATRY.definition: Injection of local anaesthetic at the base of a toe to numb it before a procedure.
PODIATRY.example: A digital nerve block was given before the nail surgery, and the toe was numb within minutes.

PODIATRY.definition: A foot with factors such as neuropathy, poor circulation or past ulcers that make serious problems more likely.
PODIATRY.example: Because of previous ulceration, she is classified as having a high-risk foot and is reviewed regularly.

PODIATRY.definition: A group of specialists from different professions who manage complex or limb-threatening foot problems together.
PODIATRY.example: The infected ulcer was escalated to the multidisciplinary foot team the same day.

PODIATRY.definition: A closely moulded cast that spreads pressure over the whole foot and lower leg to protect an ulcer or Charcot foot.
PODIATRY.example: A total contact cast was applied to offload the plantar ulcer and was changed weekly.

PODIATRY.definition: Stiffness and pain in the big toe joint caused by arthritis.
PODIATRY.example: Hallux rigidus limited his toe-off, so a rocker-sole shoe was suggested.

PODIATRY.definition: A toe that is bent at its middle joint, often rubbing on the shoe.
PODIATRY.example: A painful corn had formed on the hammer toe where it rubbed the shoe upper.

PODIATRY.definition: The force spread across the sole of the foot during standing or walking.
PODIATRY.example: In-shoe plantar pressure measurement showed peak loading under the first metatarsal head.

PODIATRY.definition: Changes made to shoes, such as extra depth or rocker soles, to reduce pressure or improve function.
PODIATRY.example: Footwear modification with extra depth was requested to accommodate his deformity.

PODIATRY.definition: A condition or factor that makes a particular treatment unsafe or unsuitable for a patient.
PODIATRY.example: Poor arterial supply was a contraindication to nail surgery until vascular review.

PODIATRY.definition: To examine something carefully in order to judge its condition or seriousness.
PODIATRY.example: The podiatrist will assess the wound depth and circulation at every appointment.

PODIATRY.definition: Happening after something else.
PODIATRY.example: Subsequent reviews showed steady reduction in ulcer size.

PODIATRY.definition: Existing or happening before a particular time or event.
PODIATRY.example: Prior to the procedure, his clotting status was checked with the referring GP.

PODIATRY.definition: To show or suggest that something is present, true or likely.
PODIATRY.example: Increased warmth and odour indicate that the wound may be infected.

PODIATRY.definition: Large or important enough to matter or to be noticed.
PODIATRY.example: There has been a significant improvement in her pain since the orthoses were fitted.

PODIATRY.definition: Enough or good enough for a particular purpose.
PODIATRY.example: Adequate blood supply must be confirmed before any surgical nail procedure.

PODIATRY.definition: Existing as a basic, built-in part of something.
PODIATRY.example: Delayed healing is an inherent risk when neuropathy and poor circulation occur together.

PODIATRY.definition: The way in which something works or happens.
PODIATRY.example: The mechanism of injury was an inversion sprain while stepping off a kerb.

PODIATRY.definition: A difference from what is usual, expected or normal.
PODIATRY.example: Any deviation from the dressing plan should be recorded in the notes.

PODIATRY.definition: Able to exist or be used together without problems.
PODIATRY.example: Her findings were compatible with early Charcot changes, so imaging was requested.

PODIATRY.definition: To suffer an injury or loss; also to keep something going over time.
PODIATRY.example: He sustained a puncture wound to the sole after stepping on a nail.

PODIATRY.definition: The state of being whole and undamaged, as in skin that is intact.
PODIATRY.example: Daily foot checks help maintain skin integrity in people with diabetes.

PODIATRY.definition: Present beneath the surface and possibly causing what is seen.
PODIATRY.example: Recurrent ulcers often reflect an underlying deformity that needs addressing.

PODIATRY.definition: To judge how good, effective or serious something is.
PODIATRY.example: We will evaluate the response to offloading after four weeks.

PODIATRY.definition: Next to or very near something.
PODIATRY.example: The ulcer had spread to the adjacent toe through an interdigital split.

PODIATRY.definition: Standard opening for a letter asking another clinician or service to see a patient.
PODIATRY.example: I am writing to refer Mrs Patel, who has a non-healing ulcer on her left heel.
PODIATRY.plain: I'm asking another specialist to see you.

PODIATRY.definition: Came to the clinic showing a particular problem or symptom.
PODIATRY.example: Mr Jones presented with a painful, red right big toe after cutting his nails.

PODIATRY.definition: Used in notes and letters to introduce what the clinician found when checking the patient.
PODIATRY.example: On examination, both foot pulses were palpable and sensation was intact.

PODIATRY.term: I would be grateful if you could
PODIATRY.definition: Polite letter phrase for asking a colleague to take an action.
PODIATRY.example: I would be grateful if you could review his blood glucose control.

PODIATRY.term: please do not hesitate to contact me
PODIATRY.definition: Polite closing that invites the reader to ask questions.
PODIATRY.example: If you require further details, please do not hesitate to contact me.
PODIATRY.plain: Get in touch if you have any questions.

PODIATRY.definition: Reports advice already given to the patient.
PODIATRY.example: She has been advised to wear the post-operative shoe until the wound heals.

PODIATRY.definition: The underside of the foot.
PODIATRY.example: There is a small ulcer on the plantar surface of the left forefoot.

PODIATRY.definition: The upper surface of the foot.
PODIATRY.example: Swelling was noted over the dorsum of the foot after the injury.

PODIATRY.definition: The medical name for the big toe.
PODIATRY.example: The nail on the right hallux is thickened and discoloured.

PODIATRY.definition: Any area of damaged or abnormal skin or tissue.
PODIATRY.example: A pigmented lesion under the nail was referred urgently for dermatology review.
PODIATRY.plain: A sore, patch or abnormal area of skin.

PODIATRY.definition: Swelling caused by fluid collecting in the tissues.
PODIATRY.example: Pitting oedema of both ankles was making his shoes too tight.

PODIATRY.definition: Abnormal feelings such as tingling, prickling or burning in the skin.
PODIATRY.example: She reports paraesthesia in both feet, especially at night.

PODIATRY.definition: Death of body tissue, often because of poor blood supply or infection.
PODIATRY.example: Dry necrosis at the tip of the second toe requires urgent vascular review.

PODIATRY.definition: Fluid that leaks from a wound.
PODIATRY.example: The ulcer produced moderate exudate, so a more absorbent dressing was chosen.
PODIATRY.plain: Fluid coming out of the wound.

PODIATRY.definition: Affecting both sides of the body.
PODIATRY.example: Bilateral heel pain has been present for six months.
PODIATRY.plain: On both sides, in both feet.

PODIATRY.definition: Showing or causing no symptoms.
PODIATRY.example: The flat feet are asymptomatic and no treatment is needed.
PODIATRY.plain: Not causing you any problems or pain.

PODIATRY.definition: A moisturising cream or ointment that softens dry skin.
PODIATRY.example: Apply an emollient to your heels daily, but not between your toes.

PODIATRY.definition: Pulses that can be felt with the fingers, suggesting blood is reaching the area.
PODIATRY.example: Palpable pulses were present in both feet, so circulation appears adequate.
PODIATRY.plain: I can feel a good pulse in your feet.

PODIATRY.definition: Loss of the ability to feel pain or pressure that normally warns of injury.
PODIATRY.example: Because of reduced protective sensation, she must check her feet every day.
PODIATRY.plain: You can't feel pain in your feet as well as you should.

PODIATRY.definition: Describing activity where the foot carries the body's weight.
PODIATRY.example: Pain is worse during weight-bearing activities such as climbing stairs.

PODIATRY.definition: Blood sugar levels that are higher or less stable than the target.
PODIATRY.example: Suboptimal glycaemic control may be delaying healing of his ulcer.
PODIATRY.plain: Your blood sugar is not as well controlled as it should be.

PODIATRY.definition: Able to walk.
PODIATRY.example: He is ambulant with one stick and lives alone.

PODIATRY.definition: Itching of the skin.
PODIATRY.example: Pruritus between the toes suggests a fungal skin infection.

PODIATRY.definition: Located between the fingers or toes.
PODIATRY.example: Interdigital maceration was found between the fourth and fifth toes.

PODIATRY.definition: Advice to look at the feet daily for cuts, redness or changes.
PODIATRY.example: Please check your feet every day, using a mirror for the soles.
PODIATRY.plain: Look at your feet each day for any changes.

PODIATRY.term: keep the area clean and dry
PODIATRY.definition: Wound and skin care advice after a procedure.
PODIATRY.example: Keep the area clean and dry until we change the dressing on Friday.
PODIATRY.plain: Don't let the dressing get wet or dirty.

PODIATRY.definition: Safety advice for people with poor feeling or circulation in their feet.
PODIATRY.example: With numb feet, it is important to avoid walking barefoot, even at home.
PODIATRY.plain: Always wear something on your feet.

PODIATRY.definition: Shoes of the correct length, width and depth that do not rub.
PODIATRY.example: Well-fitting shoes with a soft upper will help protect your toes.
PODIATRY.plain: Shoes that are the right size and don't rub.

PODIATRY.term: could you point to where it hurts
PODIATRY.definition: Simple question to locate a patient's pain.
PODIATRY.example: Could you point to where it hurts most when you first stand up?

PODIATRY.definition: Question to find out when a symptom started.
PODIATRY.example: How long have you noticed the discolouration on this nail?

PODIATRY.term: this may feel a little uncomfortable
PODIATRY.definition: Warning a patient before a procedure that could cause brief discomfort.
PODIATRY.example: This may feel a little uncomfortable while I remove the hard skin.
PODIATRY.plain: You might feel some discomfort, but it will be brief.

PODIATRY.definition: Safety-netting phrase telling the patient when to return early.
PODIATRY.example: Come back sooner if the toe becomes hot, swollen or starts to smell.
PODIATRY.plain: Return before your next visit if this happens.

PODIATRY.definition: Changes suggesting a wound or skin area is infected.
PODIATRY.example: I'll show you the signs of infection to watch for after your nail surgery.
PODIATRY.plain: Redness, heat, swelling, pus or a bad smell.

PODIATRY.definition: A later visit to check progress after assessment or treatment.
PODIATRY.example: We'll book a follow-up appointment in two weeks to check the wound.
PODIATRY.plain: Another visit to see how things are going.

PODIATRY.definition: An assessment that must happen very soon because the problem may be serious.
PODIATRY.example: A hot, swollen foot in someone with neuropathy needs urgent review.
PODIATRY.plain: You need to be seen quickly.

PODIATRY.definition: Formal letter phrase meaning because of or considering.
PODIATRY.example: In view of her absent pulses, I would value a vascular opinion.

PODIATRY.definition: Reports that a treatment has improved the patient's condition.
PODIATRY.example: His heel pain has responded well to stretching and insoles.

PODIATRY.definition: How closely a patient follows an agreed treatment plan.
PODIATRY.example: Adherence to the offloading boot has been poor, as he removes it at home.

PODIATRY.term: I'm going to test the feeling in your feet
PODIATRY.definition: Explains a sensation check before carrying it out.
PODIATRY.example: I'm going to test the feeling in your feet; just say yes each time you feel a touch.
PODIATRY.plain: I'll check how well you can feel touch.

PODIATRY.definition: The process of becoming worse.
PODIATRY.example: There has been a deterioration in the ulcer, which is now deeper and producing more fluid.

RADIOGRAPHY.definition: Radiation with enough energy to remove electrons from atoms, as used in X-ray and CT imaging.
RADIOGRAPHY.example: Every examination using ionising radiation must be justified before it is performed.

RADIOGRAPHY.definition: The documented decision that an exposure's expected benefit outweighs its radiation risk.
RADIOGRAPHY.example: Justification of the CT request was discussed with the referrer because a recent scan already existed.

RADIOGRAPHY.definition: Adjusting technique so the dose is as low as possible while still giving a diagnostic image.
RADIOGRAPHY.example: Optimisation of paediatric protocols reduced dose without losing image quality.

RADIOGRAPHY.definition: Principle that radiation doses should be kept as low as sensible effort and cost allow.
RADIOGRAPHY.example: Shielding staff behind the screen keeps their exposure as low as reasonably practicable.

RADIOGRAPHY.definition: An estimate of the overall radiation risk to the body, accounting for the sensitivity of different organs.
RADIOGRAPHY.example: The effective dose from a chest radiograph is very small compared with a CT abdomen.

RADIOGRAPHY.definition: A benchmark dose for a standard examination, used to check that practice is not unusually high.
RADIOGRAPHY.example: An audit found that lumbar spine doses regularly exceeded the local diagnostic reference level.

RADIOGRAPHY.definition: A designated zone where special rules apply because radiation levels may be significant.
RADIOGRAPHY.example: The warning light shows that the X-ray room is a controlled area during exposure.

RADIOGRAPHY.definition: Restricting the X-ray beam to the area of interest to reduce dose and scatter.
RADIOGRAPHY.example: Tight collimation to the wrist excluded the forearm and improved image contrast.

RADIOGRAPHY.definition: The settings, such as tube voltage and current-time product, that determine how an image is produced.
RADIOGRAPHY.example: Exposure factors were adjusted for the patient's large body habitus.

RADIOGRAPHY.definition: The voltage across the X-ray tube, which controls the energy and penetration of the beam.
RADIOGRAPHY.example: Increasing the tube potential improved penetration of the dense pelvis.

RADIOGRAPHY.definition: The detector plate or panel that captures the X-ray image.
RADIOGRAPHY.example: The image receptor was placed behind the knee for the lateral projection.

RADIOGRAPHY.definition: Radiation deflected from its original path within the patient, which degrades images and exposes staff.
RADIOGRAPHY.example: Scatter radiation is greatest near the patient, so staff stand well back during mobile imaging.

RADIOGRAPHY.definition: A device of thin strips placed before the detector to absorb scattered radiation and sharpen the image.
RADIOGRAPHY.example: An anti-scatter grid was used for the thick abdomen but not for the hand.

RADIOGRAPHY.definition: Reduction in beam intensity as X-rays pass through and are absorbed by tissue.
RADIOGRAPHY.example: Bone shows high attenuation, so it appears white on the radiograph.

RADIOGRAPHY.definition: A substance given to make blood vessels, organs or tissues show more clearly on images.
RADIOGRAPHY.example: Intravenous contrast medium was given to assess the liver lesion.

RADIOGRAPHY.definition: Leakage of injected fluid out of the vein into surrounding tissue.
RADIOGRAPHY.example: Swelling at the cannula site after injection suggested extravasation, and the limb was elevated.

RADIOGRAPHY.definition: A sudden fall in kidney function occurring after iodinated contrast has been given.
RADIOGRAPHY.example: Patients with poor renal function are screened for risk of contrast-associated acute kidney injury.

RADIOGRAPHY.definition: A calculated measure of how well the kidneys filter blood.
RADIOGRAPHY.example: A recent estimated glomerular filtration rate was checked before the contrast-enhanced CT.

RADIOGRAPHY.definition: An unwanted immune-type response to a substance, ranging from rash to life-threatening collapse.
RADIOGRAPHY.example: A previous hypersensitivity reaction to iodinated contrast was flagged on the request.

RADIOGRAPHY.definition: Imaging that uses a rotating X-ray beam and computer processing to produce cross-sectional slices.
RADIOGRAPHY.example: Computed tomography of the head was performed within an hour of arrival.

RADIOGRAPHY.definition: Imaging that uses a strong magnetic field and radio waves, without ionising radiation.
RADIOGRAPHY.example: Magnetic resonance imaging is preferred for assessing soft tissue injuries of the knee.

RADIOGRAPHY.definition: Strongly attracted by a magnet, and therefore dangerous near an MRI scanner.
RADIOGRAPHY.example: A ferromagnetic oxygen cylinder must never be taken into the scanner room.

RADIOGRAPHY.definition: Describes an implant or device shown to be safe in MRI only under specified conditions.
RADIOGRAPHY.example: The pacemaker was MR Conditional, so the cardiology team set it to the correct mode first.

RADIOGRAPHY.definition: Structured questioning and checks to identify implants, metal or risks before a scan.
RADIOGRAPHY.example: Safety screening revealed metal fragments in his eye from welding work.

RADIOGRAPHY.definition: The scale used in CT to express tissue density relative to water.
RADIOGRAPHY.example: The lesion measured near zero Hounsfield units, suggesting a simple fluid-filled cyst.

RADIOGRAPHY.definition: Adjusting the displayed range of grey levels to show particular tissues, such as lung or bone.
RADIOGRAPHY.example: Bone windowing showed a subtle fracture that was not visible on soft tissue settings.

RADIOGRAPHY.definition: A feature on an image that does not represent real anatomy, caused by movement, metal or equipment.
RADIOGRAPHY.example: Motion artefact made the abdominal images non-diagnostic, so the series was repeated.

RADIOGRAPHY.definition: Real-time moving X-ray imaging used to guide procedures or study swallowing and movement.
RADIOGRAPHY.example: Fluoroscopy time was kept short during the barium swallow.

RADIOGRAPHY.definition: An image taken with the beam passing from the front of the body to the back.
RADIOGRAPHY.example: An anteroposterior projection of the pelvis was taken with the patient supine.

RADIOGRAPHY.definition: An image taken with the body or beam angled, to show structures that overlap on standard views.
RADIOGRAPHY.example: An oblique projection of the foot showed the base of the fifth metatarsal clearly.

RADIOGRAPHY.definition: A side view taken with the beam parallel to the floor, often used when the patient cannot be moved.
RADIOGRAPHY.example: A horizontal beam lateral of the knee demonstrated a fat-fluid level.

RADIOGRAPHY.definition: Checking whether a patient of childbearing potential could be pregnant before certain exposures.
RADIOGRAPHY.example: The pregnancy enquiry was documented before the pelvic radiograph.

RADIOGRAPHY.definition: A registered clinician entitled to request a medical exposure and supply the clinical information.
RADIOGRAPHY.example: The referrer was contacted because the request form lacked relevant clinical details.

RADIOGRAPHY.definition: The person who takes responsibility for justifying a medical exposure under UK regulations.
RADIOGRAPHY.example: The IR(ME)R practitioner declined the request because ultrasound could answer the question.

RADIOGRAPHY.definition: A radiographer's brief written comment on an image to help the referrer while awaiting a formal report.
RADIOGRAPHY.example: The radiographer's preliminary clinical evaluation noted a possible scaphoid fracture.

RADIOGRAPHY.definition: The digital system that stores, retrieves and shares medical images across a hospital.
RADIOGRAPHY.example: Previous films were retrieved from the picture archiving and communication system for comparison.

RADIOGRAPHY.definition: An unexpected abnormality seen on imaging that is unrelated to the reason for the scan.
RADIOGRAPHY.example: An incidental finding of a renal mass was reported on the trauma CT.

RADIOGRAPHY.definition: Letting X-rays pass easily, so appearing dark on the image.
RADIOGRAPHY.example: Air in the bowel is radiolucent and appears black on the abdominal radiograph.

RADIOGRAPHY.definition: Blocking X-rays, so appearing white on the image.
RADIOGRAPHY.example: The swallowed coin was radiopaque and clearly visible in the oesophagus.

RADIOGRAPHY.definition: Inserting a thin tube into a vein to give fluids or contrast.
RADIOGRAPHY.example: Cannulation of the antecubital vein was performed before the contrast scan.

RADIOGRAPHY.definition: A set pattern of radio-frequency pulses and gradients in MRI that determines image contrast.
RADIOGRAPHY.example: A fat-suppressed pulse sequence was added to show bone marrow oedema.

RADIOGRAPHY.definition: An injected MRI contrast that brightens tissues with increased blood supply.
RADIOGRAPHY.example: A gadolinium-based contrast agent was given to characterise the brain lesion.

RADIOGRAPHY.definition: The ring-shaped part of a CT or MRI scanner that the patient passes through.
RADIOGRAPHY.example: The patient was positioned so that the head lay at the centre of the gantry.

RADIOGRAPHY.definition: Radiation intensity falls with the square of the distance from the source.
RADIOGRAPHY.example: Under the inverse square law, stepping back from the patient sharply reduces staff exposure.

RADIOGRAPHY.definition: How clearly an image shows the anatomy needed to answer the clinical question.
RADIOGRAPHY.example: Image quality was poor because the patient could not hold their breath.

RADIOGRAPHY.definition: Using pads, straps or devices to keep a patient still during imaging.
RADIOGRAPHY.example: Immobilisation with foam pads helped the child stay still for the skull series.

RADIOGRAPHY.definition: An agreed written procedure describing how an examination should be performed.
RADIOGRAPHY.example: The trauma protocol specifies which CT phases are acquired for major injuries.

RADIOGRAPHY.definition: A measurement of radiation dose multiplied by the area of the beam, used to monitor exposure.
RADIOGRAPHY.example: The dose-area product for the procedure was recorded on the system.

RADIOGRAPHY.definition: An event where a patient or staff member receives a greater or unintended exposure.
RADIOGRAPHY.example: Scanning the wrong patient was investigated as a radiation incident.

RADIOGRAPHY.definition: Low-dose X-ray imaging of the breast, used for screening and diagnosis.
RADIOGRAPHY.example: Screening mammography identified a small cluster of calcifications.

RADIOGRAPHY.definition: Minimally invasive procedures carried out using imaging guidance.
RADIOGRAPHY.example: The bleeding vessel was treated in interventional radiology by embolisation.

RADIOGRAPHY.definition: Overlapping of structures on an image, which can hide abnormalities.
RADIOGRAPHY.example: Superimposition of the ribs made the small lung nodule hard to see.

RADIOGRAPHY.definition: X-ray examinations performed at the bedside using portable equipment.
RADIOGRAPHY.example: Mobile radiography was used on the intensive care unit for a chest film.

RADIOGRAPHY.definition: A measurable setting or factor that defines how something is done.
RADIOGRAPHY.example: Scan parameters were adjusted to reduce dose for the young patient.

RADIOGRAPHY.definition: To reduce something to the smallest possible amount.
RADIOGRAPHY.example: Careful positioning and tight collimation help minimise unnecessary exposure.

RADIOGRAPHY.definition: Able to be seen.
RADIOGRAPHY.example: The fracture line was barely visible on the initial projection.

RADIOGRAPHY.definition: Able to be used safely or work together without problems.
RADIOGRAPHY.example: Only equipment confirmed as compatible with the scanner may enter the room.

RADIOGRAPHY.definition: A patient's informed agreement to an examination or procedure.
RADIOGRAPHY.example: Verbal consent was obtained after the risks of contrast were explained.

RADIOGRAPHY.definition: Coming after something else.
RADIOGRAPHY.example: Subsequent images showed resolution of the pleural effusion.

RADIOGRAPHY.definition: To show or suggest that something is present or likely.
RADIOGRAPHY.example: The clinical history should indicate why the examination is needed.

RADIOGRAPHY.term: I'm going to take an X-ray of
RADIOGRAPHY.definition: Simple way to explain which body part will be imaged.
RADIOGRAPHY.example: I'm going to take an X-ray of your wrist from two different angles.
RADIOGRAPHY.plain: I'll take a picture of this part of your body.

RADIOGRAPHY.term: please keep as still as you can
RADIOGRAPHY.definition: Instruction to avoid movement blurring the image.
RADIOGRAPHY.example: Please keep as still as you can while the table moves through the scanner.
RADIOGRAPHY.plain: Try not to move at all.

RADIOGRAPHY.definition: Instruction given for chest or abdominal images to stop movement.
RADIOGRAPHY.example: Take a deep breath in and hold your breath for a few seconds.
RADIOGRAPHY.plain: Breathe in and stop breathing for a moment.

RADIOGRAPHY.term: is there any chance you could be pregnant
RADIOGRAPHY.definition: Sensitive but necessary question before certain exposures.
RADIOGRAPHY.example: Before we start, is there any chance you could be pregnant?
RADIOGRAPHY.plain: Could you be expecting a baby?

RADIOGRAPHY.term: you may feel a warm sensation
RADIOGRAPHY.definition: Warning about a common, harmless effect of contrast injection.
RADIOGRAPHY.example: When the injection goes in, you may feel a warm sensation, as if you have passed urine.
RADIOGRAPHY.plain: You might feel warm for a short time; this is normal.

RADIOGRAPHY.definition: Instruction to take off jewellery, clips or items that affect images or safety.
RADIOGRAPHY.example: Please remove any metal objects, including hairpins and your watch.
RADIOGRAPHY.plain: Take off jewellery, keys, coins and anything metal.

RADIOGRAPHY.definition: Tells the patient how long the examination lasts.
RADIOGRAPHY.example: The scan will take about twenty minutes, and you can talk to me throughout.
RADIOGRAPHY.plain: This is how long it will last.

RADIOGRAPHY.term: the images will be reviewed by
RADIOGRAPHY.definition: Explains who will look at and report the images.
RADIOGRAPHY.example: The images will be reviewed by a radiologist, who will write a report.
RADIOGRAPHY.plain: A specialist doctor will look at your pictures.

RADIOGRAPHY.term: your doctor will receive the results
RADIOGRAPHY.definition: Tells the patient how results reach them.
RADIOGRAPHY.example: Your doctor will receive the results within a few days.
RADIOGRAPHY.plain: Your own doctor will be sent the answer.

RADIOGRAPHY.definition: Instruction on how to get help during a scan.
RADIOGRAPHY.example: If you feel unwell at any point, press the call buzzer in your hand.
RADIOGRAPHY.plain: Squeeze this button if you need us.

RADIOGRAPHY.definition: Explains why an exposure is justified despite a small radiation risk.
RADIOGRAPHY.example: For your injury, the benefit outweighs the risk from this small dose of radiation.
RADIOGRAPHY.plain: It is safer to have the scan than to miss a problem.

RADIOGRAPHY.definition: Contrast medium injected into a vein.
RADIOGRAPHY.example: Intravenous contrast will help us see the blood vessels in your chest.
RADIOGRAPHY.plain: A dye injected into your vein to make the pictures clearer.

RADIOGRAPHY.definition: A break or crack in a bone.
RADIOGRAPHY.example: The radiograph shows a fracture of the distal radius.
RADIOGRAPHY.plain: A break in the bone.

RADIOGRAPHY.definition: An abnormal collection of fluid in a body space, such as a joint or around the lung.
RADIOGRAPHY.example: A large pleural effusion was seen at the right lung base.
RADIOGRAPHY.plain: A build-up of fluid.

RADIOGRAPHY.definition: An area of lung where air spaces are filled with fluid, pus or other material.
RADIOGRAPHY.example: Consolidation in the left lower lobe is consistent with pneumonia.
RADIOGRAPHY.plain: Part of the lung is filled with fluid or infection.

RADIOGRAPHY.definition: A pale or white area on an image where X-rays have been blocked.
RADIOGRAPHY.example: A rounded opacity was seen in the right upper zone.
RADIOGRAPHY.plain: A pale patch on the X-ray.

RADIOGRAPHY.definition: An X-ray image.
RADIOGRAPHY.example: The chest radiograph was compared with last year's film.
RADIOGRAPHY.plain: An X-ray picture.

RADIOGRAPHY.definition: Lying flat on the back.
RADIOGRAPHY.example: The patient was imaged supine because she could not stand.
RADIOGRAPHY.plain: Lying on your back.

RADIOGRAPHY.definition: Lying flat on the front.
RADIOGRAPHY.example: For this view you will need to lie prone on the table.
RADIOGRAPHY.plain: Lying on your front.

RADIOGRAPHY.definition: Lying on one side, used for certain projections.
RADIOGRAPHY.example: A left lateral decubitus film was taken to look for free air.
RADIOGRAPHY.plain: Lying on your side.

RADIOGRAPHY.definition: A thin flexible tube placed in a vein.
RADIOGRAPHY.example: The nurse will place a cannula in your arm for the injection.
RADIOGRAPHY.plain: A small tube put into your vein.

RADIOGRAPHY.definition: Not involving cutting the skin or entering the body.
RADIOGRAPHY.example: An ultrasound is a non-invasive way of looking at your gallbladder.
RADIOGRAPHY.plain: It doesn't involve needles or going inside your body.

RADIOGRAPHY.definition: Not cancerous and not likely to spread.
RADIOGRAPHY.example: The radiologist thinks the lump is most likely benign.
RADIOGRAPHY.plain: Not cancer.

RADIOGRAPHY.definition: A cancerous growth or the presence of cancer.
RADIOGRAPHY.example: Further imaging is needed to exclude malignancy.
RADIOGRAPHY.plain: Cancer.

RADIOGRAPHY.definition: A small, rounded lump or spot of tissue.
RADIOGRAPHY.example: A small lung nodule will be checked again with a follow-up scan.
RADIOGRAPHY.plain: A small spot or lump.

RADIOGRAPHY.definition: A break where the bone ends have moved out of their normal line.
RADIOGRAPHY.example: The displaced fracture of the ankle will need orthopaedic review.
RADIOGRAPHY.plain: The broken bone ends have moved out of place.

RADIOGRAPHY.definition: Normal, with nothing of note found.
RADIOGRAPHY.example: The rest of the examination was unremarkable.
RADIOGRAPHY.plain: Normal.

RADIOGRAPHY.definition: Report phrase meaning no new or urgent problem was seen.
RADIOGRAPHY.example: The report says no acute abnormality detected on the head CT.
RADIOGRAPHY.plain: Nothing urgent or worrying was found.

RADIOGRAPHY.definition: Feeling anxious in small or enclosed spaces.
RADIOGRAPHY.example: If you feel claustrophobic in the scanner, we can stop at any time.
RADIOGRAPHY.plain: Scared of small, closed spaces.

RADIOGRAPHY.term: I am writing to inform you
RADIOGRAPHY.definition: Formal opening for a letter that reports an event or result.
RADIOGRAPHY.example: I am writing to inform you that the planned MRI could not be completed.
RADIOGRAPHY.plain: I'm letting you know.

RADIOGRAPHY.definition: Formal phrase explaining why a scan was stopped before completion.
RADIOGRAPHY.example: The examination was abandoned because the patient became too distressed.
RADIOGRAPHY.plain: We had to stop the scan because.

RADIOGRAPHY.definition: Polite request in a letter for a colleague to organise something.
RADIOGRAPHY.example: Please arrange a repeat chest radiograph in six weeks.
RADIOGRAPHY.plain: Please organise.

RADIOGRAPHY.definition: Report or letter phrase advising another scan.
RADIOGRAPHY.example: Further imaging is recommended to characterise the adrenal lesion.
RADIOGRAPHY.plain: You may need another scan.

RADIOGRAPHY.definition: Records a documented allergy in a referral or handover.
RADIOGRAPHY.example: She has a known allergy to iodinated contrast, so an alternative test or extra precautions may be advised.
RADIOGRAPHY.plain: Is allergic to.

RADIOGRAPHY.term: could you confirm your name and date of birth
RADIOGRAPHY.definition: Standard identity check before any exposure.
RADIOGRAPHY.example: Before we begin, could you confirm your name and date of birth?
RADIOGRAPHY.plain: Please tell me who you are so we scan the right person.

RADIOGRAPHY.definition: Aftercare advice following a contrast injection, where appropriate.
RADIOGRAPHY.example: Unless your doctor has limited your fluids, drink plenty of fluids today.
RADIOGRAPHY.plain: Drink lots of water.

RADIOGRAPHY.term: you might hear loud knocking noises
RADIOGRAPHY.definition: Prepares a patient for normal MRI scanner sounds.
RADIOGRAPHY.example: You might hear loud knocking noises, so we will give you ear protection.
RADIOGRAPHY.plain: The machine is noisy, but that's normal.

RADIOGRAPHY.definition: Taking a small sample of tissue to examine under a microscope.
RADIOGRAPHY.example: An image-guided biopsy of the liver lesion has been booked.
RADIOGRAPHY.plain: Taking a tiny piece of tissue to test.

RADIOGRAPHY.definition: Cancer deposits that have spread from where they started to other parts of the body.
RADIOGRAPHY.example: The CT showed several liver metastases.
RADIOGRAPHY.plain: Cancer that has spread to other places.

RADIOGRAPHY.term: let me know if you feel unwell
RADIOGRAPHY.definition: Invites the patient to report symptoms during or after a procedure.
RADIOGRAPHY.example: Let me know if you feel unwell after the injection, even slightly.
RADIOGRAPHY.plain: Tell me if you feel ill at all.

SPEECH_PATHOLOGY.definition: Difficulty moving food, drink or saliva safely from the mouth to the stomach.
SPEECH_PATHOLOGY.example: Following his stroke, Mr Patel developed dysphagia and was placed on a modified diet pending assessment.

SPEECH_PATHOLOGY.definition: Entry of food, fluid or saliva into the airway below the vocal folds.
SPEECH_PATHOLOGY.example: The swallow study showed aspiration of thin fluids, so thickened drinks were recommended.

SPEECH_PATHOLOGY.definition: Material entering the voice box above the vocal folds without passing below them.
SPEECH_PATHOLOGY.example: Laryngeal penetration was seen on two trials, but the patient cleared it with a strong cough.

SPEECH_PATHOLOGY.definition: Material entering the airway without the person coughing or showing any outward sign.
SPEECH_PATHOLOGY.example: Because silent aspiration cannot be detected at the bedside, an instrumental assessment was requested.

SPEECH_PATHOLOGY.definition: Lung infection caused by food, fluid or mouth bacteria reaching the lungs.
SPEECH_PATHOLOGY.example: She had two admissions with aspiration pneumonia before her swallowing was formally reviewed.

SPEECH_PATHOLOGY.definition: Unclear speech caused by weakness or poor control of the muscles used to speak.
SPEECH_PATHOLOGY.example: His dysarthria worsened when he was tired, making telephone conversations particularly difficult.

SPEECH_PATHOLOGY.definition: Difficulty planning and sequencing speech movements, though the muscles themselves are not weak.
SPEECH_PATHOLOGY.example: Apraxia of speech was suspected because her errors were inconsistent and she groped for mouth positions.

SPEECH_PATHOLOGY.definition: A language disorder after brain injury affecting speaking, understanding, reading or writing.
SPEECH_PATHOLOGY.example: Despite marked aphasia, Mrs Jones could follow simple instructions supported by gesture.

SPEECH_PATHOLOGY.definition: Difficulty retrieving the names of objects or people during speech.
SPEECH_PATHOLOGY.example: Mild anomia remained, and he often described an item's use when he could not name it.

SPEECH_PATHOLOGY.definition: A person's ability to put thoughts into words, sentences or signs.
SPEECH_PATHOLOGY.example: Her expressive language lags behind her understanding; she uses mainly two-word phrases at age four.

SPEECH_PATHOLOGY.definition: A person's ability to understand words, sentences and spoken instructions.
SPEECH_PATHOLOGY.example: Receptive language scores were within the expected range, but he struggled with longer instructions.

SPEECH_PATHOLOGY.definition: A pattern of speech-sound errors in which a child has not learned the sound rules of the language.
SPEECH_PATHOLOGY.example: A phonological disorder was diagnosed because she replaced all back sounds with front ones.

SPEECH_PATHOLOGY.definition: The physical production of speech sounds using the lips, tongue, teeth and palate.
SPEECH_PATHOLOGY.example: His articulation of the 's' sound was distorted, with the tongue resting between the teeth.

SPEECH_PATHOLOGY.definition: Any break in the smooth flow of speech, such as repetitions, prolongations or blocks.
SPEECH_PATHOLOGY.example: The frequency of disfluency increased when the child was excited or speaking to unfamiliar adults.

SPEECH_PATHOLOGY.definition: An abnormal voice quality, pitch or loudness, such as hoarseness or breathiness.
SPEECH_PATHOLOGY.example: The teacher's dysphonia had lasted three months, so laryngeal examination was arranged before voice therapy.

SPEECH_PATHOLOGY.definition: Small, usually paired, firm swellings on the vocal folds linked to voice overuse.
SPEECH_PATHOLOGY.example: Vocal fold nodules were identified, and a course of voice therapy was advised before considering surgery.

SPEECH_PATHOLOGY.definition: Too much sound resonating through the nose during speech.
SPEECH_PATHOLOGY.example: Persistent hypernasality after palate repair suggested that the soft palate was not closing fully.

SPEECH_PATHOLOGY.definition: Failure of the soft palate and throat walls to close, letting air escape through the nose.
SPEECH_PATHOLOGY.example: Velopharyngeal insufficiency was confirmed on imaging, and the cleft team discussed surgical options.

SPEECH_PATHOLOGY.definition: A gap in the roof of the mouth present from birth.
SPEECH_PATHOLOGY.example: Infants with a cleft palate may need specialised bottles to feed effectively before repair.

SPEECH_PATHOLOGY.definition: Methods such as symbol boards, signing or devices that support or replace spoken communication.
SPEECH_PATHOLOGY.example: An augmentative and alternative communication system was introduced so he could make choices at mealtimes.

SPEECH_PATHOLOGY.definition: Moving X-ray of swallowing while the person takes food and drink mixed with contrast.
SPEECH_PATHOLOGY.example: The videofluoroscopic swallowing study showed delayed swallow initiation and residue in the throat.

SPEECH_PATHOLOGY.definition: Viewing the throat during swallowing through a thin flexible camera passed through the nose.
SPEECH_PATHOLOGY.example: Fibreoptic endoscopic evaluation of swallowing was carried out at the bedside because she could not travel to radiology.

SPEECH_PATHOLOGY.definition: Food or fluid left in the throat after a swallow is complete.
SPEECH_PATHOLOGY.example: Pharyngeal residue increased with puree, so a second dry swallow was taught as a strategy.

SPEECH_PATHOLOGY.definition: The movement of a prepared mouthful from the front of the mouth to the throat.
SPEECH_PATHOLOGY.example: Oral transit was prolonged because reduced tongue control left food pocketed in the cheek.

SPEECH_PATHOLOGY.definition: Food prepared to a set softness or consistency to make swallowing safer.
SPEECH_PATHOLOGY.example: A texture-modified diet was recommended, and the kitchen was informed of the required level.

SPEECH_PATHOLOGY.definition: Drinks with added thickener so they flow more slowly and are easier to control.
SPEECH_PATHOLOGY.example: Thickened fluids reduced coughing at meals, but the team monitored her hydration closely.

SPEECH_PATHOLOGY.definition: Relating to movement and strength of the lips, tongue, jaw and soft palate.
SPEECH_PATHOLOGY.example: The oromotor examination revealed reduced lip seal and weak tongue elevation on the left.

SPEECH_PATHOLOGY.definition: Testing the nerves that control face, mouth and throat function.
SPEECH_PATHOLOGY.example: A cranial nerve examination showed facial weakness and reduced gag on the right side.

SPEECH_PATHOLOGY.definition: A surgical opening in the front of the neck into the windpipe, often holding a tube.
SPEECH_PATHOLOGY.example: While the tracheostomy tube was in place, speech was only possible with the cuff deflated.

SPEECH_PATHOLOGY.definition: A valve on a tracheostomy tube letting air in but sending exhaled air through the voice box.
SPEECH_PATHOLOGY.example: A one-way speaking valve was trialled for twenty minutes, and she produced clear voice throughout.

SPEECH_PATHOLOGY.definition: Surgical removal of the voice box, usually as treatment for cancer.
SPEECH_PATHOLOGY.example: Before the laryngectomy, the therapist explained the options for producing voice afterwards.

SPEECH_PATHOLOGY.definition: Reduced hearing because sound is blocked in the outer or middle ear.
SPEECH_PATHOLOGY.example: Fluctuating conductive hearing loss from glue ear may have contributed to her speech delay.

SPEECH_PATHOLOGY.definition: Long-term language difficulties in children that are not explained by another known condition.
SPEECH_PATHOLOGY.example: Developmental language disorder was diagnosed after his difficulties persisted despite good hearing and learning opportunities.

SPEECH_PATHOLOGY.definition: Using language socially, such as taking turns, staying on topic and reading context.
SPEECH_PATHOLOGY.example: Pragmatic language difficulties meant he often interrupted peers and missed hints in conversation.

SPEECH_PATHOLOGY.definition: Sharing focus on an object or event with another person, often by looking or pointing.
SPEECH_PATHOLOGY.example: Joint attention was limited; she rarely followed her mother's point to a toy.

SPEECH_PATHOLOGY.definition: How easily a listener can understand what a speaker says.
SPEECH_PATHOLOGY.example: Intelligibility to unfamiliar listeners rose from about half to most of his words after therapy.

SPEECH_PATHOLOGY.definition: Communication problems caused by difficulties with attention, memory, reasoning or planning.
SPEECH_PATHOLOGY.example: After his head injury, a cognitive-communication disorder made it hard for him to follow group conversations.

SPEECH_PATHOLOGY.definition: The brain's capacity to reorganise and form new connections, especially after injury or through practice.
SPEECH_PATHOLOGY.example: Intensive practice is thought to support neuroplasticity in the months following stroke.

SPEECH_PATHOLOGY.definition: Describing a condition in which nerve cells gradually lose function over time.
SPEECH_PATHOLOGY.example: Because the condition is neurodegenerative, the plan focuses on maintaining communication as speech declines.

SPEECH_PATHOLOGY.definition: A technique that works around a difficulty rather than treating it directly.
SPEECH_PATHOLOGY.example: Turning the head to the weaker side was taught as a compensatory strategy for safer swallowing.

SPEECH_PATHOLOGY.definition: An initial measurement used to compare later progress or change.
SPEECH_PATHOLOGY.example: A baseline of naming accuracy was recorded before therapy began.

SPEECH_PATHOLOGY.definition: A standard tool or score used to judge the effect of care.
SPEECH_PATHOLOGY.example: A functional outcome measure was completed at discharge to show change in communication.

SPEECH_PATHOLOGY.definition: A test given and scored the same way every time, allowing comparison with a reference group.
SPEECH_PATHOLOGY.example: A standardised assessment placed his vocabulary well below that of other children his age.

SPEECH_PATHOLOGY.definition: Scores from a typical population used to judge whether a result is expected.
SPEECH_PATHOLOGY.example: Normative data for this test were collected in another country, which limits interpretation.

SPEECH_PATHOLOGY.definition: Use of a newly learned skill in new settings, with new people or new material.
SPEECH_PATHOLOGY.example: Generalisation of the new sound into classroom speech was slower than in clinic.

SPEECH_PATHOLOGY.definition: Combining research findings, clinical expertise and patient values to guide decisions.
SPEECH_PATHOLOGY.example: Evidence-based practice requires the therapist to weigh trial findings alongside the family's goals.

SPEECH_PATHOLOGY.definition: How well a treatment works under controlled research conditions.
SPEECH_PATHOLOGY.example: Evidence on the efficacy of this approach for adult stammering remains limited.

SPEECH_PATHOLOGY.definition: An additional condition present in the same person alongside the main one.
SPEECH_PATHOLOGY.example: Comorbidity with attention difficulties is common in children with language disorder.

SPEECH_PATHOLOGY.definition: A group of professionals from different specialties who plan care together.
SPEECH_PATHOLOGY.example: The multidisciplinary team agreed that tube feeding should be discussed with the family.

SPEECH_PATHOLOGY.definition: The number of patients a clinician or service is responsible for at one time.
SPEECH_PATHOLOGY.example: A growing caseload has lengthened waiting times for paediatric assessment.

SPEECH_PATHOLOGY.definition: The average number of meaningful units per utterance in a speech sample.
SPEECH_PATHOLOGY.example: His mean length of utterance increased from two to three units over six months.

SPEECH_PATHOLOGY.definition: To examine something carefully to judge its nature, level or quality.
SPEECH_PATHOLOGY.example: The therapist will assess her swallowing at lunchtime, when she is usually most alert.

SPEECH_PATHOLOGY.definition: Planned action, such as therapy, taken to improve a condition or situation.
SPEECH_PATHOLOGY.example: Early intervention for late-talking toddlers may reduce later literacy problems.

SPEECH_PATHOLOGY.definition: To hold back, slow or prevent something from happening.
SPEECH_PATHOLOGY.example: Anxiety about speaking may inhibit participation in class discussions.

SPEECH_PATHOLOGY.definition: To arrange or produce things in the correct order.
SPEECH_PATHOLOGY.example: Children with speech apraxia often find it hard to sequence sounds in longer words.

SPEECH_PATHOLOGY.definition: Enough in amount or quality for a particular purpose.
SPEECH_PATHOLOGY.example: Oral intake was not adequate to meet his needs, so supplementary feeding was discussed.

SPEECH_PATHOLOGY.definition: Continuing for a long time or recurring despite attempts to change it.
SPEECH_PATHOLOGY.example: Persistent hoarseness lasting more than three weeks should be examined by an ear, nose and throat specialist.

SPEECH_PATHOLOGY.definition: To change often and irregularly, rising and falling.
SPEECH_PATHOLOGY.example: Her swallowing tends to fluctuate during the day, depending on fatigue and medication timing.

SPEECH_PATHOLOGY.definition: The likely course and outcome of a condition.
SPEECH_PATHOLOGY.example: The prognosis for further language recovery is reasonable, given her age and motivation.

SPEECH_PATHOLOGY.definition: The cause or origin of a disease or disorder.
SPEECH_PATHOLOGY.example: The aetiology of his speech difficulty is unclear, so a genetics referral has been made.

SPEECH_PATHOLOGY.definition: An instruction that a person must not eat or drink anything orally.
SPEECH_PATHOLOGY.example: He is currently nil by mouth until his swallow is reassessed tomorrow morning.
SPEECH_PATHOLOGY.plain: nothing at all to eat or drink, not even sips of water

SPEECH_PATHOLOGY.definition: Bringing the chin down towards the chest while swallowing to protect the airway.
SPEECH_PATHOLOGY.example: Please remind her to do a chin tuck every time she swallows a drink.
SPEECH_PATHOLOGY.plain: bend your head forward a little when you swallow

SPEECH_PATHOLOGY.definition: A short period of using the voice as little as possible to let it recover.
SPEECH_PATHOLOGY.example: I'd recommend two days of voice rest after the concert before you start teaching again.
SPEECH_PATHOLOGY.plain: using your voice as little as possible for a short time

SPEECH_PATHOLOGY.definition: Everyday habits that protect and look after the voice.
SPEECH_PATHOLOGY.example: We discussed vocal hygiene, including drinking water regularly and avoiding shouting in the gym.
SPEECH_PATHOLOGY.plain: habits that keep your voice healthy

SPEECH_PATHOLOGY.definition: A set of exercises given to a patient or family to do between sessions.
SPEECH_PATHOLOGY.example: I have enclosed a home practice programme for Amir's parents to use for ten minutes each day.
SPEECH_PATHOLOGY.plain: exercises to do at home between appointments

SPEECH_PATHOLOGY.definition: The process of finding and saying the word you intend.
SPEECH_PATHOLOGY.example: Word retrieval is still difficult for Mr Evans, so allow him extra time to find words.
SPEECH_PATHOLOGY.plain: finding the right word when you want to say it

SPEECH_PATHOLOGY.definition: Meals changed in texture so that they are safer to swallow.
SPEECH_PATHOLOGY.example: She should continue on a modified diet, and her family have been shown how to prepare it.
SPEECH_PATHOLOGY.plain: food made softer or mashed so it is easier to swallow

SPEECH_PATHOLOGY.definition: A food texture that is tender, moist and cut into small pieces.
SPEECH_PATHOLOGY.example: Meals should be soft and bite-sized, with no hard or crunchy pieces.
SPEECH_PATHOLOGY.plain: soft food cut into small pieces

SPEECH_PATHOLOGY.definition: Fluids thickened slightly so they flow more slowly than water.
SPEECH_PATHOLOGY.example: Please give all mildly thick drinks from a cup, not through a straw.
SPEECH_PATHOLOGY.plain: drinks thickened a little so they move more slowly

SPEECH_PATHOLOGY.definition: An instruction to drink a little at a time.
SPEECH_PATHOLOGY.example: Try to take small sips and swallow each one before taking the next.
SPEECH_PATHOLOGY.plain: drink a little at a time

SPEECH_PATHOLOGY.definition: Advice to keep the body straight, ideally in a chair, for eating and drinking.
SPEECH_PATHOLOGY.example: Make sure he is able to sit upright for meals and for thirty minutes afterwards.
SPEECH_PATHOLOGY.plain: sit up straight

SPEECH_PATHOLOGY.definition: Any board, book or device that helps a person express themselves.
SPEECH_PATHOLOGY.example: Her communication aid should go with her to every appointment and stay within reach.
SPEECH_PATHOLOGY.plain: a board or device that helps someone get their message across

SPEECH_PATHOLOGY.definition: A speech difficulty where sounds or words are repeated, stretched or blocked.
SPEECH_PATHOLOGY.example: Many children with a stammer improve, and we can support you at home in the meantime.
SPEECH_PATHOLOGY.plain: getting stuck on, repeating or stretching sounds when speaking

SPEECH_PATHOLOGY.definition: Language developing later than usual but along a typical pattern.
SPEECH_PATHOLOGY.example: Lily has a language delay, so we will see her again in three months to check progress.
SPEECH_PATHOLOGY.plain: starting to talk later than most children of the same age

SPEECH_PATHOLOGY.definition: A voice that sounds rough, strained or croaky.
SPEECH_PATHOLOGY.example: If your hoarse voice has not improved in three weeks, please see your GP.
SPEECH_PATHOLOGY.plain: a rough or croaky voice

SPEECH_PATHOLOGY.definition: Everyday term for an infection in the airways or lungs.
SPEECH_PATHOLOGY.example: Food going down the wrong way can sometimes lead to a chest infection, which is why these steps matter.
SPEECH_PATHOLOGY.plain: an infection in the lungs

SPEECH_PATHOLOGY.definition: Everyday way to describe food or drink entering the airway.
SPEECH_PATHOLOGY.example: The test showed that thin drinks sometimes go down the wrong way into his windpipe.
SPEECH_PATHOLOGY.plain: food or drink going into the breathing tube instead of the food pipe

SPEECH_PATHOLOGY.definition: The individual sounds that are combined to form spoken words.
